explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient presents with knee pain, swelling, reduced range of motion, and mechanical locking, which are hallmark features of synovial chondromatosis.
  • The X-ray showing multiple calcified loose bodies and the MRI confirming lobular cartilage nodules with areas of calcification further support this diagnosis.
  • Given the severe symptoms (pain, limited motion, and locking) and imaging findings of calcified loose bodies, arthroscopic synovectomy and removal of the loose bodies is the recommended treatment. This approach addresses both symptom relief and prevents further joint damage.

Imaging

  • Radiographs: Standard anteroposterior (AP) and lateral views of the affected joint are recommended. Findings vary by disease stage and may show stippled calcification.

[[figure-2]]

  • MRI: Initially, cartilage nodules are visible only on MRI, appearing lobular. In later stages, there is a signal drop-out indicating calcification.

Histology

  • Displays discrete hyaline cartilage nodules at various stages of calcification and ossification, with mild atypia, binucleate cells, and occasional mitoses.

  • Operative: Open or arthroscopic synovectomy and loose body resection are indicated for severe symptoms impacting range of motion.

Observation and conservative management (Option A) is reserved for mild cases not affecting joint function.

Total knee replacement (Option C) is not typically indicated unless severe degenerative changes are present, which is not mentioned in this case.

Physical therapy only (Option D) alone would not resolve the mechanical issues caused by the loose bodies.

question: A 45-year-old male presents with progressive knee pain, swelling, reduced range of motion, and occasional mechanical locking. An X-ray of the knee is given below. MRI confirms the presence of lobular cartilage nodules with areas of calcification. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Presenting with progressive knee pain, swelling, reduced range of motion, and mechanical locking, with X-ray showing multiple calcified loose bodies in the joint space are features consistent with synovial chondromatosis, a condition where loose chondroid bodies form in the joint.
  • The absence of active synovial involvement on imaging, combined with the presence of calcified loose bodies, classifies this case as Class III (Final stage) of Milgram's classification.

Synovial Chondromatosis

  • Synovial chondromatosis is a benign condition where the synovial membrane of joints forms multiple loose chondroid bodies, leading to joint pain, swelling, and decreased range of motion.
  • Sites:
    • Knee: Most common
    • Shoulder
    • Hip
    • Elbow
  • Presents with joint pain as the chief complaint, often accompanied by swelling, reduced range of motion, and occasionally crepitus and mechanical locking during movement.
  • Milgram Classification
    • Early stage (Class I) - Synovial symptoms without any loose bodies visible on X-Rays. (Option A)
    • Intermediate stage (Class II) - Reunites both clinical symptoms and images of calcified loose bodies within the synovial membrane. (Option B)
    • Final stage (Class III) - Calcified loose bodies without any synovial involvement

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cleidocranial Dysostosis is characterized by the partial or complete absence of the clavicles, often leading to shoulder abnormalities discovered incidentally. X-ray findings confirm the diagnosis, and while treatment is usually unnecessary, surgery may be considered if pain occurs.

Cleidocranial Dysostosis

  • Rare condition with partial or complete absence of the clavicles.
  • Exact cause unknown, possibly due to disruption of membranous bone development during early embryonic life.

Types:

  • Pseudarthritic gap between ends of bones
  • Partial defect, usually at the acromial end
  • Complete absence of clavicle

Associated Muscle Variations:

  • Trapezius may be absent
  • Pectoralis major may be underdeveloped
  • Other congenital malformations may occur

Clinical Features:

  • Shoulder abnormalities discovered accidentally
  • Mimics un-united fracture or complete absence of the clavicle
  • Shoulders can be approximated
  • X-rays of both clavicles are essential for diagnosis.

Treatment:

  • No treatment usually required
  • Surgery (removal of part of the clavicle) if pain occurs
  • No significant disability or discomfort

Sprengel’s Deformity (Option A): This condition is characterized by an elevated scapula due to improper descent during embryonic development, not a clavicular abnormality. The deformity is noticeable at birth, with limited shoulder movement, which is not consistent with this scenario.

Klippel–Feil Syndrome (Option B): This syndrome involves cervical vertebrae abnormalities and results in a short, stiff neck with low hairline and webbing, leading to significant neck movement limitations. It does not relate to clavicle absence or shoulder positioning.

Madelung's Deformity (Option C): This deformity affects the distal radial epiphysis and is unrelated to the clavicles or shoulder positioning. It presents with forearm deformities rather than shoulder abnormalities and does not fit the clinical findings in this case.



Reference:

Textbook of Orthopedics, Ebenezar, 5th Edition, Page 474, 475

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Halo fixation for 6 to 12 weeks is the correct treatment for Type 2 fractures of Levin and Edward Classification with subluxation greater than 3 mm but less than 5 mm. It provides sufficient immobilization for the fracture to heal.

C2 Traumatic Spondylolisthesis (Hangman’s Fracture)

  • Cause: Traditionally from judicial hanging; now more commonly due to hyperextension injuries (e.g., force to the forehead, Forsyth mechanism).
  • Injury: Results in anterior translation at C2, leading to pars fractures and possible C2/3 disc disruption.
  • Neurological Injury: Uncommon, as the fractures can expand the spinal canal.
  • Stability Assessment: Depends on C2/3 disc status and facet integrity.

Levine & Edward Classification

Treatment

Type 1: Less than 3 mm subluxation, stable

Rigid cervical collar (Option A)

Type 2: Greater than 4 mm subluxation, unstable

-Less than 5 mm - Reduction in axial traction and halo fixation for 6 to 12 weeks

-Greater than 5 mm - Require surgery (Option C)

Type 2a: Unstable with flexion injury and angular deformity

Halo fixation

Type 3: Unstable with facet and anterior longitudinal ligament disruption

Require surgery (Option C)

Conservative management with analgesics and observation (Option D): This approach would not be appropriate for an unstable fracture like Type 2, as it requires immobilization to ensure proper healing and to prevent further displacement.



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 845
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519496/

question: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident where his forehead struck the steering wheel. He complains of neck pain but no neurological deficits. Imaging reveals a fracture of the pars interarticularis of C2 with anterior displacement of the vertebra. There is 4 mm of subluxation at the C2/3 level. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Apply pelvic binders and initiate resuscitation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient is suspected to have pelvic fractures due to significant swelling and bruising in the lower abdomen and thighs, tenderness indicating possible intraperitoneal bleeding, a positive pelvic compression test and an inability to void suggesting a potential bladder rupture.
  • Applying pelvic binders helps stabilize the pelvis and reduce hemorrhage while initiating resuscitation is critical for managing potential hemorrhagic shock.

Clinical Features of Pelvic Fractures

  • Swelling and Bruising: Lower abdomen, thighs, perineum, scrotum, or vulva.
  • Abdominal Tenderness: Indicates intraperitoneal bleeding.
  • Extraperitoneal Bladder Rupture: Suspect if unable to void or palpate bladder; may lead to significant hemorrhage.
  • Neurological Damage: Assess for lumbosacral plexus injury, especially in unconscious patients

[[figure-1]]

Treatment of Pelvic Ring Fractures:

  1. Initial Management:
    • Follow ATLS protocol (Advanced Trauma Life Support).
    • Immediate resuscitation and management of hemorrhagic shock using blood products.
  2. Pelvic Binders:
    • Applied at the level of the greater trochanters, not the iliac crest.
    • Temporarily stabilizes the pelvis and reduces pelvic volume, limiting blood loss.
    • Should not be left on for more than 24 hours due to the risk of pressure sores.
    • May need to be loosened if over-reduced (excessive internal rotation of the hemipelvis).
    • Reapplication is possible after checking pressure areas.
  3. Management of Hemorrhage:
    • If the patient remains hemodynamically unstable despite a binder and resuscitation:
      • Exclude other sources of bleeding (chest, abdomen, external).
      • Two main options:
        1. Angiography and Embolization: Targets arterial bleeding, controls vessels like the internal iliac and superior gluteal arteries. Risks include muscle necrosis (gluteals).
        2. Pre-peritoneal Packing: Requires rapid application of an external fixator and abdominal packing (Stoppa approach). May be followed by angiography if needed.
  4. Conservative Management:
    • Used for stable fractures such as avulsion fractures and LC I fractures.
    • Early mobilization and partial weight-bearing are encouraged to avoid complications (e.g., VTE, chest infections).
  5. Operative Fixation:
    • Converts unstable fractures to stable configurations using open reduction, internal fixation (plates, screws), or percutaneous iliosacral screws.
    • Sacral fractures and sacroiliac dislocations may require closed or open reduction.

Immediate surgery for internal fixation (Option A): Immediate surgery for internal fixation is not the first step in trauma management. Stabilization and resuscitation are prioritized.

Order a CT scan of the pelvis (Option C): While imaging may be necessary, the immediate management should focus on stabilization and addressing hemodynamic stability first.

Initiate strict bed rest and monitor vital signs (Option D): Strict bed rest is not appropriate in this scenario. Active intervention to stabilize the pelvis and manage shock is essential.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 870-872, 864, 865

question: A 35-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a high-impact motorcycle accident. He presents with significant swelling and bruising in the lower abdomen and thighs. During the examination, he exhibits tenderness upon palpation of the abdomen. Pelvic compression test is positive. The patient is unable to void, and the bladder is not palpable. What is the most appropriate initial management step for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Sacro-iliac ligament, Ilio-lumbar ligament, and Superior pubic ligament– all of these ligaments work together to reinforce the pelvic ring, enhance stability, and protect against injuries, particularly during movements or forces applied to the pelvis. Thus, all are essential for pelvic stability.

Pelvis Anatomy

  • Pelvic ring is a ring-shaped structure.
  • Front: joined by pubic symphysis.
  • Back: joined by sacro-iliac joints.
  • Features iliac wings, a common fracture site.
  • Continuity: pubic symphysis → pubic crest → pectineal line of pubis → arcuate line of ilium → ala and promontory of sacrum.
  • Anterior fractures may involve posterior injuries, causing instability.
  • Obturator nerve and sacral plexus cross the pelvic brim.
  • These nerves are at risk of injury during pelvic fractures.

[[figure-1]]

Stability of the Pelvis

  • Stability depends on:
    • Posteriorly: sacro-iliac joints.
    • Anteriorly: symphysis pubis.
  • Sacro-iliac joints supported by strong sacro-iliac ligaments, ilio-lumbar, sacro-tuberous, and sacro-spinous ligaments.
  • Pubic symphysis reinforced by superior pubic ligament and the arcuate pubic ligament.

Mechanism of the Injury

  • Low energy injuries
    • Result from sudden muscular contractions in young athletes that cause an avulsion injury.
    • Low energy fall in an elderly with osteoporosis which may fracture the pelvic bones.
  • High energy injuries: Most common
    • RTA
    • Fall from heights.
    • Crush injuries


Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 863, 867, 868

question: A newborn presents with weakness in the left arm. On examination, the infant's hand shows a claw-like deformity like shown in the image below. Which of the following statements is most likely true regarding this condition?

correctAnswer: D. MRI, early physiotherapy and hydrotherapy, reassess for surgical intervention if no improvement by 3-6 months
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In this scenario, the infant presents with weakness in the right arm, an inability to abduct the shoulder or flex the elbow, and the arm is held in internal rotation with the forearm pronated.
  • These findings are characteristic of Erb's Palsy, which occurs due to an injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, primarily affecting the C5 and C6 nerve roots.



After diagnosis of Erb’s Palsy, the management approach includes:

  1. Early immobilization followed by passive and active range of motion exercises
  2. Hydrotherapy: Provides an anti-gravity environment for strengthening muscles
  3. Physiotherapy: Includes gentle stretching, sensory stimulation, and strength exercises
  4. Occupational therapy: For long-term cases to help with daily activities
  5. Reassessment: If no improvement is seen by 3-6 months, surgical intervention may be considered
  6. Surgical options: Include nerve graft and nerve decompression if conservative management fails

Management of Erb’s Palsy

Diagnosis

  • Clinical diagnosis based on history and physical examination
  • MRI of brachial plexus and cervical cord (best imaging technique)
  • X-ray to exclude fractures
  • Electromyography (EMG) to assess muscle electrical activity
  • Nerve conduction studies (NCS) to measure nerve signal transmission
  • CT myelography for detailed imaging of spinal cord and nerve roots

Management
  • Conservative management done in most cases
  • Early immobilization followed by range of motion exercises
  • Hydrotherapy: Anti-gravity environment for muscle strengthening
  • Physiotherapy: Stretching, sensory stimulation, range of motion exercises
  • Occupational therapy: For long-term cases to assist with daily activities
  • Surgical intervention: Considered if no functional recovery with conservative management
    • Nerve graft
    • Nerve decompression
  • Medical therapy: Botulinum toxin injections for contracture relief

Prognosis
  • Generally favorable if treated early
  • About 90% of infants show recovery with time
  • 10% may continue to have a dysfunctional arm
  • Neglected cases may lead to 20-30% permanent deficit of nerve function


Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513260/

question: A 1-month-old infant presents with weakness in the right arm, inability to abduct the shoulder or flex the elbow, and the arm is held in internal rotation with the forearm pronated. An image of the infant is given below. Which of the following sequences best represents the appropriate management approach?

correctAnswer: C. Injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5-C6)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The clinical presentation described is characteristic of Erb's Palsy, which is caused by an injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, specifically involving the C5 and C6 nerve roots.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Erb’s Palsy - Pathophysiology and Clinical Features

Aspect

Details

Pathophysiology
  • Injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5-C6)
  • Most commonly caused by traction of the neck during delivery
  • Severity ranges from neuropraxia (least severe) to neurotmesis (most severe)
  • Can involve C7 in more severe cases (Extended Erb's Palsy)

Clinical Features
  • Weakness of the arm
  • Loss of sensation in the arm
  • Paralysis and atrophy of deltoid, biceps, and brachialis muscles
  • Limited shoulder abduction- Deltoid, Supraspinatus
  • Inability to flex the elbow- Biceps brachii, Brachialis
  • Internal rotation and pronation of the arm- Subscapularis, Pronator teres, Pectoralis major.
  • "Waiter's tip" posture
  • Absent Moro reflex on the affected side
  • Present grasp reflex

Injury to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1) (Option A) causes Klumpke's palsy, which primarily affects the hand and presents with a "claw hand" appearance.

Compression of the median nerve at the carpal tunnel (Option B) would not cause the shoulder and elbow symptoms described in Erb's Palsy.

Avulsion of the cervical nerve roots from the spinal cord (Option D): While avulsion of cervical nerve roots can occur in severe brachial plexus injuries, it's not the typical pathophysiology of Erb's palsy and would likely result in more extensive deficits.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513260/

question: A newborn presents with weakness in the right arm, inability to abduct the shoulder or flex the elbow, and the arm is held in internal rotation with the forearm pronated. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Sprengel's Deformity involves the failure of the scapula to descend properly, resulting in an elevated scapula, noticeable at birth. The features of painless shoulder movements with some limitation in abduction align perfectly with the described condition.

Sprengel’s Deformity

  • A congenital condition where the scapula fails to descend properly during embryonic development.
    • Imperfect descent of the shoulder girdle by the third month of pregnancy
    • Possible presence of a fibrous band between the skull and scapula
  • Elevated scapula (2–10 cm higher than normal)
  • Hypoplastic and abnormally shaped scapula
  • Neck may appear shorter; potential for kyphosis or scoliosis
  • Deformity noticeable at birth
  • Shoulder movements are painless, but abduction and elevation may be limited
  • Torticollis present in ~10% of cases
  • Associated congenital anomalies (e.g., cervical rib, spina bifida)
  • Potential absence or alterations in the trapezius and other shoulder muscles
  • Treatment:
    • Mild cases require no treatment
    • Severe cases may necessitate surgery after age three, involving muscle release or trapezius muscle origin transfer

[[figure-1]]

Klippel–Feil Syndrome (Option A)

  • A widespread disorder characterized by abnormalities in the cervical spine and occipital bones.
  • Congenital short and stiff neck due to fused or deformed cervical vertebrae.
  • Key Features:
    • Bilateral failure of scapular descent.
    • Appearance of having no neck.
    • Low hairline and bilateral neck webbing.
    • Significant limitation of neck movement.

[[figure-2]]

Madelung's Deformity (Option B):

  • This deformity affects the distal radial epiphysis, leading to a deformity of the radius and dislocation of the ulna.
  • It is unrelated to scapular positioning or shoulder movement and therefore is not applicable to the scenario.

[[figure-3]]

Fig. Comparison of Madelung’s deformity with normal anatomy

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

Fig. Madelung’s deformity on physical examination and radiograph

Cleidocranial Dysostosis (Option C):

  • An autosomal dominant disorder characterized by hypoplasia or absence of the clavicles and flat bones.
  • Patients typically have drooping shoulders and a narrow chest.
  • While it does involve skeletal abnormalities, it does not fit the presentation of an elevated scapula or shoulder movement limitations.

[[figure-6]]

Fig. Cleidocranial Dysostosis

Factors Affecting Fracture Healing:

Faster Healing

Slower Healing

Age: Fractures unite faster in children than in adults (Option A)

Fracture Type: Open fractures and comminuted fractures often go into delayed union and non-union (Option D)

question: Regarding fracture healing, which of the following statements is INCORRECT?

correctAnswer: D. The Ilizarov technique is ineffective in correcting deformities or treating non-unions.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The Ilizarov technique is versatile and can be used for multiple purposes such as correcting deformities, not just limb lengthening.

[[figure-1]]

Key points on Ilizarov technique:

  • The Ilizarov technique is mainly used for management of difficult non-unions and limb lengthening.
  • It's based on the principle that osteogenesis requires a dynamic state, achieved through controlled distraction or compression. (Option B)
  • Intramembranous Ossification: This is the primary method of bone formation during distraction osteogenesis. Osteoblasts directly form bone without an intermediate cartilage stage (unlike endochondral ossification, seen in long bone growth).
  • The technique uses a ring fixator that stabilizes the limb while allowing controlled movement of bone fragments. (Option A)
  • Distraction or compression is typically done at a rate of 1 mm per day, in four 0.25 mm increments. (Option C)
  • First corticotomy is done to expose the metaphyseal bone. Then 10 days are given for a latent period for hematoma formation.

The technique is effective for:

  • Limb lengthening, especially when shortening is associated with deformity.
  • Non-union treatment, particularly those resistant to conventional methods.
  • Correction of deformities, which can be done simultaneously with lengthening.


Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 331, 337

question: Regarding the Ilizarov technique for distraction osteogenesis, which of the following statements is incorrect?

correctAnswer: B. Hematoma formation, Inflammation, Callus formation, Remodeling, Modeling
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

STAGES IN FRACTURE HEALING OF CORTICAL BONE:

Stage of hematoma
  • The initial stage lasts up to 7 days.
  • Blood leaks from torn vessels and forms a hematoma around the fracture.
  • The periosteum and soft tissues are stripped away from the fracture ends.
  • Fracture ends suffer from ischemic necrosis over a few millimeters.
  • Some osteocytes die, while others become active and help in healing.

Stage of granulation tissue
  • The granulation tissue stage lasts 2-3 weeks.
  • Precursor cells produce blood vessels, fibroblasts, and osteoblasts.
  • Soft granulation tissue forms between fracture fragments.
  • It provides support without structural rigidity.
  • A fibrous mesh from the blood clot supports fibroblast and capillary growth.
  • Macrophages and giant cells remove the blood clot.
  • In bone healing, granulation tissue differentiates into osteoblasts to form new bone.

Stage of callus
  • This stage lasts 4-12 weeks, during which granulation tissue differentiates into osteoblasts.
  • These cells create an intercellular matrix that becomes impregnated with calcium salts, forming the callus, or woven bone.
  • This callus, visible on X-rays about 3 weeks post-fracture, provides initial strength and indicates union.

Stage of remodeling

  • Formerly known as the consolidation stage.
  • Woven bone is replaced by mature lamellar bone.
  • This occurs in multicellular units, with callus replaced by lamellar bone.
  • The process is slow, taking 1 to 4 years.

Stage of modeling

  • Formerly known as the remodeling stage.
  • Bone is gradually strengthened.
  • Cortices sharpen at the endosteal and periosteal surfaces.
  • Local bone strains from weight-bearing stresses and muscle forces stimulate this process.
  • More noticeable in children with angulated fractures.

question: Identify the correct sequence of the mentioned stages of fracture healing:

correctAnswer: B. Primary healing occurs with absolute stability and direct bone remodeling, while secondary healing is a process involving callus formation and occurs with relative stability.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Primary healing requires absolute stability (surgical fixation) and healing occurs without a callus. Secondary healing occurs with relative stability (e.g., casting) and involves callus formation.

Feature

Primary (Direct) Healing

Secondary (Indirect) Healing

Process

Direct bone healing without callus formation. (Option A)

Involves the classical stages of healing: hematoma, callus formation, and remodeling.

Mechanism

Lamellar bone forms directly across the fracture line by direct extension of osteons.

Healing occurs through endochondral and intramembranous ossification with callus formation.

Fracture Hematoma

Occurs when the fracture hematoma is disturbed, usually in surgically treated fractures. (Option D)

Occurs when the fracture hematoma remains undisturbed, typical of non-operative treatment.

Callus Formation

No callus formation; difficult to evaluate on X-rays due to direct healing.

Callus formation is visible on X-rays and bridges the fracture site.

Stability Requirement

Requires absolute stability with rigid internal fixation (e.g., surgical plates).

Requires relative stability, often managed with casting or external fixation.

Healing Speed

Slower healing due to the direct remodeling of bone. (Option C)

Faster healing, as callus provides early mechanical strength.

Mechanical Continuity

Mechanical continuity is reestablished without callus formation.

Strength is restored by the callus, which provides initial stability.

Bone Contact

Direct contact between bone cortices (anatomical reduction).

Gaps between bone fragments are bridged by callus formation.

Clinical Use

Used in surgically treated fractures requiring perfect alignment.

Common in non-surgically treated fractures (e.g., casting, external fixation).

X-ray Evaluation

Hard to evaluate healing on X-rays due to lack of callus formation.

Callus formation makes healing progress visible on X-rays.

[[figure-1]]


Reference:

Campbell’s Operative Orthopaedics, 14th Edition, Page 2776-77

The patient's presentation aligns with slipped capital femoral epiphysis based on the clinical features.

  • SCFE occurs when the femoral head becomes displaced due to slippage at the growth plate, often linked to factors such as mechanical stress and hormonal influences during periods of rapid growth.
  • This displacement leads to altered hip mechanics and can cause pain, limited mobility, and long-term joint complications if not addressed.

SCFE presents with the following characteristics:

  1. Age: 13 years old, which falls within the typical age range for SCFE (12-14 years)
  2. Gender: Male, which is more common in SCFE
  3. Body habitus: Obese, a known risk factor for SCFE
  4. Symptoms: Gradual onset of hip and knee pain with a limp
  5. Physical examination: External rotation of the affected leg, limited hip internal rotation, and abduction
  6. Associated with Hypothyroidism and Hypogonadism.

[[figure-1]]

Fig. Plain X-ray of Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)

Definition

Displacement of the upper femoral epiphysis at the growth plate, usually postero-medially, resulting in coxa vara

Age & Gender
  • Occurs at puberty (between 12-14 years)
  • More common in boys

Risk Factors
  • Obesity
  • Endocrine abnormalities
  • Short and obese children

Clinical Features
  • Pain in the groin, often radiating to the thigh and knee
  • Limp
  • External rotation of the affected leg, Shortening of the limb.
  • Limitation of hip movements, especially abduction and internal rotation
  • Positive Trendelenburg's sign
  • Drehmann's Sign is characterized by external rotation and abduction of the hip when the knee is flexed, indicating instability or weakness in the hip joint

Radiological Features
  • Best seen on the X-ray: lateral view of the hip
  • AP view: Growth plate displaced towards metaphyseal side
  • Lateral view: Head is angulated on the neck
  • Klein's Line: This is an imaging line drawn on an X-ray of the hip, where a line is drawn along the superior aspect of the femoral neck. The line should intersect the capital femoral epiphysis. If the epiphysis is above this line, it indicates a potential displacement or abnormality in the femoral head.
  • Trethowan Sign: This sign is observed on an X-ray when there is a widening of the medial joint space of the hip, indicating a possible displacement of the femoral head. It may also suggest a higher likelihood of osteonecrosis in the affected hip.

Treatment
  • Acute slip: Closed reduction and pinning
  • Gradual slip: Depends on severity; in situ fixation or corrective osteotomy
  • Prophylactic pinning of unaffected side in unilateral cases

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (Option A) typically affects younger children (4-10 years) and typically presents with limping, hip or knee pain, reduced hip mobility, and possible leg length discrepancy in children aged 4-10 years. In Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, decreased movements typically include hip abduction, internal rotation, external rotation, and flexion.

Septic arthritis of the hip (Option B) usually has an acute onset with fever and severe pain, which is not described in this case.

Definition

A condition characterized by pain and tenderness at the lateral epicondyle of the humerus due to non-specific inflammation at the origin of the extensor muscles of the forearm

  • Maudsley's test: This test involves the patient pronating their forearm and resisting extension of the third digit of their hand while the examiner stabilizes the humerus. The test is positive if the patient experiences sudden pain on the lateral epicondyle.

question: A 55-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse presents to the clinic with difficulty in straightening his right middle finger as shown in the image below. He mentions that this has progressively worsened over the past year. Which of the following statements is false regarding the condition he may be experiencing?

correctAnswer: C. Atrophy of the thenar eminence.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms of tingling and numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, worsening at night are classic signs of carpal tunnel syndrome.
  • Atrophy of the thenar eminence indicates significant nerve dysfunction and is commonly seen in advanced cases of carpal tunnel syndrome.

Carpal tunnel syndrome

Definition

Compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel in the wrist

Symptoms
  • Numbness, tingling in thumb, index, and middle fingers
  • Pain in hand and wrist
  • Weakness in grip
  • Symptoms often worse at night and improve during the day.
  • Advanced cases may lead to constant symptoms, hand weakness, clumsiness, and muscle atrophy.

Structures Affected
  • Median Nerve: Compressed within the carpal tunnel, leading to symptoms and signs.
  • Flexor Tendons: The nine flexor tendons passing through the carpal tunnel can become inflamed, further compressing the median nerve.

Structures Spared
  • Thenar Eminence: Sensory loss generally spares this area because its nerve (palmar sensory cutaneous nerve) bypasses the carpal tunnel.

Clinical Signs
  • Weakness: Notable weakness in thumb abduction and opposition. (Option A)
  • Atrophy: Possible atrophy of the thenar eminence in advanced cases.
  • Sensory Loss: Loss typically affects the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the fourth digit). (Option B)

Causes
  • Idiopathic- commonest cause
  • Inflammatory causes- Rheumatoid arthritis, wrist osteoarthritis
  • Post-traumatic causes- Bone thickening after a Colles' fracture
  • Endocrine causes- Myxoedema, Acromegaly

Diagnostic Tests
  • Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS) - primary diagnostic test
  • Electromyography (EMG)
  • Carpal Compression Test: Positive if pain/paresthesias occur during pressure application over the carpal tunnel.
  • Phalen Test: Positive if pain/paresthesias arise during wrist flexion. (Option D)
  • Tinel Test: Positive if tapping over the carpal tunnel elicits symptoms.

Treatment
  • Conservative: Wrist splinting, NSAIDs, activity modification
  • Corticosteroid injections
  • Surgical: Carpal tunnel release (for severe or refractory cases)


Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448179/

Correct Option A - Primary Healing:

  • The type of fracture healing you can expect in a fracture treated with rigid internal fixation, as shown in the X-ray, is primary healing. This type of healing is characterized by the direct formation of bone across the fracture site with minimal callus formation, due to the stable and precise alignment of the fracture fragments provided by rigid internal fixation.

Incorret Options:

Option B - Secondary Healing:

  • This process involves the formation of a callus and is associated with more motion at the fracture site compared to primary healing. Secondary healing occurs in two stages: the formation of a soft callus followed by a hard callus, and finally, remodeling of the callus into mature bone. This type of healing is more common with fractures treated with casts or less stable fixation.

Option C - Creeping Substitution:

  • This term refers to the gradual replacement of fibrocartilage or woven bone with lamellar bone during the healing process, often observed in secondary healing. It is not a distinct type of fracture healing on its own but rather a part of the secondary healing process.

Option D - Intramembranous Ossification:

  • This type of bone formation occurs directly within a membrane-like layer of connective tissue and is commonly seen in flat bones of the skull and the clavicle. It is not typically associated with fracture healing but rather with the development of bone during embryonic growth and the healing of certain types of fractures like those involving the skull.

Salter-Harris Classification of growth plate fractures:

[[figure-1]]

Type

Description

Treatment and Prognosis

Type I (Option A)

Separation of the physis (growth plate), without involvement of the metaphysis or epiphysis.
  • Excellent prognosis if treated promptly
  • Treated with immobilization and observation.

Type II (Option B)

Fracture through the physis and part of the metaphysis. The metaphyseal fragment is displaced, forming a triangle (known as the Thurston-Holland sign).
  • Good prognosis with proper treatment.
  • Treated with reduction and casting.
  • Rarely affects future growth.

Type III (Option C)

Fracture through the physis and epiphysis, with the epiphysis displaced.
  • May result in joint deformity or growth disturbance if not managed well.
  • Surgical intervention required for proper alignment and fixation.

Type IV

Fracture through the physis, metaphysis, and epiphysis. Involves all three areas.
  • Can lead to growth disturbances or joint deformity.
  • Treatment typically involves surgical fixation.

Type V (Option D)

Crushing injury of the physis (growth plate), resulting in compression and loss of the growth plate. No fracture line visible.
  • Risk of growth arrest and long-term deformities.
  • Surgical intervention required.

The tests that are not commonly used in osteoporosis are bone scan (option 2) and quantitative CT (option 3).

Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA or DEXA):

  • Measures bone mineral density (BMD) at various sites, typically the hip and spine.
  • Findings: T-score and Z-score values are reported, indicating the deviation of the patient's BMD from the average for their age and sex. Lower T-score values indicate lower bone density.

  • Findings: Provides direct measurement of mineral content and bone quality.

  • Findings: X-rays may show signs of osteoporosis such as vertebral compression fractures or decreased bone density.

Blood tests:

  • Measure various markers of bone turnover and metabolism, such as serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D levels.
  • Findings: Abnormal levels of these markers may suggest underlying bone disorders.

Explanation:

  • Dyspnea, and the presence of petechiae all over the body in a male patient who has broken a long bone in a car accident could be signs of the hazardous medical disorder known as fat embolism syndrome (FES)
  • Fat embolism syndrome (FES) is a serious medical condition that can occur after a bone fracture or other traumatic injury.
  • Symptoms of FES include dyspnea, decreased oxygen saturation, and petechiae all over the body.

Gurd and Wilson's Diagnostic Criteria:

One major criterion, four minor criteria, and the presence of macroglobulinemia are required for the diagnosis.

Major criteria

Minor criteria
  • Respiratory insufficiency (symptoms and radiologic evidence)
  • Cerebral dysfunction not caused by head injury or other conditions
  • Petechial rash
  • Tachycardia (>110 beats/min)
  • Pyrexia (temperature >38.5°C)
  • Retinal changes (fat or petechiae)
  • Renal dysfunction
  • Jaundice
  • Acute drop in haemoglobin
  • Sudden thrombocytopenia
  • Elevated ESR
  • Fat macroglobulinemia.

Air embolism (Option B) occurs when air bubbles obstruct blood flow, risking organ damage or death.

Venous thromboembolism (VTE) (Option C) forms blood clots in veins, often traveling to the lungs, leading to pulmonary embolism and potential fatality.

Pulmonary hypertension (PH) (Option D) causes high blood pressure in lung arteries, straining the heart and leading to eventual failure

Painful Arc Syndrome:

Description

correctAnswer: C. Abnormal mobility in a long bone
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Abnormal mobility in a long bone (movement at a site other than a joint) is pathognomonic for a fracture, as it indicates loss of structural continuity.
  • Pain, swelling, ecchymosis, and loss of function can occur with severe soft tissue injuries or dislocations and are not specific to fractures.
  1. Definition: Abnormal mobility refers to movement at a site of the bone where no joint normally exists, indicating loss of bony continuity.
  2. Pathognomonic Nature: It is considered pathognomonic for fracture, meaning its presence confirms the diagnosis without the need for further clinical doubt.
  3. Mechanism: Occurs due to a complete or unstable break in the bone shaft, allowing independent movement of fragments.
  4. Clinical Detection: Assessed gently during examination; forceful testing is avoided to prevent pain and further injury.

Pain and tenderness (Option A): Nonspecific-seen in fractures, soft-tissue injuries, sprains, and contusions.

Swelling and ecchymosis (Option B): Common but not diagnostic; occurs with hematoma, ligament injury, and muscle tears.

Loss of function (Option D): Suggestive but not pathognomonic; also seen in dislocations, nerve injury, and severe pain without fracture.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 716

question: Which clinical finding is considered pathognomonic for a fracture?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • An avulsion fracture occurs when a tendon or ligament pulls a fragment of bone away from the main bone, e.g., olecranon or patellar fractures.

Avulsion Fracture

  • Definition: An avulsion fracture occurs when a fragment of bone is pulled off by a sudden, forceful contraction of a muscle or ligament attached to it.
  • Mechanism: Usually results from acute trauma, rapid acceleration/deceleration, or sports injuries involving jumping or sprinting.
  • Common Sites: Frequently seen at the pelvis (ASIS, AIIS, ischial tuberosity), ankle (medial malleolus), fifth metatarsal, and finger phalanges.
  • Population: More common in adolescents due to open apophyses, but also occurs in athletes and adults.
  • Clinical Features: Presents with sudden, sharp pain, localised tenderness, swelling, and loss of function at the affected site.
  • Diagnosis: Confirmed by X-ray; MRI or CT may be needed for small or occult fragments.
  • Management: Most cases are treated conservatively with rest and immobilisation; surgery is indicated if there is significant displacement.

Impacted fracture (Option A): Occurs when one bone fragment is driven into another, usually due to axial compression, not due to muscle or ligament pull.

Comminuted fracture (Option B): Characterised by the bone being broken into multiple fragments, typically from high-energy trauma.

Greenstick fracture (Option D): An incomplete fracture seen in children where one cortex bends and the other breaks.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 711

  • Pain at the site usually precedes the fracture due to progressive weakening of the bone
  • Pathological fractures often show an abnormal transverse fracture pattern through diseased bone, sometimes referred to as a “banana fracture,” resembling breaking a segment from a banana.

[[figure-1]]

  • FDG-PET/CT (Option C) is considered the gold standard for evaluating bony metastases.
  • The risk of fracture in metastatic bone lesions is assessed using Mirel's score (Option B)
  • A Mirel's score ≥ 8 generally indicates the need for prophylactic fixation.

question: A 70-year-old woman with a history of malignancy reports that while turning in bed, she suddenly experienced severe pain and was unable to move her leg. An X-ray of the hip is shown below. Which of the following statements regarding this type of fracture is false?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Fabry disease (alpha‑galactosidase deficiency) causes angiokeratomas, neuropathic pain, and renal/cardiac involvement, but not bone weakening or pathological fractures.
  • Fabry Disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by α-galactosidase A deficiency, leading to the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3).

Causes of Pathological Fracture

  • Generalized Bone Diseases
    • Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option A): Characterised by defective type I collagen, leading to brittle bones and recurrent pathological fractures.
    • Postmenopausal osteoporosis
    • Metabolic bone diseases (e.g., osteomalacia, renal osteodystrophy)
    • Myelomatosis (multiple myeloma)
    • Paget’s disease of bone
    • Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia
  • Primary Malignant Bone Tumours
    • Osteosarcoma
    • Chondrosarcoma
    • Ewing’s sarcoma
  • Metastatic Bone Disease
    • Carcinoma of:
      • Breast
      • Lung
      • Prostate
      • Kidney
      • Thyroid
      • Colon
  • Local Benign Bone Lesions
    • Chronic Infection
    • Solitary (simple) bone cyst
    • Aneurysmal bone cyst
    • Fibrous cortical defect
    • Chondroma
    • Chondromyxoid fibroma
    • Monostotic fibrous dysplasia

Gaucher disease (Option B): Causes bone marrow infiltration, osteopenia, and Erlenmeyer flask deformity, predisposing to pathological fractures.

Hyperparathyroidism (Option D): Results in osteitis fibrosa cystica with subperiosteal bone resorption and brown tumours, increasing fracture risk.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 747
question: Which of the following conditions is not typically associated with pathological fractures?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The X-ray shows a distal radius fracture where alignment can be restored by applying traction across the wrist joint, allowing the intact ligaments and capsule to pull the fracture fragments into alignment - the principle known as ligamentotaxis.

  • Ligamentotaxis is the technique of applying traction via ligaments and capsules to realign fracture fragments indirectly, commonly used in distal radius and spinal fractures.
  • It is commonly used in orthopaedic trauma, especially for intra-articular and metaphyseal fractures.
  • Continuous traction is applied, which transmits force via surrounding ligaments and soft tissues.
  • This traction helps restore length, alignment, and joint congruity without directly manipulating fragments.
  • Most effective when ligaments are intact, and fracture fragments are large enough to be guided.
  • Commonly achieved using external fixators (e.g., wrist spanning fixator in distal radius fractures).
  • Particularly useful in comminuted fractures where direct reduction is difficult.
  • Advantages include minimal soft tissue disruption and preservation of fracture biology.
  • Limitations include poor effectiveness in severely displaced fractures or ligament injury.
  • Prolonged use may lead to joint stiffness.
  • It is often a temporary or adjunct method before definitive fixation.

Callotaxis (Option A): Refers to gradual distraction to stimulate callus formation, not indirect fracture reduction.

Arthrodesis (Option C): Surgical fusion of a joint, unrelated to fracture alignment.

Osteotaxis (Option D): Alignment achieved by direct manipulation of bone, not via soft-tissue traction.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 331 ,719
question: A patient with a distal radius fracture undergoes treatment using external fixation with traction across the wrist joint. The radiograph of the wrist is shown. The principle of using traction through surrounding soft tissues (ligaments and joint capsule) to indirectly align fracture fragments is known as:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a thumb spica cast, which immobilises the wrist and thumb to stabilise the scaphoid bone during healing.

The scaphoid cast (or thumb spica cast) is applied with the wrist in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb in abduction (glass‑holding position) to immobilise a scaphoid fracture.

  • Definition: A scaphoid fracture is a break in the scaphoid bone, the most commonly fractured carpal bone of the wrist.
  • Mechanism: Usually occurs due to a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with the wrist in extension.
  • Anatomy: The scaphoid spans the proximal and distal carpal rows, making it crucial for wrist stability.
  • Blood Supply: Supplied mainly by the radial artery in a retrograde fashion, predisposing the proximal pole to avascular necrosis.
  • Clinical Features: Pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, swelling, and reduced wrist motion.
  • Diagnosis: X-ray may be initially normal; MRI or CT is more sensitive in early fractures.
  • Complications: Non-union, avascular necrosis, and scaphoid non-union advanced collapse (SNAC) wrist.
  • Management: Immobilisation in a thumb spica cast or surgical fixation, depending on displacement and location.

Colles fracture (Option A): Managed with a cast in palmar flexion and ulnar deviation, not dorsiflexion with thumb abduction.Hand shaking cast is used.

Boxer’s fracture (Option C): Treated with ulnar gutter splint with MCP joints flexed; thumb position is not relevant.

Monteggia fracture (Option D): Requires above-elbow immobilisation with elbow flexion and forearm supination.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 806-808
question: A patient with wrist trauma is immobilised using the cast shown in the image above, with the wrist in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb positioned in abduction. This type of cast is most commonly used for which fracture?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The tibial diaphysis is one of the most common sites for open fractures due to its subcutaneous location.
  • Phalanges are common overall

Tibial Diaphysis (Shaft of Tibia) fracture

  • Most commonly fractured long bone
  • Most common site of open fracture among long bones
    • ~23.5% are open
  • Reason:
    • Tibia is subcutaneous along:
      • Anterior border
      • Medial surface
  • Common mechanisms:
    • Road traffic accidents (esp. motorcycle)
    • Falls
    • Sports injuries
  • High risk of open fracture because:
    • Minimal soft-tissue cover
    • Sharp anterior border (“shin”) easily pierces skin

Femoral shaft (Option A): Deeply surrounded by bulky muscle, so it is less likely to become open despite high-energy trauma.

Humeral shaft (Option C): Has better soft-tissue coverage and a lower incidence of open fractures compared to the tibia.

Pelvis (Option D): Pelvic fractures are usually closed; open pelvic fractures are rare and associated with severe multisystem trauma, not the most common site.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 929
question: Which of the following is the most common site for an open fracture?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Type IIIB open fractures have extensive soft‑tissue loss (>10 cm) with periosteal stripping, contamination, and usually require flap coverage, but vascularity is intact.

Gustilo-Anderson Classification (Open Fractures)

  • Purpose: Classifies open fractures based on wound size, soft-tissue damage, contamination, and vascular injury, guiding management and prognosis.
  • Type I:
    • Wound < 1 cm, clean.
    • Minimal soft-tissue damage, simple fracture pattern.
    • Low contamination and infection risk.
  • Type II:
    • Wound 1-10 cm, without extensive soft-tissue injury.
    • Moderate contamination, no flaps or avulsions.
    • Fracture is moderately comminuted.
  • Type III: High-energy injuries with extensive damage. Subdivided into:
    • Type IIIA:
      • Adequate soft-tissue coverage despite severe injury.
      • Extensive laceration or flaps, heavy contamination.
    • Type IIIB:
      • Extensive soft-tissue loss with periosteal stripping.
      • Bone exposure requires flap coverage.
    • Type IIIC:
      • Open fracture with arterial injury requiring repair, regardless of wound size.


Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 929
question: An open fracture with extensive soft tissue loss (>10 cm) with periosteal stripping, severe contamination, and adequate vascularity is classified as Gustilo‑Anderson type:

correctAnswer: B. Surgical intervention for vascular compromise
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A capillary refill time (CRT) exceeding 3 seconds in trauma indicates critical tissue ischemia, necessitating immediate neurovascular evaluation and Doppler assessment.
  • Suggests vascular compromise, which may be due to arterial injury, severe oedema, compartment syndrome, or shock.

Compartment syndrome

Feature

Clinical Detail

Pathophysiology

Reduced arterial inflow or venous outflow due to vessel damage or compression.

Clinical Red Flags

Cold, pale limbs, absent pulses, pain out of proportion, and paresthesia.

Common Causes

Arterial transection, compartment syndrome, crush injuries, or tight casts.

Immediate Action

Urgent neurovascular exam, Doppler assessment, and comparison with the contralateral limb.

Management

Stabilisation, removal of constrictive dressings, and urgent surgical referral (vascular/ortho).

Prognosis

Early intervention is critical to prevent limb loss and tissue necrosis.

Need for analgesia (Option A): Analgesia is important for pain control, but prolonged CRT >3 s indicates impaired perfusion/ischemia, not pain; analgesia does not restore arterial flow and is not the urgent action.

Routine fracture immobilisation (Option C): Immobilisation stabilises the fracture,it doesn't address arterial compromise.

Antibiotic administration (Option D): Antibiotics prevent or treat infection, but prolonged CRT reflects ischemia, not infection.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 680
question: In a patient with a traumatic limb injury, a capillary refill time >3 seconds most urgently indicates:

correctAnswer: B. Impaired nerve supply in the limb
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a severe open fracture with extensive soft-tissue injury.

Associated neurovascular compromise, such as impaired nerve supply, indicates significant soft-tissue damage and increases the risk of infection and poor healing, making primary closure inappropriate.

Other contraindications to Primary Closure of an Open Fracture Wound

  1. Gross contamination: Presence of soil, faeces, farmyard contamination, or foreign material increases infection risk if closed primarily.
  2. Severe soft-tissue damage: Extensive muscle crushing, devitalized tissue, or skin loss prevents safe tension-free closure.
  3. Delayed presentation: Wounds presenting >6-8 hours after injury have a higher bacterial load, making primary closure unsafe.
  4. Inadequate debridement: If thorough excision of devitalized tissue cannot be confidently achieved, closure should be avoided.
  5. Active infection: Signs such as pus, foul smell, erythema, or systemic sepsis contraindicate primary closure.
  6. High-energy injuries: Gustilo-Anderson type III fractures, especially IIIB and IIIC, are not suitable for primary closure.
  7. Vascular injury: Associated arterial damage requiring repair increases the risk of wound breakdown and infection.

Primary closure of open fractures may be considered after meticulous debridement, particularly when the injury-to-debridement interval is <12 hours, contamination is minimal, and stable fixation is achievable.

Injury-to-debridement interval <12 hours (Option A): Early debridement actually favours primary closure, so this is not a contraindication.

Absence of systemic injuries (Option C): This is favourable for primary closure, not a contraindication.

Ability to achieve stable fracture fixation (Option D): Stable fixation is required for primary closure, so this is not a contraindication.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 729

options.text: Impaired nerve supply in the limb
Ability to achieve stable fracture fixation

question: A patient presents with a severe open fracture of the leg following trauma, as shown in the image. After thorough debridement, the surgical team considers primary wound closure. Which of the following is a contraindication to primary closure in this situation?

correctAnswer: B. Monteggia fracture (ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Monteggia fracture-dislocation (ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation) has poor results with conservative treatment due to the risk of chronic radial head instability, nonunion, and stiffness; thus, surgical fixation is standard.
  • Undisplaced distal radius, stable tibial shaft, and clavicular shaft fractures often heal well with conservative management. (Option A, C and D ruled out)

Monteggia Fracture-Dislocation

  • A Monteggia fracture-dislocation consists of a fracture of the proximal or middle third of the ulna associated with dislocation of the radial head at the elbow.
  • Mechanism of Injury: Usually caused by a fall on an outstretched hand, direct blow to the forearm, or high-energy trauma.
  • Bado Classification is used to categorise the Monteggia fractures.
  • Clinical Features: Pain, swelling, forearm deformity, and restricted elbow movement.
  • Neurovascular Injury: Posterior interosseous nerve palsy may occur.
  • Diagnosis: Confirmed by X-ray of the elbow and forearm, ensuring the radiocapitellar line alignment.

  • Management: Anatomical reduction and fixation of the ulna usually leads to spontaneous reduction of the radial head.

Fractures of Necessity

These are fractures that almost always require operative management because satisfactory outcome with conservative treatment is unlikely.

Common examples include:

  1. Neck of femur fracture (especially displaced intracapsular)
  2. Fracture shaft femur
  3. Both-bone forearm fractures in adults
  4. Displaced intra-articular fractures
  5. Patellar fracture with disrupted extensor mechanism
  6. Olecranon fracture with displacement
  7. Fracture lateral condyle of humerus in children
  8. Monteggia fracture-dislocation
  9. Galeazzi fracture-dislocation
  10. Unstable pelvic fractures
  11. Open fractures (after debridement ± fixation)
  12. Fractures associated with vascular injury
  13. Nonunion or malunion requiring correction
  14. Certain spinal fractures with instability/neurological deficit


Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 793-794

options.text: Monteggia fracture (ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation)

question: Which fracture-dislocation is known to have poor functional outcomes with conservative management, typically necessitating surgery?

correctAnswer: B. Severe type III open fracture
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a circular external fixator used to stabilise fractures while minimising additional soft-tissue injury.

  • Such devices are commonly used in severe open fractures (Gustilo type III) where there is extensive soft-tissue damage, contamination, or swelling, making immediate internal fixation unsafe.

External fixation

  • Fracture stabilised by pins/wires above & below the fracture connected to an external frame
  • Commonly used
    • Tibia, pelvis
    • Also femur, humerus, distal radius, hand
  • Indications
    • Severe soft-tissue injury / open fractures (Type III)
    • Contaminated or infected fractures
    • Polytrauma (damage control)
    • Gross swelling → temporary stabilisation
    • Non-union / bone loss → compression or bone transport
  • Principle
    • Pins in safe corridors
    • Frame provides length, alignment, and stability
    • Allows adjustment & dynamization
    • Enables early partial weight-bearing
  • Advantages
    • Preserves soft tissue
    • Allows wound care & staged surgery
    • Minimal fracture site exposure
  • Complications
    • Pin-tract infection (most common)
    • Neurovascular injury
    • Joint stiffness
    • Over-distraction → non-union

Type I open fracture (Option A): These have minimal soft-tissue injury and are usually managed with internal fixation or casting, not external fixation.

Undisplaced closed tibial fracture (Option C): Such fractures are stable and typically treated with conservative immobilisation, making external fixation unnecessary.

Isolated radial styloid fracture (Option D): This is a low-energy, localised injury and is commonly treated with casting or simple internal fixation, not external fixation.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 726, 929
question: Which of the following is a common indication for the procedure below?

correctAnswer: C. The tension-stress effect induces new bone formation between the gradually separated bony surfaces.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows an Ilizarov circular external fixator used for distraction osteogenesis. During gradual distraction, the tension-stress effect stimulates new bone formation in the gap between the separated bone ends.

  • The Ilizarov method relies on the principle of distraction osteogenesis, where gradual, controlled traction (tension‑stress) is applied to a healing bone segment to stimulate neovascularisation and new bone formation (regeneration) between the separated bone ends.

Ilizarov Method

  • The Ilizarov method is a circular external fixation technique used for bone lengthening, deformity correction, non-union, and limb reconstruction.
  • Principle: It is based on distraction osteogenesis, where gradual mechanical distraction stimulates new bone formation.
  • Device: Uses an Ilizarov ring fixator consisting of circular rings, tensioned wires, and rods attached to bone.
  • Procedure: After a corticotomy, distraction is started at about 1 mm/day, usually in 4 increments.
  • Biology: Controlled tension induces regeneration of bone, muscles, nerves, vessels, and skin.
  • Indications: Non-union, malunion, limb length discrepancy, bone loss, deformities, and infected non-union.
  • Advantages: Allows simultaneous correction, early weight bearing, and treatment of infection.
  • Complications: Pin-tract infection, pain, joint stiffness, malalignment, and prolonged treatment time.
  • Outcome: Highly effective when patient compliance and meticulous follow-up are ensured.

The presence of chronic osteomyelitis is an absolute contraindication for this procedure (Option A): Not an absolute contraindication; the Ilizarov technique is commonly used in infected non-unions.

The distraction should be carried out at a rate of 2.0 mm per day to accelerate bone formation (Option B): Excessive rate; standard is ~1 mm/day to allow proper regeneration formation.

The total daily distraction should be performed in a single daily adjustment to ensure stability (Option D): Incorrect; distraction is done in multiple small increments (e.g., 0.25 mm × 4/day) for optimal bone formation.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 334

question: A 28-year-old man sustains a severe tibial injury with segmental bone loss following a motor vehicle accident. Reconstruction is planned using the device shown below. A corticotomy is performed, followed by a latency period before gradual bone distraction is started. Which of the following statements regarding the distraction phase of this procedure is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Autologous bone graft (usually from iliac crest) is the gold standard because it provides osteogenesis (living osteoblasts), osteoinduction (growth factors like BMPs), and osteoconduction (scaffold).
  • Common donor sites: Iliac crest (most common), fibula, tibia, distal radius, ribs.
  • Biological properties: Provides osteogenesis, osteoinduction, and osteoconduction (gold standard).
    • Osteogenesis: Contains living osteoblasts and progenitor cells that directly form new bone.
    • Osteoinduction: Has growth factors (BMPs) that stimulate differentiation of mesenchymal cells into osteoblasts.
    • Osteoconduction: Acts as a scaffold for new bone growth.
  • Indications: Non-union fractures, spinal fusion, bone defects, and revision surgeries.
  • Advantages: No immunological rejection, excellent incorporation, and high success rate.
  • Disadvantages: Donor site morbidity (pain, infection, hematoma), limited quantity.
  • Types: Cancellous (rapid healing), cortical (structural support), or corticocancellous.

Allograft (Option A): Provides osteoconduction and limited osteoinduction, but lacks osteogenesis because viable osteogenic cells are absent.

Synthetic hydroxyapatite (Option B): Acts only as an osteoconductive scaffold with no osteogenic cells or inductive proteins.

Demineralised bone matrix (Option D): Has osteoinductive properties due to bone morphogenetic proteins, but lacks osteogenesis and provides limited structural conduction.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 332-334
question: Which type of bone graft provides osteogenesis, osteoinduction, and osteoconduction?

correctAnswer: C. Boyd’s involves talectomy and fusion; Syme’s uses a posterior flap.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Boyd’s amputation involves talectomy and calcaneotibial arthrodesis, while Syme’s amputation uses a long posterior flap.

Syme’s Amputation

Boyd’s amputation
  • Syme’s amputation is performed above the ankle. (Option D ruled out)
  • The level of bone section is 0.6 cm proximal to the ankle joint.
  • It preserves the distal physis, providing good function.
  • Children benefit greatly from this procedure (Option A ruled out)
  • Men generally accept it well, but women may find it cosmetically unappealing.
  • The indications for the surgery are limited and it is technically difficult.
  • A long posterior flap is used, including the heel skin and fat pad.
  • The bones are cut just above the malleoli for stability.
  • Boyd’s amputation involves
    • Removal of the talus (talectomy)
    • The fusion of the calcaneus to the tibia (calcaneotibial arthrodesis) (Option B ruled out)
  • It enables full weight-bearing.
  • It offers stabilization of the heel pad while providing support for a prosthesis.



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page. 342
  2. Ebenezer Orthopaedics. 5th edition. Page. 774

Boyd’s involves talectomy and fusion; Syme’s uses a posterior flap.

question: A 10-year-old boy requires an amputation due to severe trauma to his ankle. The surgeon discusses two options: Syme’s amputation and Boyd’s amputation. Which statement accurately describes a key feature of each procedure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Calcium sulfate (plaster of Paris) is osteoconductive, biodegradable, and resorbable, making it suitable for filling contained bone defects.
  • Composition: It is usually available as calcium sulfate hemihydrate (plaster of Paris), which hardens after mixing with fluid.
  • Mechanism: Acts as an osteoconductive scaffold, allowing bone ingrowth along its structure, but does not induce osteogenesis or osteoinduction.
  • Resorption: It is rapidly resorbed (within 4-12 weeks), matching early phases of bone healing.
  • Advantages: Biocompatible, easy to handle, injectable, and can be combined with antibiotics for local drug delivery.
  • Clinical Uses: Used in contained metaphyseal defects, benign bone tumours, fracture voids, and osteomyelitis dead space management.
  • Limitations: Low mechanical strength, not suitable for load-bearing defects, and rapid resorption may cause serous wound drainage.

Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement (Option A): PMMA is non-biodegradable and not osteoconductive; it acts only as a space filler and structural support.

Demineralised bone matrix (DBM) (Option C): DBM is mainly osteoinductive, with variable and weak osteoconductive properties, and is not a predictable structural scaffold like calcium sulfate

Cobalt-chrome alloy (Option D): This is a metallic implant material, neither biodegradable nor osteoconductive.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 332, 333
question: Which agent is both osteoconductive and biodegradable, often used as a bone graft substitute in contained defects?

correctAnswer: C. Recurrence can be prevented with indomethacin or radiotherapy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Myositis ossificans is a benign ectopic bone formation seen commonly after elbow dislocation or trauma. Recurrence prevention is done using indomethacin or radiotherapy.
  • Aetiology: Most commonly follows blunt trauma, muscle contusion, fractures, surgery, or repeated micro-trauma.
  • Types:
    • Myositis ossificans traumatica (most common)
    • Progressive myositis ossificans (Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva - rare, genetic)
  • Common Sites: Thigh (quadriceps), brachialis, gluteal muscles.
  • Clinical Features: Pain, swelling, localised warmth, and progressive restriction of movement.
  • Radiology: X-ray shows peripheral calcification with central lucency (“zonal phenomenon”) after 3-6 weeks.
  • Management: Mostly conservative - rest, NSAIDs, physiotherapy after the acute phase.
  • Surgery: Reserved for mature lesions causing functional limitation.
  • Prognosis: Generally self-limiting with a good outcome.

Early vigorous massage helps prevent progression (Option A): Vigorous massage and aggressive physiotherapy in the early phase can worsen heterotopic ossification, so this is incorrect.

Condition is malignant and requires urgent excision (Option B): This is myositis ossificans / heterotopic ossification, a benign reactive process, not a malignancy.

Surgical excision should be done immediately after diagnosis (Option D): Excision in the active phase leads to high recurrence; surgery is delayed until maturation (≈6-12 months).



Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 187
  • Essential Orthopaedics by Maheshwari, 6th Edition, Page 52
