Nailing of tibia with external fixation of femur
Nailing of femur with external fixation of tibia
External fixation for both femur and tibia

question: A child sustains multiple injuries following a road traffic accident. On examination, vitals are unstable, and the London sign is positive. Bilateral femoral and tibial fractures are noted along with tenderness over the right upper limb. After adequate hemodynamic stabilization, what is the most appropriate immediate orthopedic management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Radial nerve injury is common in shaft of humerus fractures and presents with wrist drop and finger drop due to loss of wrist extensors.
  • Sensory loss over the dorsoradial hand and dorsal proximal parts of the radial 3½ digits (excluding the fingertips).
  • Anatomy: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humerus, making it susceptible to injury in mid-shaft fractures.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Motor: Weakness or inability to extend the wrist, fingers, and thumb (“wrist drop”).
    • Sensory: Numbness over the dorsal hand, dorsoradial forearm, and radial 3½ fingers. (excluding the fingertips)
  • Diagnosis: Clinical assessment supported by electromyography (EMG) if recovery is delayed.
  • Management:
    • Conservative: Most closed fractures with radial nerve palsy recover spontaneously within 3-4 months.
    • Surgical Exploration: Indicated for open fractures, sharp bone fragments, or no recovery on EMG.

Median nerve (Option A): Injury causes weak wrist/finger flexion, thenar wasting, and sensory loss over the lateral palm and radial 3½ fingers; this does not match dorsiflexion weakness.

Ulnar nerve (Option B): Injury causes weakness of finger abduction/adduction, claw hand, and sensory loss over the medial 1½ fingers; dorsiflexion is unaffected.

Musculocutaneous nerve (Option D): Injury causes weak elbow flexion and sensory loss over the lateral forearm; wrist and finger movements are normal.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 770-772
question: A 40-year-old man presents after a road traffic accident with pain and swelling of the arm. X-ray shows a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus. He is unable to dorsiflex the wrist and fingers, and has numbness over the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and radial 3½ digits. Which nerve is most likely injured, shown in the X-ray below?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario and the distinct line observed in the lateral condyle on the X-ray indicate a lateral condylar fracture.
  • The Milch classification is specifically used for lateral condylar fractures.

Lateral Condylar Fracture:

  • Mechanism of Injury: Typically occurs due to a fall on an outstretched hand with the elbow extended and forced into varus, leading to a shearing or avulsion fracture of the lateral condyle.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Swelling and deformity of the elbow.
  • Tenderness over the lateral condyle & pain during passive wrist flexion.
  • Milch Classification:
    • Type I: Fracture occurs lateral to the trochlea.
      • The ulnohumeral joint is not involved, making the fracture stable.
      • Generally, these fractures can be treated conservatively without surgical intervention, as they tend to maintain alignment.
    • Type II: Fracture runs through the middle of the trochlea and is more common.
      • The elbow is unstable due to compromised lateral restraint that includes the lateral trochlea ridge.
      • The fragment is partly cartilaginous and is larger than it seems on x-ray.

[[figure-1]]

Pauwel’s Classification (Option A) is used for femoral neck fractures and classifies fractures based on the angle of the fracture line relative to the horizontal plane.

Garden’s Classification (Option B) assesses femoral neck fractures based on the degree of rotational displacement. It evaluates changes in the direction of the medial trabecular stream of the neck relative to the bony trabeculae and the corresponding part of the acetabulum.

Gustilo-Anderson Classification (Option D) classifies open fractures into three grades based on the size of the wound, the degree of contamination, and the soft tissue injury.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 785
question: A 7-year-old child presents to the emergency department after falling on an outstretched hand. The examination reveals swelling and tenderness over the lateral aspect of the elbow. X-rays show the findings as shown in the image. What classification system is used to categorize this condition?

correctAnswer: D. Fracture of the medial epicondyle
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A fracture of the medial epicondyle is not included in the terrible triad of the elbow.

Terrible Triad of the Elbow: It refers to a specific injury pattern involving three components, commonly seen in elbow dislocations, particularly after trauma:

  • Posterior elbow dislocation (Option A)
  • Fracture of the radial head (Option B)
  • Fracture of the coronoid process (Option C)

[[figure-1]]

  • Mechanism of Injury: Typically results from a fall on an outstretched hand with the elbow slightly flexed. A valgus twist can lead to a posterolateral dislocation.
  • Treatment: The standard treatment involves reduction under anaesthesia, followed by immobilisation in an above-elbow cast.



Reference:

John Ebnezar and Rakesh John, Textbook of Orthopedics, 5th Edition, Page 142

Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th Edition, Page 105
question: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a fall while playing rugby. He has severe pain and swelling in his elbow, and the physician suspects injury to the terrible triad. Which of the following is NOT a component of the terrible triad of the elbow?

correctAnswer: B. Pain that intensifies with passive finger extension
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The first sign of impending compartment syndrome is typically pain that worsens with passive stretching of the muscles in the affected compartment. (Stretch Test)

Compartment Syndrome:

  • It occurs when increased pressure within a limb's muscle compartments compromises blood flow to the muscles and nerves, potentially leading to severe complications.
  • Causes:
    • Common in children: Most frequently caused by supracondylar fractures.
    • Adults: Often due to crush injuries; other causes include:
      • Fractures of both bones of the forearm and elbow dislocations
      • Vascular injuries and Subfascial hematomas.

[[figure-1]]

  • The flexor muscles, particularly the flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus, are most commonly affected.
  • Volkmann's ischemic contracture (VIC) may develop due to arterial spasm, leading to muscle ischemia and eventual fibrosis. The 6 Ps of Impending Volkmann’s Ischemia:
    • Pain
    • Pallor
    • Paresthesia
    • Paralysis
    • Pulselessness
    • Positive passive stretch test
  • Diagnosis:
    • Severe, poorly localised pain disproportionate to injury.
    • Swelling, redness, warmth, tenderness, and tension in the forearm
    • Stretch test: Pain occurs when ischemic muscles are stretched - the first sign of impending compartment syndrome.
    • Other signs:
      • Initially, palpable peripheral pulses may later become absent.
      • Nerve involvement (Median nerve > Ulnar nerve)
  • Treatment:
    • Preventive measures, such as limb elevation and active finger movements, can help mitigate risks.
    • Acute stage (Surgical Emergency): Removing any tight bandages & monitor intracompartmental pressure:
      • Pressure > 30 mm Hg - Emergency fasciotomy
      • Pressure < 30 mm Hg - Continuous monitoring

  • Absence of the radial pulse on examination (Option A) indicates severe ischemia, which occurs when blood flow is critically compromised due to elevated compartment pressure & is not an early sign.

  • Immediate improvement in pain with elevation of the arm (Option C) is not typical of compartment syndrome. Pain is not alleviated unless pressure is reduced in the compartment.

  • Numbness in the forearm (Option D) can occur as a result of nerve compression due to increased compartment pressure, but it is a later sign.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 784

Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th Edition, Page 47

options.text: Absence of the radial pulse on examination
Pain that intensifies with passive finger extension
Immediate improvement in pain with elevation of the arm

question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after falling from a tree. X-rays reveal a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus. The child is experiencing severe pain, and upon examination, the forearm appears swollen and tense. Which of the following is the first sign of impending compartment syndrome??

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario described, including the reported symptoms and the lateral deviation of the forearm when the arm is extended, points to a diagnosis of Cubitus Valgus.

Description

An acquired deformity due to reduced growth on the lateral side of the distal humeral epiphysis.

Cause

Non-union of lateral condylar fracture

Clinical feature
  • A carrying angle of the elbow greater than 15 degrees
  • Asymmetry between the two side
  • Lateral deviation of the forearm during arm extension

[[figure-1]]

Management

  • Usually, no treatment is required
  • Supracondylar osteotomy (in severe cases)

Complication

Tardy ulnar nerve palsy: Managed by anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve.

Gunstock deformity (Option A) is also known as cubitus varus. It is caused by malunion of a supracondylar fracture in childhood.

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Dinner fork deformity (Option C) occurs due to a Colles' fracture. In this condition, the radial styloid process is positioned at or slightly above the level of the ulnar styloid process, creating the characteristic appearance of a dinner fork.

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

Coxa vara (Option D) is a hip deformity characterised by a reduced angle between the neck and shaft of the femur. This condition can be congenital or acquired (Inter-trochanteric fracture).

[[figure-6]]

[[figure-7]]



Reference:

Apley & Solomon’s System of Orthopaedic and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 386.
question: A 28-year-old female with a history of a left lateral condylar fracture presents with left elbow pain, especially during lifting or reaching overhead. She notices her left arm appears straighter than her right. Examination shows lateral deviation of the forearm when her arms are extended. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The scenario describes Tsuge’s type I Volkmann’s Ischemic Contracture (VIC) involving only the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP).
  • The appropriate management in this case would be the use of a Turn Buckle splint.

Volkmann’s Ischemic Contracture (VIC) Management

Type

Management

Mild

(Tsuge's Type-I)
  • Turn Buckle's splint (Volkmann's splinting) (Option A)

[[figure-1]]

  • Physiotherapy
  • Total excision (single muscle involved)

Moderate

(Tsuge's Type-II)
  • Max page's operation (Soft tissue sliding operation) (Option B)

[[figure-2]]

  • Excision of cicatrix
  • Neurolysis (freeing the peripheral nerves from the surrounding fibrous tissue)

Severe

(Tsuge's Type-III)
  • Seddon's carpectomy: (Option C)

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

  • Excision of the scar
  • Arthrodesis of the wrist
  • Amputation (cases with gangrene) (Option D)



Reference:

Apley & Solomon’s System of Orthopaedic and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 434.
question: A 34-year-old female presents to the emergency department with severe pain and swelling in her right forearm after a biking accident. She has difficulty flexing her ring and pinky fingers. Examination reveals swelling, limited flexion of the fourth and fifth fingers, pallor, diminished pulse, and paresthesia in the affected fingers. What is the appropriate management?

explanationHtml:
Option A: Ulnar

[[figure-1]]

  • The ulnar nerve (C8-T1) arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus.
  • It descends downward in the upper arm medial to the axillary artery.
  • At the elbow, it runs posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
  • It passes through the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris and enters the flexor compartment of the forearm.
  • At the wrist, the ulnar nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum and enters the hand through Guyon’s canal.
  • On the hand, it terminates by dividing into superficial and deep branches.
  • It supplies the following muscles:
  • Flexor carpi ulnaris.
  • Medial half of the flexor digitorum profundus.
  • Intrinsic muscles of the hand except for the thenar muscles and two lateral lumbricals.
  • The sensory supply of the ulnar nerve includes:
  • Palmar and dorsal aspects of the medial side of the hand.
  • Palmar and dorsal aspects of the ulnar one and half fingers.

[[figure-2]]

  • As it passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, the ulnar nerve is susceptible to injury in case of its fracture.

Option B: Median

  • The median nerve is injured in case of supracondylar fracture of the humerus.

Option C: Radial

  • The radial nerve is most commonly injured in case of a fracture of the humerus shaft.

Option D: Axillary

  • The axillary nerve is most commonly injured in case of a fracture of the humerus neck.


Reference:

Orthopaedics Quick Review (OPQR) pg. 77
question: A 25-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department after he fell while playing football and hit his right elbow. Physical examination reveals severe pain and tenderness in his elbow with a limited range of motion. An x-ray was performed that showed a fracture of the medial epicondyle of the right humerus. Which is the most common nerve injured in the given clinical scenario?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has a fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus, which most commonly injures the ulnar nerve because it passes posterior to the medial epicondyle in the cubital tunnel, making it particularly vulnerable to trauma at this site.

  • The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8-T1) and supplies the flexor carpi ulnaris, the medial half of the flexor digitorum profundus, and most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand.
  • It also provides sensation to the medial one-and-a-half fingers and the adjacent medial aspect of the hand.
  • Injury to the ulnar nerve results in weak finger abduction and adduction, reduced grip strength, sensory loss over the medial one-and-a-half digits, and, in chronic cases, an ulnar claw hand due to paralysis of the interossei and medial lumbricals.

[[figure-1]]

Median nerve (Option B): The median nerve is most commonly injured in supracondylar fractures of the humerus, particularly the anterior interosseous nerve branch. It does not lie directly behind the medial epicondyle.

Radial nerve (Option C): The radial nerve is most commonly injured in fractures of the shaft of the humerus, especially at the spiral groove, resulting in wrist drop due to paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors.

Axillary nerve (Option D): The axillary nerve is most commonly injured in fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus and anterior shoulder dislocations. Injury causes weakness of shoulder abduction and sensory loss over the regimental badge area of the lateral shoulder.



Reference:

Orthopaedics Quick Review, 8th Edition, Page 77
question: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department after falling while playing football and landing on his right elbow. Examination reveals severe pain, tenderness, and restricted elbow movements. An X-ray shows a fracture of the medial epicondyle of the right humerus. Which nerve is most commonly injured in this patient?

correctAnswer: C. Weight of the ipsilateral arm and pull of the sternocleidomastoid
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The lateral fragment is displaced inferiorly due to the weight of the ipsilateral arm, while the medial fragment is elevated by the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Mechanism of displacement:

  • The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) attaches to the medial clavicle superiorly and tends to pull the medial fragment upward.
  • The weight of the ipsilateral arm pulls the shoulder girdle downward, contributing to the inferior displacement of the lateral fragment.
  • The trapezius cannot counteract the downward pull of the arm, so the lateral fragment displaces inferiorly.

Pull of trapezius on the lateral fragment (Option A): Trapezius acts to elevate the shoulder, but the lateral fragment is displaced inferiorly mainly due to the weight of the arm, not the trapezius pull.

Pull of pectoralis major on the medial fragment (Option B): Pectoralis major inserts on the humerus, not the medial clavicle, so it does not elevate the medial fragment.

Spasm of the deltoid muscle (Option D): Deltoid primarily abducts the arm and does not cause the characteristic clavicular fragment displacement.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 755-757

Pull of pectoralis major on the medial fragment
Weight of the ipsilateral arm and pull of the sternocleidomastoid

question: A 25-year-old male presents after a fall on the shoulder. X-ray shows a fracture at the junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third of the clavicle. The lateral fragment is displaced inferiorly, while the medial fragment is elevated. What is the most likely reason for this pattern of displacement?

correctAnswer: B. Avulsion fracture of the anteroinferior glenoid rim
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A bony Bankart lesion is an avulsion fracture of the anteroinferior glenoid rim associated with anterior shoulder dislocation.
  • A soft‑tissue Bankart lesion involves only labral tearing.
  • Mechanism: Occurs due to forceful anterior dislocation, where the inferior glenohumeral ligament complex pulls off a fragment of bone from the glenoid.
  • Pathoanatomy: Involves both bone and labrum, unlike a soft-tissue Bankart, which affects only the labrum.
  • Common Population: Seen commonly in young athletes and patients with recurrent anterior shoulder instability.
  • Clinical Features: Patients present with recurrent dislocations, apprehension, and instability, especially in abduction and external rotation.
  • Imaging: Best visualised on CT scan with 3D reconstruction; MRI helps assess associated soft-tissue injuries.
  • Management: Small lesions may be treated conservatively; large defects require surgical fixation or bone augmentation procedures.

Fracture of the humeral greater tuberosity (Option A): This is associated with rotator cuff avulsion or shoulder dislocation but is not a Bankart lesion.

Tear of the glenoid labrum without bony injury (Option C): This describes a soft-tissue (classic) Bankart lesion, not a bony Bankart.

Fracture of the coracoid process (Option D): Seen in specific trauma patterns but unrelated to Bankart lesions.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 762-764

question: A 22-year-old rugby player presents to the emergency department after a traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation sustained during a tackle. After successful reduction, an X-ray reveals a small bone fragment displaced from the anteroinferior aspect of the glenoid rim. Which of the following best describes this finding?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Laterjet‑Bristow procedure transfers the coracoid process with attached conjoined tendon to the anteroinferior glenoid rim to augment bony stability.
  • Approach: Deltopectoral incision to expose the coracoid process.
  • Coracoid osteotomy: The coracoid process is osteotomized at its base, along with the conjoint tendon (short head of biceps + coracobrachialis).
  • Preparation: The undersurface of the coracoid is decorticated to promote bone healing.
  • Subscapularis split: The subscapularis muscle is split horizontally to access the anterior glenoid neck.
  • Graft placement: The coracoid graft is positioned at the anteroinferior glenoid rim
  • Fixation: Fixed using screws (usually 1-2) to achieve a stable bone block.
  • Capsular repair: The capsule and labrum may be sutured over the graft to augment stability.
  • Biomechanical effect: Provides bony extension of the glenoid and dynamic sling from the conjoint tendon to prevent anterior dislocation.

Bankart repair (Option A): Involves reattachment of the detached anteroinferior labrum to the glenoid; no bone transfer is performed.

Putti‑Platt procedure (Option B): Shortens and tightens the subscapularis and anterior capsule; does not involve coracoid transfer.

Neer capsular shift (Option D): Tightens a lax joint capsule to improve stability; no bony procedure is performed.



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 370
  2. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26231148/
question: Which surgical procedure for recurrent anterior shoulder instability involves transfer of the coracoid process to the anterior glenoid rim?

correctAnswer: B. Posterior dislocation of the shoulder
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Posterior shoulder dislocation typically occurs after seizures or electric shock due to violent internal rotation and adduction, with the arm locked in internal rotation.

Posterior Shoulder Dislocation

  • Dislocation of the humeral head posteriorly relative to the glenoid fossa; rare, accounting for ~2-5% of all shoulder dislocations.
  • Aetiology: Usually due to seizures, electric shocks, or trauma with forceful internal rotation and adduction.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Pain and limited shoulder movement
    • Arm held in adduction and internal rotation
    • The anterior shoulder appears flattened with posterior fullness
    • Posterior fullness on palpation
  • Special Signs:

  • Axillary or scapular Y view confirms the diagnosis
  • Complications: Chronic dislocation, reverse Hill-Sachs lesion, rotator cuff injury, arthritis
  • Management:
  • Acute: Closed reduction under sedation
  • Chronic: Open reduction, possible bone grafting or arthroplasty

Russell's Traction (Option B) is commonly used in intertrochanteric fractures. It provides a combination of longitudinal traction and counter traction to maintain proper alignment of the fracture while allowing for some movement of the joints, preventing stiffness.

question: A 10-year-old patient presents to the emergency department after falling onto an outstretched hand. X-rays reveal a finding, as shown in the image. Traction is applied as part of the management, as depicted in the accompanying image. What is the name of the traction being used?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cubitus varus (gunstock deformity) is the most common late complication of pediatric supracondylar humerus fractures, resulting from malunion.
  • Cubitus varus is a deformity of the elbow characterised by decreased or reversed carrying angle, causing the forearm to deviate medially when the arm is extended.
  • Pathophysiology: Results from medial tilt, medial rotation, and posterior angulation of the distal humeral fragment rather than growth disturbance.
  • Clinical Features: Usually, cosmetic deformity; elbow function is often preserved. Some patients may develop posterolateral rotatory instability or ulnar nerve symptoms later.
  • Diagnosis: Primarily clinical, confirmed by AP and lateral X-rays showing altered humeral alignment.
  • Complications: Increased risk of lateral condyle fractures, elbow instability, and tardy ulnar nerve palsy.
  • Management: Corrective supracondylar osteotomy is the treatment of choice for significant deformity or functional issues.

Cubitus valgus (Option A): More commonly associated with lateral condyle fractures of the humerus, not supracondylar fractures.

Radial nerve palsy (Option C): A neurological complication, usually acute and transient, not the most common long-term sequela.

Myositis ossificans (Option D): Can occur after repeated manipulations, but is uncommon compared to deformity.

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 784
question: What is the most common long‑term complication of the condition below, seen on X-ray, in children?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lateral condyle fractures in children usually involve the physis, epiphysis, and metaphysis, crossing the growth plate into the joint, making them Salter‑Harris type IV injuries.

Salter-Harris Classification (Physeal Injuries)

  • Salter-Harris fractures are epiphyseal plate (growth plate) injuries seen in children and adolescents, occurring before physeal closure.
  • They are clinically significant because damage to the physis can cause growth arrest, limb length discrepancy, or angular deformity.
    • Type I (Option A): Fracture through the physis only; epiphysis separates from metaphysis. Prognosis is excellent.
    • Type II (Option B) (most common): Fracture through physis + metaphysis; growth plate usually preserved. Good prognosis.
    • Type III (Option C): Fracture through physis + epiphysis, extending into the joint; may affect growth and joint surface.
    • Type IV: Fracture through metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis; high risk of growth disturbance.
    • Type V: Crush injury to the physis; often radiologically occult initially, and has the worst prognosis.


Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 750, 785
question: A child presents with a displaced fracture of the lateral condyle of the humerus. Which Salter‑Harris classification does this fracture typically represent?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In a pulled elbow, the child holds the arm with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated, resisting supination.

Pulled Elbow (Nursemaid’s Elbow)

  • Pulled elbow, also called nursemaid’s elbow, is a subluxation of the radial head due to displacement of the annular ligament.
  • Age group: Common in children aged 1-5 years, rare after 7 years as the ligament strengthens.
  • Mechanism: Occurs due to sudden longitudinal traction on the pronated, extended forearm (e.g., pulling a child by the hand).
  • Pathophysiology: The annular ligament slips over the radial head and becomes interposed between the radius and capitellum.
  • Clinical features: Child presents with sudden pain and the arm is held more or less immobile with the elbow fully extended and the forearm pronated; any attempt to supinate the forearm is resisted
  • Examination: Local tenderness may be present, but neurovascular status is normal.
  • Imaging: X-ray is usually normal and not routinely required unless a fracture is suspected.
  • Management: Treated by closed reduction-supination-flexion or hyperpronation manoeuvre.
  • Prognosis: Excellent; child regains arm use within minutes.


Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 387

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Posterior dislocation accounts for over 90% of elbow dislocations, typically resulting from a fall on an outstretched hand with the elbow extended.

Posterior Elbow Dislocation

  • Posterior elbow dislocation is the displacement of the ulna (± radius) posteriorly relative to the distal humerus; it is the most common elbow dislocation.
  • Mechanism of injury: Usually due to a fall on an outstretched hand with the elbow in extension, causing axial load and valgus stress.
  • Anatomy involved: Disruption of the capsule, lateral collateral ligament complex, and sometimes the medial collateral ligament.
  • Clinical features: Severe pain, swelling, and gross deformity with the elbow held in slight flexion; loss of normal elbow contour.
  • Neurovascular status: Ulnar nerve is commonly involved
  • Associated injuries: May include coronoid fracture, radial head fracture, or epicondylar fractures.
  • Diagnosis: Confirmed on AP and lateral X-rays showing posterior displacement of the ulna.
  • Management: Urgent closed reduction, followed by short immobilisation and early mobilisation.
  • Complications: Stiffness, recurrent instability, heterotopic ossification, and neurovascular injury.


Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 779
question: What is the most common type of elbow dislocation?

correctAnswer: B. Rupture of the extensor pollicis longus tendon
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Rupture of the extensor pollicis longus tendon is a late complication of Colles fracture, due to tendon ischemia or attrition over the fracture site, leading to loss of thumb interphalangeal joint extension.

Colles’ Fracture

  • Colles’ fracture is an extra-articular fracture of the distal radius, occurring about 2-3 cm proximal to the wrist joint, with dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation of the distal fragment.
  • Mechanism of injury: Commonly caused by a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with the wrist in extension.
  • Epidemiology: Seen most frequently in elderly patients, especially postmenopausal women, due to osteoporosis.
  • Clinical features: Pain, swelling, tenderness around the wrist, and characteristic “dinner-fork” or “silver-fork” deformity due to dorsal tilt.
  • Associated injuries: May be associated with ulnar styloid fracture, median nerve compression, or carpal instability.
  • Radiological features: X-ray shows dorsal displacement, dorsal angulation, radial shortening, and impaction of the distal radius.
  • Management: Treated by closed reduction and cast immobilisation; unstable fractures may require surgical fixation.
  • Complications: Malunion, stiffness, carpal tunnel syndrome, EPL rupture and post-traumatic arthritis.

Radial nerve injury (Option A): Radial nerve palsy causes wrist and finger extension weakness, not an isolated inability to extend the thumb IP joint, weeks after a Colles fracture.

Carpal tunnel syndrome (Option C): Involves median nerve compression, leading to sensory symptoms and thenar weakness, not loss of thumb IP extension.

Malunion causing mechanical block (Option D): Malunion may restrict wrist movement, but it does not selectively block thumb IP extension.



Reference:

Textbook of Orthopedics by Ebnezar, 5th Edition, Page 631

question: A patient who sustained a Colles fracture 6 weeks ago now presents with the inability to extend the thumb at the interphalangeal joint. The most likely cause is:

correctAnswer: B. Traction → Palmar flexion → Ulnar deviation → POP
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Traction is first applied to disimpact the fracture fragments against counter-traction. The distal fragment is then brought into palmar flexion and ulnar deviation to correct dorsal displacement, followed by immobilisation in a Colles’ cast (POP).

Colles’ Fracture Treatment

  • Initial assessment: Evaluate neurovascular status, skin integrity, and associated injuries; obtain AP and lateral wrist X-rays.
  • Pain control: Provide analgesia and usually a hematoma block or short general anaesthesia before reduction.
  • Closed reduction: Reduction is done by traction, then palmar flexion and ulnar deviation (with or without correction of rotation), followed by casting.
  • Immobilisation: Apply a below-elbow plaster cast with wrist in palmar flexion and ulnar deviation for stability.
  • Post-reduction check: Repeat X-ray to confirm acceptable alignment (radial height, radial inclination, volar tilt).
  • Follow-up: Regular radiographs (1 and 2 weeks) to detect redisplacement, especially in elderly patients.
  • Surgical management: Indicated for unstable, comminuted, intra-articular, or redisplaced fractures; options include percutaneous K-wires, external fixation, or volar locking plate.
  • Rehabilitation: Start finger movements immediately; after cast removal, begin wrist physiotherapy to restore motion and strength.


Reference:

Textbook of Orthopedics by Ebnezar, 5th Edition, Page 624

question: A 65-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after a fall on an outstretched hand. X-ray shows a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture consistent with a Colles’ fracture. Closed reduction is planned. What is the correct sequence of movements during the reduction of a Colles’ fracture before application of a plaster cast?

correctAnswer: C. Open reduction and internal fixation of the radius with a plate
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In adults, Galeazzi fracture‑dislocation requires open reduction and internal fixation of the radial shaft fracture with a compression plate; this usually reduces the distal radioulnar joint.
  • A Galeazzi fracture-dislocation is a fracture of the distal or middle third of the radius associated with disruption or dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ).
  • Mechanism of injury:Usually due to a fall on an outstretched hand with rotational force (pronation or supination), causing radial shaft fracture with DRUJ disruption
  • Epidemiology: More common in adults; considered an unstable injury pattern.
  • Clinical features: Pain, swelling, and deformity of the forearm; tenderness over the DRUJ, restricted forearm rotation, and possible ulnar head prominence.
  • Radiological findings: X-ray shows radial shaft fracture with signs of DRUJ disruption, such as ulnar styloid fracture, widened DRUJ, or dorsal/volar displacement of ulna.
  • Management: Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of the radius with a plate is the standard treatment; DRUJ stability is assessed post-fixation.
  • Complications: DRUJ instability, malunion, non-union, and reduced forearm rotation.

Closed reduction and casting (Option A): In adults, Galeazzi fractures are inherently unstable, and closed treatment leads to high rates of malunion and persistent DRUJ instability.

Closed reduction with percutaneous K-wire fixation (Option B): K-wires do not provide adequate rotational and length stability of the radial shaft and are insufficient in adult patients.

Isolated fixation of the distal radioulnar joint (Option D): The primary pathology is the radial shaft fracture; DRUJ instability usually reduces spontaneously after anatomical fixation of the radius.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 794

Explanation:

  • Reverse (volar) Barton’s fracture is usually caused by axial load on a flexed wrist, leading to shearing of the volar rim
  • The volar lip fragment stays aligned with the carpus (maintains articular contact), and both displace together volarly.

Reverse (Volar) Barton’s Fracture

  • Intra-articular fracture of the distal radius involving the volar rim, with the carpus displaced volarly along with the fragment.
  • Mechanism: Usually due to axial load on a flexed wrist producing a volar rim shear fracture.
  • Radiographic Features:
    • Volar rim fragment with volar subluxation of the carpus
    • Intra-articular involvement with volar rim fracture.
    • The articular surface may remain in contact with the carpus.
  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Volar wrist swelling, pain, and deformity.
    • Limited wrist motion.
    • Possible median nerve compression if the fragment displaces.
  • Treatment:
    • Open reduction and volar plate fixation are preferred for stability.
    • Conservative casting is usually not recommended due to instability.
  • Complications:
    • Malunion, post-traumatic arthritis, chronic pain.
    • Median nerve injury if the volar fragment compresses the nerve.

Colles’ fracture (Option A): Extra-articular fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the distal fragment - does not involve the volar rim or intra-articular displacement, so this is incorrect.

Smith’s fracture (Option B): Extra-articular distal radius fracture with volar displacement, but the articular surface is not involved separately, unlike in Barton’s fracture.

Dorsal Barton’s fracture (Option C): Intra-articular fracture of the dorsal rim of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the carpus, opposite to this case.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 800

question: A 32-year-old man presents after a fall on a flexed wrist with wrist pain and swelling. He has pain on dorsiflexion of the wrist. Radiographs of the wrist are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Tension band wiring is the preferred technique for displaced, non‑comminuted transverse olecranon fractures because it converts distracting forces into compressive forces.
  • Olecranon fractures involve the proximal ulna at the elbow, often caused by direct trauma or a fall on an outstretched hand.
    • Clinical Features: Pain, swelling, loss of elbow extension, palpable step deformity, and sometimes comminution.
    • Indication for Surgery: Displaced fractures (>2 mm), loss of extension, or comminuted fractures.
    • Tension Band Wiring Principle: Converts tensile forces from the triceps into compressive forces at the fracture site during elbow movement.
    • Technique:
      • Fracture reduction and K-wire fixation.
      • A figure-of-eight stainless steel wire passed through the olecranon and around K-wires.
      • Wire tightened to achieve stable compression.
    • Advantages: Early mobilisation, good functional recovery, minimal hardware if properly placed.
    • Complications: Wire migration, infection, non-union, hardware irritation, and, rarely, elbow stiffness.
    • Post-op Care: Early range-of-motion exercises while protecting fracture stability.

Non‑operative immobilisation (Option A): Only suitable for non-displaced fractures; a displaced fracture in an active adult risks loss of extension, so immobilisation is inadequate.

Plate fixation (Option C): Reserved for comminuted or unstable fractures, not simple transverse fractures.

Olecranon excision with triceps advancement (Option D): Rarely indicated; used for severely comminuted fractures or failed fixation, not primary management.



Reference:

Textbook of Orthopedics by Ebnezar, 5th Edition, Page 150

Hippocrates technique (Option A) is an outdated method for shoulder dislocation reduction. The surgeon pulls firmly on the semi-abducted arm while placing a foot in the axilla, using it as a fulcrum to guide the humeral head back into place.

Milch technique (Option C) involves manipulating the humeral head by applying traction to the arm, combined with external rotation and abduction, facilitating the repositioning of the humeral head into the glenoid cavity.

question: A 32-year-old male arrives at the emergency department with severe right shoulder pain after a fall during a workout. His shoulder appears deformed, with swelling and bruising. An orthopaedic manoeuvre is performed, as shown in the image. What is the name of this technique?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario of a fall onto the shoulder with tenderness and swelling, as well as the X-ray findings, points towards a left clavicle fracture.
  • Clavicular fracture most commonly occurs at the junction of the middle two-third and outer (lateral) thirds of the clavicle. This area is most vulnerable to injury due to the natural curvature of the bone and the forces exerted during trauma.
  • It is the most common bone to be fractured in children.
  • Displacement:
    • The outer fragment tends to displace medially and downward due to gravity and the pull of the pectoralis major muscle.
    • The inner fragment displaces upward because of the sternocleidomastoid muscle's pull.

Radiographs: The following views are recommended for evaluating clavicle fractures:

  • Routine Anteroposterior (AP) View of the clavicle.

  • Lordotic View if the fracture is uncertain.

  • Special Radiographic Techniques like CT Scans are required for assessing the distal clavicle.
  • Findings:
    • Fracture Line: A clear line usually located in the middle third of the clavicle.
    • Displacement of Fragments
    • Overlapping Fragments: D/t muscle pull
    • No Medullary Cavity

Early Complications

Management of Clavicular Fracture:

  • Clavicle fractures typically heal well; fragment reduction is not necessary, even if displaced.
  • For minimal displacement, a triangular sling is adequate.
  • Active shoulder exercises should begin once severe pain diminishes, usually around 10-14 days post-injury.

Figure-of-‘8’ bandage (Option A): This provides immobilisation and pain relief for young adults with displaced fractures and is not preferred for age <2 years.

question: A one-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after a fall, and the caregiver reports mild pain over the right shoulder while the child remains active. An X-ray is provided. What is the most appropriate treatment option for managing this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Among the given options, the Capsule (marked as c) serves as a static stabilizer of the shoulder joint, while the Supraspinatus(a), the long head of the biceps(d), and Teres minor(b) act as dynamic stabilizers.

Shoulder Joint: (Glenohumeral joint)

  • It is formed by the articulation of the head of the humerus with the glenoid cavity of the scapula.
  • While it is the most mobile joint in the body, its wide range of motion contributes to its instability, resulting in a high risk of dislocations.

Static Stabilizers

Dynamic Stabilizers
  • Glenoid labrum: Enhances stability by deepening the glenoid cavity.
  • Glenohumeral ligaments (Superior, Middle, and Inferior Ligaments) form the glenohumeral joint capsule (c), connecting the glenoid fossa to the humerus.
  • Coracoclavicular ligament
  • Coracohumeral ligament
  • Long Head of the Biceps Tendon (d): Provides stability and support.
  • Rotator Cuff Muscles:
    • Supraspinatus (a): Assists in the abduction and stabilises the head of the humerus.
    • Infraspinatus: External rotation and stabilisation.
    • Teres Minor (b): External rotation and stabilisation.
    • Subscapularis: Internal rotation and stabilization.
  • Deltoid (Option D): It facilitates arm movements such as abduction, flexion, and rotation while stabilizing the shoulder joint.
  • Periscapular muscles: Stabilize the scapula & shoulder joint during movement.

Acromioclavicular joint dislocation (Option C): A fall onto the shoulder with the arm adducted can strain or tear the acromioclavicular ligaments, leading to dislocation. It presents with severe pain and a palpable "step." A comparative X-ray of both sides aids in diagnosis, and surgical management is often necessary.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 762- 766.

Tests of Shoulder dislocation

Measures the distance from the acromion to the lateral epicondyle with the arm in a neutral position. A lack of gap between the arm and the ruler indicates dislocation.

The inability to touch the opposite shoulder with a shoulder dislocation is typically observed in anterior dislocations.

[[figure-2]]

The circumference of the axilla is checked bilaterally using a measuring tape. An increased circumference on the affected side is diagnostic of dislocation.

[[figure-3]]

It involves observing the anterior axillary fold, displaced inferiorly on the affected side in shoulder dislocation.

Loss of sensation over the deltoid on the affected side due to axillary nerve damage.

question: A 36-year-old male with shoulder pain and recurrent anterior dislocations reports instability and weakness during overhead activities. An X-ray is advised. What lesion was observed?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Based on the clinical presentation and mechanism of injury, a subcoracoid dislocation is suspected. This is the most common type of anterior shoulder dislocation, where the humeral head typically displaces forward and downward toward the coracoid process.

Anterior Shoulder dislocation

Subtypes
  • Subglenoid (Option C): The humeral head lies below the glenoid fossa.
  • Subclavicular (Option B): The humeral head is displaced beneath the clavicle.
  • Intrathoracic(Option A): The humeral head dislocates into the thoracic cavity, which is rare.
  • Subcoracoid (Option D): The humeral head lies below the coracoid process.

[[figure-1]]

Clinical findings
  • Loss of the deltoid contour (loss of shoulder roundness)
  • The shoulder is extended, abducted and externally rotated.

Clinical tests
  • Duga’s test is the inability to touch the opposite shoulder.
  • Hamilton ruler test is where the gap between the ruler and the arm is lost.
  • Callaway’s test is increased girth of the axilla on the dislocated side.
  • Bryant’s Test is where the anterior axillary fold is displaced downward on the affected side.
  • Regiment batch sign is loss of sensation due to axillary nerve damage.

Imaging
  • X-ray reveals that the humeral head is displaced anteriorly and inferiorly, often under the coracoid process ("subcoracoid" position)
  • An MRI is necessary to assess soft-tissue injuries and identify Bankart and Hill-Sachs lesions, which are complications of shoulder dislocations and increase the risk of recurrence due to joint instability.

[[figure-2]]

Management
  • Kocher's method (Most common method) is the reduction by traction, external rotation, adduction, and medial rotation.
  • In Hippocrates' method, the surgeon pulls the semi-abducted arm firmly while using his foot in the axilla as a fulcrum to reduce the dislocation.
  • Stimson’s technique is the reduction by applying weight for traction, using the body as counter traction.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 762, 763.
question: A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a motorcycle accident with severe pain and immobility in his right shoulder. Examination reveals a flattened shoulder, and he is unable to abduct or externally rotate the arm. An X-ray was taken. What type of dislocation is suspected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Recurrent shoulder dislocation is the most common complication following an initial dislocation.
  • It occurs due to repeated trauma, capsular laxity, bone changes, muscle weakness, inadequate rehabilitation, or high-risk activities.
  • Hill-Sachs and Bankart lesions, associated with shoulder dislocations, contribute to joint instability and increase the risk of recurrence.

Complications of Shoulder Dislocation:

Early Complications

Delayed Complications
  • Rotator cuff tear - Common in the elderly due to degenerative changes in the tendons and less common in younger patients. (Option B)
  • Axillary artery injury - Rare; Occurs with severe trauma (Option B)
  • Nerve injury - The axillary nerve is most commonly affected; other nerve injuries and complete brachial plexus palsy are rare. (Option A)
  • Recurrence - Most common, due to instability.
  • Joint stiffness - Results from prolonged immobility.
  • Unreduced dislocation - Due to missed or undiagnosed dislocation.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 763, 764, 386.

question: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency after a soccer match with severe right shoulder pain following a fall. He reports a "pop" in his shoulder and is unable to lift his arm or touch the opposite shoulder. An X-ray has been taken. What is the appropriate management for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario with X-ray findings points towards a right Clavicular fracture, most commonly caused by a fall directly onto the shoulder.

Clavicle or Collarbone:

  • It is a long, slightly S-shaped bone located horizontally at the junction of the neck and trunk. It articulates medially with the sternum and the cartilage of the first rib and laterally with the acromion process of the scapula.
  • Structural features: It is the only long bone that lies horizontally, does not contain a medullary cavity, and remains subcutaneous along its entire length.
  • Ossification:
    • It is the first bone to begin ossifying (between the fifth and sixth week of fetal development) and the last to finish ossification (around 25 years of age).
    • It is the only long bone that ossifies from two primary centers.
    • It primarily ossifies in the membrane, except for its medial end, which ossifies in cartilage (unlike other long bones).

Mechanism of Injury:

  • Fall on the shoulder: The most common mechanism is a fall directly onto the point of the shoulder, accounting for 91% of cases.

Direct injury (Option A):
Incorrect because direct trauma (such as a blow or impact over the clavicle) is a less common mechanism than indirect force from a shoulder fall.

Fall onto an outstretched hand (Option B):
Incorrect because this mechanism typically causes scaphoid fractures, distal radius fractures, or shoulder dislocations, not clavicle fractures.

Fall from a height (Option D):
Incorrect because while it can result in clavicle fractures, it is not the most common cause. It usually leads to multiple injuries, and the clavicle is not selectively involved unless the person lands on their shoulder.



Reference:

Vishram Singh, Textbook of Anatomy, Upper Limb & Thorax, 2nd Edition, Page 11

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 755
question: A 26-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with severe pain and tenderness after sustaining an injury from a fall. An X-ray of the region is provided below. Considering the mechanisms of injury, what is the most common cause associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation: The scenario along with the attitude showing abducted arm above the head with external rotation suggests Inferior shoulder dislocation.

The Sulcus sign is specifically designed to assess inferior shoulder instability by evaluating the presence of a gap between the humeral head and the acromion. A positive sulcus sign indicates inferior instability or laxity in the shoulder joint.

Tests for shoulder instability:

a) Anterior instability

Test

Description

Image

Apprehension test

(Option D)

With the patient seated or supine, the examiner abducts the arm and externally rotates it. The patient may feel the humeral head about to slip anteriorly, leading to tension and apprehension.

Fulcrum test

(Option A)

With the patient lying supine and the arm abducted to 90°, the examiner uses one hand behind the shoulder as a fulcrum to lever the humeral head forward by extending and laterally rotating the arm, leading to immediate apprehension.

Crank test

With the arm flexed at 90°, the examiner applies an axial load to the humerus and rotates it while elevating the shoulder.

A positive test shows pain or a clicking sensation.

Jobe’s relocation test (or) Supraspinatus test

(Option B)

Positioning the shoulder at 90° of abduction and 30° of forward flexion with the thumb down, resistance testing reveals supraspinatus weakness, indicating a possible tear or rotator cuff impingement.

Surprise test

In the relocation test, a posterior force is applied to the humeral head and then suddenly released. The test is considered positive if the patient experiences apprehension or fear of dislocation.

b) Posterior instability:

Jerk test: With the patient seated, the examiner stabilises the scapula while abducting and internally rotating the arm. Applying axial and horizontal adduction forces, sharp pain or a clunk indicates a positive test.

c) Inferior instability:

Sulcus test (Option C): With the arm at 0 and 45 degrees of abduction, the examiner pulls distally, checking for a sulcus or dimple between the humeral head and acromion that persists with external rotation.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 368, 369.

Campbell’s Operative Orthopaedics, 14th Edition, Page 2443
question: A 30-year-old male presents with recurrent shoulder dislocations after playing basketball & shows the attitude as shown in the image. Which of the following tests is specifically used to assess this shoulder instability?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The X-ray is suggestive of a proximal humerus (surgical neck) fracture, common in elderly after falls.
  • Mechanism here is direct fall on the shoulder, as given in the history (not FOOSH).
  • The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of humerus, making it the most vulnerable.
  • Injury leads to deltoid weakness + loss of shoulder abduction (15–90°).
  • Also causes sensory loss over regimental badge area.

FOOSH, Axillary nerve: Axillary nerve fits dislocation, but mechanism is wrong (no FOOSH in history)

FOOSH, Radial nerve (Option B):

  • FOOSH → more typical for shoulder dislocation, not this fracture pattern
  • Radial nerve → associated with shaft fractures, not proximal humerus

Direct trauma, Radial nerve (Option C): Mechanism may fit, but wrong nerve (radial nerve not related to surgical neck)



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pg no, 766-769.

question: A 55-year-old female fell on her left shoulder while walking and now presents with severe pain, swelling, and bruising. Based on the X-ray shown below, what is the most common mechanism of injury and the likely affected structure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario describes a humeral shaft fracture, with management options including a U-slab, hanging cast, and plate osteosynthesis. However, a Velpeau bandage is used for proximal humerus fractures, not shaft fractures.

Management of fracture of shaft of the humerus:

a) Conservative management

Type

Description

Image

U-slab

(Option A)
  • Supported with a triangular sling
  • Moulded on the lateral side of the arm (prevent lateral angulation)

Hanging arm cast

(Option B)
  • Used in lower 1/3rd fractures of the humerus
  • The limb's weight and the cast provide traction to keep the fracture aligned.

Chest-arm bandage
  • The arm is strapped to the chest

b) Surgical management:

Technique

Description

Image

Internal fixation with plate and screw

It consists of:

  • Compression plate and screws
  • Interlocking intramedullary nail or semi-flexible pins
  • External fixator

Minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis (MIPO)

(Option D)
  • The plate is placed over the comminution without disturbing the fragments, and no graft is utilised.
  • Fracture alignment is preserved without compression.

Russell-Taylors (RT) nailing technique

This procedure avoids radial nerve injury (wrist drop).

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 767-769.
question: A 29-year-old boxer received a blow to his arm and presented to the emergency department with severe pain, swelling, and deformity in his left upper arm. He reports difficulty moving his elbow and hand and weakness in his wrist. An X-ray was taken. All the following are management options for this condition except?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given X-ray image depicts 2 part fracture of Neer’s classification which says 1 displaced part with fracture line involving 2 or 3 parts.
  • Neer’s classification of Proximal humerus fractures is based on the number of displaced fragments, where displacement is angulation > 45° or a separation > 1 cm and is helpful in guiding the treatment decisions.
  • The four parts of the proximal humerus are
    • Greater tuberosity
    • Lesser tuberosity
    • Head of the humerus
    • Shaft of the humerus

Neer’s Classification

Management

1 Part Fracture

The fracture line involves 1 part and no displacement.

Conservative with an arm sling for 6 weeks, followed by exercises.

  • Triangular arm sling

  • Velpeau bandage

2 Part Fracture

The fracture line involves two parts and displacement of 1 part.
  • Surgical neck displacement: Closed reduction and immobilization with arm-sling or k-wire.
  • Greater tuberosity displaced (mostly associated with shoulder dislocation): Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF).
  • In anatomical neck fractures,
    • Older patients: Hemiarthroplasty (replacement of the humeral head)

3 Part Fracture

The fracture line involves 3 parts and displacement of 2 parts.

Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with Proximal humerus interlocking system plate (PHILOS).

4 Part Fracture

The fracture line involves all 4 parts and displacement of 3 parts.

(High chances of avascular necrosis).

Arthroplasty with shoulder joint replacement.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 766 - 768
question: A 48-year-old female fell on her outstretched right hand and reported shoulder pain. A bruise was noted during the examination, and an X-ray was performed. How would you classify this fracture according to Neer's classification based on the X-ray findings?

correctAnswer: B. Junction of the middle and distal third
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This fracture, known as a Holstein-Lewis fracture, typically occurs at the junction of the middle and distal third of the humeral shaft and is associated with radial nerve injury, leading to wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand.
  • Mechanism of injury: Fall on outstretched hand or direct trauma to the arm.

Management:

  • Conservative: There is no role for conservative management in Holstein-lewis fracture
  • The treatment of choice is emergency decompression
  • For stable fractures, the initial management may include:
    • U-slab or Hanging cast
    • Chest arm bandage to immobilise the arm
  • Surgical Intervention: In cases of displaced fractures or complicated cases:
    • Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF)
    • Intramedullary nailing
    • Compression plating and screws
    • External fixation
  • Dynamic cock-up splint is used primarily to support the wrist and hand while allowing for some movement. It is designed to maintain the wrist in a neutral position (slightly extended) while permitting the fingers to flex and extend.
  • Nerve damage is usually temporary, but in case of open fractures exploration might be needed.

[[figure-1]]

Supracondylar region (Option A): Fractures in the supracondylar region typically affect the median nerve, leading to symptoms such as weakness in wrist flexion and the "hand of benediction" sign. These fractures are more common in children and are less likely to cause wrist drop.

Junction of the proximal and middle third (Option C) & Surgical neck of the humerus (Option D): Fractures at these locations primarily affect the axillary nerve. This results in weakness of the deltoid muscle, causing difficulty in arm abduction and sensory loss over the lateral shoulder.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 772

options.text: Junction of the middle and distal third
Junction of the proximal and middle third

question: A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department with severe pain in his left upper arm and wrist drop after a fall while playing football. Examination reveals weakness in wrist extension and numbness over the dorsum of his hand. Radiographs show a humeral fracture. Which part of the humerus is most likely involved in this fracture?

correctAnswer: C. Bony relationship is unaffected by elbow fractures.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The X-ray shows a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, where the three-point bony relationship is usually normal (Option D) due to the fracture's location above the elbow joint or minimal displacement.
  • In a normally flexed elbow at 90°, these three bony points form a nearly isosceles triangle (Option A).

  • The three-point bony relationship consists of the medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and tip of the olecranon (Option B), which is crucial for diagnosing elbow injuries
  • It shows increased intercondylar distance in lateral epicondyle fractures
  • Supracondylar fractures are more common in children, with a higher incidence in boys.

Type of Injury

Supracondylar Fracture

Elbow Dislocation

Frequency

Common fracture in children

Common dislocation in children

Mechanism of injury

Fall on outstretched hand, hyperextension

Fall on outstretched hand, posterior force on flexed elbow

Three bony points relationship

Maintained

Reversed (Option B)
(Bowstringing of Triceps tendon)

Length of forearm

Normal

Shorter

Types

Gartland classification (3 types: I, II, III)

No specific classification

Nerve damage

Anterior interosseous nerve

Median nerve

X-ray

Anterior humeral line displaced, visible fracture.

Dislocation of radius and ulna with displaced humeral condyle.

Complications and Deformities
  • Compartment syndrome (Volkmann's ischemic contracture)
  • Brachial artery injury
  • Gunstock deformity (cubitus varus) in untreated cases.
  • Medial collateral ligament (MCL) or lateral collateral ligament (LCL) damage resulting in recurrent dislocations or subluxations.
  • Posterior olecranon deformity (abnormal prominence of the olecranon process)



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Pages 781, 782

question: An 11-year-old girl is brought to the clinic after falling on her outstretched hand, resulting in severe pain in her left elbow. The examination shows swelling and tenderness in the elbow, and she is reluctant to move her arm. An x-ray has been taken. Which of the following is false regarding the 3 bony point relationship in this fracture?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation and X-ray suggest a supracondylar humerus fracture, which commonly affects the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve.
  • This nerve innervates the flexor pollicis longus and the lateral half of the flexor digitorum profundus, which is responsible for flexing the distal phalanx of the index and middle fingers. Weakness in thumb opposition and forearm pronation further indicates this nerve's involvement.

Supracondylar Fractures

Mechanism of injury

Fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH)

Location

Humerus fractures just above the condyles.

Displacements

The distal fragment of the humerus is usually displaced by

  • Posterior shift (Due to Impaction)
  • Posterior Tilt
  • Proximal shift
  • Medial shift/ Tilt
  • Internal rotation

Types
  • Type 1: Undisplaced fracture
  • Type 2: Partially displaced fracture with displacement of only anterior cortex
  • Type 3: Completely displaced anterior and posterior cortex.

Clinical Presentation
  • Severe elbow pain, swelling, deformity, and loss of function may occur, and neurological symptoms like weakness in wrist flexion or the "hand of benediction" sign may also occur if the median nerve is affected.
  • Unusual posterior prominence of the olecranon in the backward tilt (S-shaped deformity)
  • The skin around the fracture has a dimpled appearance (Dimple sign)

X-ray Findings
  • Three bony parts relationship is maintained.
  • Fat Pad or Sail sign: A translucent shadow-like appearance representing anterior and posterior fat pads.

  • Disturbed tear drop sign: An abnormal appearance of the fat pad, suggesting the presence of an injury, such as a fracture or joint effusion.

  • Fishtail sign: The ends of the proximal fragment are slightly widened and serrated, resembling a fishtail.

  • Crescent sign: The normal radiolucent gap of the elbow joint is replaced by a crescent-shaped shadow from the capitulum overlapping the olecranon, indicating varus or valgus tilt of the distal fragment.

Management

Based on the type of fracture

  • Undisplaced fracture: Immobilisation in above-elbow plaster slab with the elbow in 90-degree flexion.
  • Displaced fractures
    • Closed reduction with percutaneous K-wire fixation. (for Type 2 fracture)
    • Open reduction internal fixation with K-wire. (for Type 3 fracture)
  • In Late presentation with swelling
    • Dunlop traction (skin)
    • Smith traction (skeletal)

Complications
  • Early complications
    • Vascular injury (commonly Brachial artery)
    • Nerve injury (commonly Anterior Interosseous nerve)
  • Delayed complications
    • Cubitus varus or Gunstock deformity (Malunion)
    • Volkmann's Ischemia and compartment syndrome.
    • Elbow stiffness
    • Myositis ossificans.

Radial nerve (Option A) deficit typically results in loss of sensation over the posterior aspect of the arm, forearm, and part of the hand, particularly the dorsal surface of the thumb and index finger, and it's very rarely affected in supracondylar fracture.

Posterior interosseous nerve (Option B) is a branch of the radial nerve, it innervates the extensor muscles of the forearm. Damage causes wrist drop but does not affect thumb opposition or flexor function.

Ulnar nerve (Option C) results in loss of sensation over the medial aspect of the hand, including the little finger and half of the ring finger, along with the corresponding palmar area, but it does not impact the index and middle fingers or forearm pronation.



Reference:

Maheshwari’s Essential Orthopedics, 5th edition, Pages 52, 101, 102

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Pages 783, 784
question: An 18-year-old male presents with difficulty flexing the distal phalanx of her index and middle fingers, along with weakness in thumb opposition and forearm pronation. He also reports pain, swelling, and limited movement in his elbow following a fall on his left hand. An X-ray was taken. Which of the following nerves is commonly affected in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The radiograph shows an extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus, the most common elbow fracture associated with injury to the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), a pure motor branch of the median nerve.

  • AIN supplies:
    • Flexor pollicis longus (FPL)
    • Flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger (and often the middle finger)
    • Pronator quadratus
  • Patients have difficulty making the "OK" sign because they cannot flex the distal phalanx of the thumb and index finger.
  • There is no sensory loss, as the AIN has no cutaneous sensory distribution.
  • Clinical Features
    • Pain and swelling around the elbow
    • Deformity with restricted elbow movement
    • Positive anterior and/or posterior fat pad (sail) sign on lateral radiographs

[[figure-1]]

    • Preserved relationship of the three bony points around the elbow
  • Management
    • Gartland Type I: Immobilisation in an above-elbow cast or splint.
    • Gartland Type II and III: Closed reduction and percutaneous K-wire fixation (CRPP) is the standard treatment.
  • Complications
    • Early
      • Brachial artery injury
      • Anterior interosseous nerve palsy (most common nerve injury)
      • Compartment syndrome
    • Late
      • Cubitus varus (gunstock deformity)
      • Volkmann ischemic contracture
      • Elbow stiffness

Radial nerve (Option A): Injury causes wrist and finger extension weakness (wrist drop) with sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand. It is less commonly injured in supracondylar fractures.

Posterior interosseous nerve (Option B): A motor branch of the radial nerve supplying the forearm extensors. Injury produces finger extension weakness without sensory loss and does not impair thumb-index pinch.

Ulnar nerve (Option C): Injury causes weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles with sensory loss over the little finger and medial half of the ring finger. It is more commonly associated with flexion-type supracondylar fractures or medial pin placement.



Reference:
  1. Maheshwari’s Essential Orthopaedics, 5th Edition, Pages 52, 101, 102
  2. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Pages 783, 784

question: A 9-year-old boy fell on his outstretched hand and was presented with pain, swelling and restricted movement of the elbow, along with an S-shaped deformity. An X-ray was performed; What is the most common type of below fracture diagnosed?

correctAnswer: C. Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The scenario of a fall on an outstretched hand, with an X-ray showing a supracondylar fracture of the humerus and completely displaced fractures, indicates a Type III Gartland fracture.
  • Management involves closed reduction followed by percutaneous pinning for stabilization

[[figure-1]]

Gartland Classification of Supracondylar Fractures

Type I

Nondisplaced fractures.

Long arm cast immobilisation

(Option A) for 3 weeks, followed by a period of protected activity

[[figure-2]]

Type II

Fracture with an intact posterior hinge.

Type IIA

Stable fractures with no significant

translation or rotation

Closed reduction & casting (Option B)

Closed reduction and percutaneous K-wire fixation

[[figure-3]]

Closed reduction and pinning

Open reduction (Option D) is indicated in supracondylar fractures when there is failed closed reduction, compound or comminuted fractures, or when brachial artery exploration is needed due to suspected vascular injury.

question: A 6-year-old child presents to the emergency department after falling onto an outstretched hand. X-ray shows the following findings. What is the most appropriate management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The child's presentation with the head tilt and mass over the sternocleidomastoid suggests Congenital Torticollis.
  • Plagiocephaly, characterised by an asymmetrical head shape, is commonly associated with congenital torticollis due to the child's consistent head position.

Deformities associated with Congenital Torticollis:

[[figure-1]]

  • These features worsen & become more evident as the child grows.
  • Cervicothoracic Scoliosis (Option C) may be rarely associated with Congenital Torticollis.
  • Kyphosis (Option B) & Lordosis (Option D) are not generally associated with congenital torticollis.

question: A 6-month-old child with a noticeable head tilt is found to have a mass over the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The clinician is considering potential secondary deformities that may develop due to the condition. Which of the following deformities is most commonly associated with the condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Kienböck’s disease is due to avascular necrosis of the lunate, presenting with progressive wrist pain, stiffness, and increased lunate sclerosis on X-ray.
  • Etiology: Caused by compromised blood supply to the lunate; associated with negative ulnar variance, trauma, or repetitive loading.
  • Epidemiology: Common in young adults (20-40 years), more frequent in manual labourers.
  • Pathophysiology: Ischemia leads to lunate sclerosis, collapse, and fragmentation, followed by secondary carpal instability.
  • Clinical Features: Presents with dorsal wrist pain, swelling, reduced grip strength, and restricted wrist movements.
  • Imaging: X-ray shows lunate sclerosis/collapse; MRI detects early ischemic changes.
  • Staging: Classified by Lichtman stages (I-IV) based on radiologic progression.
  • Management: Early stages-immobilization or revascularization; advanced stages-radial shortening, proximal row carpectomy, or wrist fusion.

Sever disease (Option A): A traction apophysitis of the calcaneal apophysis in children, causing heel pain, not wrist pathology.

Köhler disease (Option C): Avascular necrosis of the navicular bone of the foot in children, unrelated to the lunate or wrist.

Osgood-Schlatter disease (Option D): Traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in adolescents, presenting with knee pain, not wrist symptoms.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 413, 599, 640, 641, 643

question: A 35-year-old manual labourer presents with chronic wrist pain and stiffness. Examination reveals localised tenderness over the lunate. X-ray of the wrist as seen below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Jersey finger results from avulsion of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon from the distal phalanx, leading to loss of active DIP flexion, commonly seen in rugby and football players.
  • Mechanism of injury: Occurs due to forceful hyperextension of a flexed DIP joint, classically when a player grabs an opponent’s jersey.
  • Commonly affected finger: Ring finger is most commonly involved due to its anatomical length and weaker independent motion.
  • Clinical features: Pain and swelling over the volar aspect of the distal finger, inability to actively flex the DIP joint, and tenderness along the flexor sheath.
  • Examination finding: DIP joint rests in extension while PIP joint flexion is preserved.
  • Imaging: X-ray to detect avulsion fracture; ultrasound/ MRI to assess tendon retraction.
  • Management: Early surgical repair is the treatment of choice.

Mallet finger (Option A): Caused by extensor tendon injury at the DIP joint, leading to inability to extend the DIP - not flex - so this does not fit.

Boutonnière deformity (Option B): Involves central slip extensor tendon rupture, causing flexion of PIP and hyperextension of DIP, not isolated loss of DIP flexion.

Swan neck deformity (Option D): Characterised by hyperextension of PIP with flexion of DIP, usually a chronic deformity, not an acute traumatic presentation



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 821
lessonTitle: Upper Limb Trauma II & Congenital Torticollis
question: A 26-year-old rugby player presents with pain and swelling of the ring finger after grabbing an opponent’s jersey. On examination, he is unable to actively flex the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint of the affected finger. Passive flexion is possible. X-ray shows no fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Mallet finger - dorsal hyperextension splint
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Mallet finger is caused by disruption of the extensor tendon at the DIP joint, leading to a flexed fingertip with preserved passive extension.
  • It is best treated with continuous immobilisation in a dorsal hyperextension splint to allow tendon healing.
  • Mechanism: Commonly caused by sudden forced flexion of an extended fingertip (e.g., ball striking the finger).
  • Types:
    • Tendinous mallet: Rupture of extensor tendon without fracture.
    • Bony mallet: Avulsion fracture of the dorsal base of distal phalanx.
  • Clinical Features: Flexion deformity at DIP joint, pain, swelling, and inability to actively extend the fingertip.
  • Diagnosis: Primarily clinical, confirmed by X-ray to detect avulsion fracture or joint subluxation.
  • Treatment: Continuous splinting of DIP joint in extension for 6-8 weeks; surgery if large fracture fragment or volar subluxation.
  • Complications: Swan-neck deformity, residual extensor lag, and joint stiffness.

Jersey finger - surgical repair (Option A): Involves FDP tendon avulsion causing loss of DIP flexion, not extension.

Swan neck deformity - volar splinting (Option C): Characterised by PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion, usually a chronic deformity, not an acute injury.

Boutonniere deformity - PIP joint splint (Option D): Due to central slip injury, leading to PIP flexion and DIP hyperextension, opposite of this presentation.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 434
lessonTitle: Upper Limb Trauma II & Congenital Torticollis
question: A 30-year-old man presents after a cricket injury with the inability to actively extend the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint of the index finger, as given below. The fingertip rests in flexion, but passive extension is possible. X-ray shows no fracture. What is the most appropriate diagnosis and management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A chauffeur's fracture (or Hutchinson fracture) is an intra‑articular fracture of the radial styloid, historically associated with a backfire injury while cranking a car.
  • Mechanism of injury: Caused by direct axial compression of the scaphoid against the radial styloid, classically when a crank handle backfires.
  • Common causes today: Seen in road traffic accidents, falls on an outstretched hand, and sports injuries.
  • Anatomy involved: Involves the radial styloid, often extending into the radiocarpal joint.
  • Clinical features: Presents with pain, swelling, tenderness over radial wrist, and restricted wrist movements.
  • Associated injuries: May be associated with scaphoid fractures, ligament injuries, or carpal instability.
  • Radiology: X-ray shows vertical or oblique fracture line through radial styloid.
  • Treatment:
    • Undisplaced fractures → immobilization
    • Displaced fractures → ORIF with screws or K-wires.
  • Complications: Post-traumatic arthritis, malunion, and wrist stiffness if untreated.

[[figure-1]]

Barton fracture (Option A): An intra-articular fracture of the distal radius rim (volar or dorsal) with radiocarpal subluxation, not an isolated radial styloid fracture.

Smith fracture (Option C): A reverse Colles’ fracture with volar displacement of the distal radial fragment, not confined to the styloid.

Rolando fracture (Option D): A comminuted intra-articular fracture of the base of the first metacarpal, unrelated to the radius.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 800

question: A fracture, as shown below, of the radial styloid process is also known as:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The radiograph shows a fracture involving the radial styloid process of the distal radius. Such fractures are known as Chauffeur’s fracture, also called Hutchinson fracture.

  • Mechanism of injury: Caused by direct axial compression of the scaphoid against the radial styloid, classically when a crank handle backfires.
  • Common causes: Road traffic accidents, falls on an outstretched hand, and sports injuries.
  • Anatomy: Involves the radial styloid, often extending into the radiocarpal joint.
  • Clinical features: Presents with pain, swelling, tenderness over radial wrist, and restricted wrist movements.
  • Associated injuries: May be associated with scaphoid fractures, ligament injuries, or carpal instability.
  • Radiology: X-ray shows vertical or oblique fracture line through radial styloid.

  • Treatment:
    • Undisplaced fractures → immobilization
    • Displaced fractures → ORIF with screws or K-wires.
  • Complications: Post-traumatic arthritis, malunion, and wrist stiffness if untreated.

Barton fracture (Option A): An intra-articular fracture of the distal radius rim (volar or dorsal) with radiocarpal subluxation, not an isolated radial styloid fracture.

Smith fracture (Option C): A reverse Colles’ fracture with volar displacement of the distal radial fragment, not confined to the styloid.

Rolando fracture (Option D): A comminuted intra-articular fracture of the base of the first metacarpal, unrelated to the radius.
