question: A 67-year-old diabetic patient presented with swelling around the knee, restriction of movement and minimal or no pain. The x-ray of the knee is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Young male with lower backache and morning stiffness are suggestive of Ankylosing spondylitis.

Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) / Marie Strumpell Disease

Definition

Chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the axial skeleton (spine and sacroiliac joints), leading to pain, stiffness, and spinal fusion (bamboo spine).

Etiology

Idiopathic; genetic (HLA-B27) and environmental factors involved. HLA-B27 is positive in 90% of cases, but not all carriers develop AS.

Pathophysiology

Inflammation at entheses → Erosive changes → New bone formation → Syndesmophytes → Spinal fusion (ankylosis).

Clinical Features

Musculoskeletal Symptoms:

  • Chronic low back pain (worse after inactivity, better with activity)
  • Limited spinal mobility
  • Enthesitis (Achilles, plantar fascia)
  • Peripheral arthritis (hips, shoulders, knees)

Extra-articular Symptoms:

  • Ocular: Anterior uveitis (pain, redness, photophobia)
  • Cardiovascular: Aortic regurgitation, conduction issues
  • Pulmonary: Apical fibrosis
  • Gastrointestinal: Associated with IBD

Clinical tests:

  • Schober/ Modified Schober test (for lumbar spine)
  • Gaenslen’s test
  • Patrick/FABER test
  • Figure of 4 test
  • Pump handle test

Diagnosis

Based on clinical features, imaging studies, and HLA-B27 gene presence. Modified New York Criteria:

Clinical Criteria:

  • Low back pain > 3 months (improves with exercise, not with rest)
  • Limited lumbar spine motion (sagittal/frontal planes)
  • Reduced chest expansion (relative to age/sex)

Radiographic Criteria (X-ray):

  • Bilateral sacroiliitis (grade 2-4) or unilateral sacroiliitis (grade 3-4)

Radiological Features:

  • Blurring/haziness of sacroiliac joint
  • Squaring of vertebrae
  • Bamboo spine
  • Dagger sign

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

MRI: Early detection of inflammation

Laboratory Tests
  • HLA-B27 positive (90% of cases)
  • ESR, CRP: Elevated during active disease, but can be normal

Treatment

Non-Pharmacological:

  • Physical therapy (mobility/posture exercises)
  • Patient education on disease and exercise importance

Pharmacological:

  • NSAIDs (first-line for pain, stiffness)
  • TNF inhibitors/IL-17 inhibitors (Secukinumab)
  • Sulfasalazine (for peripheral arthritis)
  • Corticosteroids (short-term flare control)

Surgical:

  • Hip replacement (for severe hip involvement)
  • Spinal surgery (for severe deformities/fractures)

Complications
  • Spinal fractures (minimal trauma)
  • Cardiac issues (aortic regurgitation, conduction defects)
  • Osteoporosis leading to fracture risk

Incorrect Options:

Tuberculosis of the spine (Option A): Tuberculosis of the spine also known as Pott's disease, is a potential differential diagnosis, particularly in regions where tuberculosis is endemic. However, in this case, the patient's age, chronicity of symptoms, and the absence of constitutional symptoms such as weight loss and night sweats make ankylosing spondylitis more likely.

Disc prolapse (Option C): Disc prolapse can cause lower back pain and radicular symptoms radiating down the leg due to nerve root compression. However, the presence of morning stiffness and bilateral heel pain in this patient suggests an inflammatory condition such as ankylosing spondylitis rather than a disc prolapse.

Mechanical Pain (Option D): Mechanical pain resulting from musculoskeletal strain or injury, can certainly cause lower back pain. However, the chronicity of symptoms, morning stiffness, and the involvement of sacroiliac joints and heels make ankylosing spondylitis a more likely diagnosis in this case.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 72-76.

question: A patient presented with pain in the hand. The joints involved were proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint and first carpometacarpal joint. The wrist and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints were spared. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• OA typically affects the distal interphalangeal (DIP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, especially in the hands. It often spares the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and wrists, making it characteristic of OA in the hands.

Osteoarthritis (OA):

  • It is the most common form of arthritis in the world.
  • It mainly affects the hips, knees, spine, hands and feet.

Clinical manifestations

Symptoms:

  • Pain (Nature and severity are variable)
  • Joint stiffness (short-lasting stiffness after a period of inactivity)
  • Fatigue
  • Sleep disturbance
  • Reduced functional ability and activities

Signs:

  • Tenderness of the joint
  • Bony swelling
  • Reduced range of movement with pain at the end of the range
  • Crepitus on movement of the joint
  • Weakness and wasting of muscles around the joint
  • Signs of inflammation (mild)
  • In severe cases - deformity and instability
  • Varus deformity and fixed flexion deformity of the knee

Varus deformity

  • Classical findings in hand:
    • Heberden’s nodes (posterolateral swellings of DIP joints)

[[figure-2]]

  • Bouchard’s nodes (posterolateral swellings of PIP joints)

[[figure-3]]

  • Squaring at the base of the thumb (first CMC joints)

Kashin Beck disease:

  • An extremely rare polyarticular form of OA.
  • Seen in the people of Northern China and Eastern Siberia.
  • Symptoms:
    • Joint pain
    • Polyarticular swelling
    • Deformity from childhood
    • Short stature
  • X-ray:
    • Distorted epiphyses and tubular long bones.

Rheumatoid Arthritis (Option B): Affects MCP joints and wrists symmetrically, not typically sparing them.

Psoriasis (Option C): Psoriatic arthritis can affect DIP joints but often involves other joints, including MCP joints.

Hyperparathyroidism (Option D): Causes bone changes but does not specifically affect DIP and PIP joints in the same pattern as OA.

Explanation:

Gout

  • Inflammatory arthritis caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and tissues due to hyperuricemia

Clinical Presentation:

  • Acute Gouty Attack- Sudden onset of intense joint pain, typically affecting the big toe, but can also involve other joints such as the ankle, knee, wrist, or elbow
  • Chronic Gout- Recurrent attacks of joint inflammation, development of tophi (deposits of urate crystals) in joints and soft tissues

Diagnosis:

  • Medical History- History of recurrent joint pain, sudden onset, and self-limiting nature of attacks.
  • Physical Examination- Joint examination revealing signs of inflammation (redness, swelling, warmth)
  • Synovial Fluid Analysis-Detection of monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid aspirated from an affected joint
  • Serum Uric Acid Level- Elevated serum uric acid levels (>6.8 mg/dL) may support the diagnosis, but levels can be normal during an acute attack.

Treatment:

  • Acute Attack- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), colchicine, corticosteroids for pain relief and inflammation control
  • Long-term Management- Lifestyle modifications (dietary changes, weight loss), medications to lower uric acid levels (allopurinol, febuxostat) to prevent further attacks.

Serum Uric Acid Level (Option A): While elevated serum uric acid levels are often seen in individuals with gout, they are not sufficient to confirm the diagnosis on their own.

Urine Uric Acid Levels (Option C): Urine uric acid levels are not typically used as a diagnostic test for gout. Although increased urinary excretion of uric acid may be observed in some cases of gout, it is not a specific or reliable marker for diagnosing the condition.

X-Ray Changes (Option D): X-ray changes, such as the presence of joint erosions or bone damage, may occur in advanced stages of gout or if there have been recurrent episodes of inflammation over time.

Structure of Nerve:

  • Neuron (Nerve Cell): The basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system, consisting of a cell body, dendrites, and an axon.
  • Axon: A long projection from the neuron that carries electrical impulses away from the cell body.The basic unit of nerve
  • Endoneurium: A delicate connective tissue that surrounds individual axons within a nerve.
  • Fascicle: A bundle of axons grouped together, surrounded by the perineurium.
  • Perineurium: A protective sheath of connective tissue that encases each fascicle within the nerve.
  • Epineurium: The outermost layer of dense connective tissue that surrounds the entire nerve, protecting the bundled fascicles.

[[figure-1]]

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Pages 230-231, 279-280

explanationHtml:
Axon regeneration in the PNS typically occurs at a rate of about 1 mm per day or 1 inch/month under optimal conditions.

  • Part of the neuron distal to the point of injury undergoes secondary or Wallerian degeneration.
  • The proximal part of the injury undergoes primary or retrograde degeneration up to a single node.

Nerve regeneration:

  • Begins with the growth of the axonal stump from the proximal segment, which starts to grow distally.
  • If the endoneurial tube (which contains Schwann cells) is intact, the axonal sprout can follow its path to reinnervate the end-organ.
  • The rate of recovery of the axon is approximately 1 mm per day.
  • If the endoneurial tube is interrupted, multiple sprouts (up to 100) may migrate aimlessly into the surrounding tissues (epineurium, perineurium, or adjacent tissues), forming a neuroma.

Signs of nerve regeneration

  • The muscle nearest to the injury site recovers first, followed by others in sequence, as the nerve reinnervates muscles from proximal to distal, known as the motor march.
  • Tinel’s sign/ Hoffman’s sign: With progressive regeneration, Tinel sign move distally which indicates axonal regeneration and sensory restoration.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 281

explanationHtml:
The Seddon classification is a system used to categorize peripheral nerve injuries based on the degree of damage to the nerve and its components.

Type

Description

Prognosis

Neurapraxia

(Grade I)
  • Temporary conduction block, myelin damage only.
  • No neuroma and no degeneration.
  • Recovery is complete within 6 weeks.

Axonotmesis

(Grade II)
  • Axonal damage, connective tissue intact.
  • Neuroma in continuity.
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Recovery can take up to months
  • Complete recovery may not occur.
  • Motor march present

Neurotmesis

(Grade III)
  • Complete nerve disruption.
  • End or side neuroma.
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Spontaneous recovery never occurs.
  • Repair is required (poor recovery)

[[figure-1]]

Neurapraxia:

Definition
  • Physiological disruption of conduction in nerve fibre with temporary loss of motor and sensory function without any structural damage to the nerve.

[[figure-2]]

Cause

Commonly caused by compression, stretching, or blunt trauma to a nerve, often seen in sports injuries, falls, or prolonged pressure.

Mechanism

Involves disruption of the myelin sheath surrounding the nerve fibers, which leads to a temporary conduction block while preserving the axon’s structure.

Symptoms

Temporary numbness, weakness, or tingling in the affected area.

Decreased reflexes and muscle strength, but usually not complete paralysis.

Diagnosis

Based on clinical examination and patient history; electrodiagnostic tests (e.g., nerve conduction studies) may confirm the diagnosis.

Classification

Classified as a first-degree nerve injury, indicating the least severe type of nerve injury.

Prognosis

Typically good, with recovery occurring within 6 weeks.

Treatment

Generally conservative; may include rest, physical therapy, and avoiding activities that could further irritate the nerve.


Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 281

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Seddon classification is a system used to categorize peripheral nerve injuries based on the degree of damage to the nerve and its components.

Type

Description

Prognosis

Neurapraxia

(Grade I)
  • Temporary conduction block, myelin damage only.
  • Segmental demyelination due to mechanical pressure (Option D)
  • No neuroma and no degeneration.
  • Recovery is complete within days or weeks (Option A)

Axonotmesis

(Grade II)
  • Axonal damage, connective tissue intact.
  • Loss of conduction within an intact neural tube - Neuroma in continuity (Option C)
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Recovery may occur spontaneously or take many months.
  • Complete recovery may not occur.
  • Motor march (nerve re-innervates muscles from proximal to distal) present

Neurotmesis

(Grade III)
  • Complete nerve disruption (Option B)
  • End or side neuroma.
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Spontaneous recovery never occurs.
  • Repair is required (poor recovery)
  • Function maybe adequate but never complete

[[figure-1]]

Axonotmesis: A type of nerve injury that involves damage to the axon, but the surrounding connective tissue structures (such as the epineurium, perineurium, and endoneurium) remain intact.

Key Features of Axonotmesis:

Axonal Damage

The axon is disrupted, causing Wallerian degeneration distal to the site of injury.

Intact Connective Tissues

The epineurium and perineurium remain intact, which facilitates axonal regrowth.

Wallerian Degeneration

Occurs distal to the injury, involving degeneration of the axon and myelin sheath.

Regeneration

The nerve has the potential to regenerate because the pathway for axonal growth is preserved, typically at a rate of 1-3 mm per day.

Crush Injuries

This is a common mechanism leading to axonotmesis, where the nerve is compressed or crushed, causing axonal damage.

Motor and Sensory Deficits

Loss of motor function and sensation distal to the injury.

Absent Reflexes

Reflexes in the affected region are typically absent.

Conservative Management

In most cases, surgical intervention is not necessary. Recovery occurs as the axon regenerates.

Physical therapy.

Prognosis

Good prognosis for recovery since the structural framework of the nerve is preserved, allowing for regrowth and reconnection of the nerve fibers.

Recovery can take weeks to months.



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 281
  2. Axonotmesis

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Neurotmesis is the most severe form of nerve injury, involving complete disruption of both the axon and the surrounding connective tissues.
  • This results in total loss of motor and sensory function distal to the injury, as seen in this patient.

The Seddon classification is a system used to categorize peripheral nerve injuries based on the degree of damage to the nerve and its components.

Type

Description

Prognosis

Neurapraxia

(Grade I)
  • Temporary conduction block, myelin damage only.
  • No neuroma and no degeneration.
  • Recovery is complete within 6 weeks.

Axonotmesis

(Grade II)
  • Axonal damage, connective tissue intact.
  • Neuroma in continuity.
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Recovery may occur spontaneously or take many months.
  • Complete recovery may not occur

Neurotmesis

(Grade III)
  • Complete nerve disruption.
  • End or side neuroma.
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Complete recovery never occurs

[[figure-1]]

Neurotmesis:

  • The most severe form of nerve injury is characterized by the complete severance of the nerve, including both the axon and the surrounding connective tissues.
  • This results in a total loss of nerve function distal to the site of injury, with both motor and sensory deficits.

Key features
  • Complete Disruption: Both the axon and the nerve's supportive structures are completely severed.
  • Loss of Function: This leads to total loss of motor and sensory function in the region supplied by the affected nerve.
  • Wallerian Degeneration: The portion of the axon distal to the injury undergoes Wallerian degeneration, where the axon and myelin sheath break down.

Common Causes
  • Severe Trauma: Penetrating injuries such as cuts, gunshot wounds, or severe crush injuries are common causes.

Clinical Presentation
  • Complete Motor and Sensory Loss: There is no movement or sensation distal to the injury. Reflexes in the affected area are absent.
  • No Spontaneous Recovery: Unlike less severe nerve injuries, neurotmesis does not allow for spontaneous recovery because the nerve's structural continuity is disrupted.

Diagnosis
  • Clinical Examination
  • Electromyography (EMG) and Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS)
  • MRI or ultrasound

Treatment
  • Surgical Repair: Nerve ends are surgically reconnected, or nerve grafting is performed to bridge the gap between the severed ends. Tendon transfer procedures are also done.
  • Physical Therapy: Post-surgical therapy is crucial to maintain muscle tone and promote recovery once the nerve starts regenerating.

Prognosis

Without Surgical Repair:

  • The prognosis is poor, with no chance of functional recovery.

With Surgical Repair:

  • Recovery depends on the extent of the injury, the length of time between injury and surgery, and the success of the repair.
  • Even with surgery, full recovery may not be possible, especially in cases of long nerve gaps or severe trauma.


Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 281
  2. Neurotmesis

Management of nerve injury:

Conservative Treatment
  • Required in all types of nerve injury
  • Aimed at preserving limb mobility during nerve recovery
  • Types:
  • Splintage of the Paralysed Limb
  • Preserve Joint Mobility
  • Skin and Nail Care
  • Physiotherapy
  • Pain Relief

Operative Treatment

Nerve Suture
  • Techniques include epineural, epi-perineural, perineural, and group fascicular repair.
  • Methods for achieving an end-to-end suture: Mobilization, joint positioning, nerve course alteration, stripping branches, and sacrificing unimportant branches.

Nerve Grafting
  • For gaps greater than 10 cm or when tension is likely at the suture line.
  • The sural nerve is used as a graft.

Neurolysis
  • External Neurolysis: Freeing nerve from surrounding scar tissue. (Option A)
  • Internal Neurolysis: Dissecting nerve sheath to relieve internal pressure. (Option B ruled out)

Reconstructive Surgery
  • When there’s no hope of nerve recovery
  • Usually after 18 months
  • Types:
    • Tendon transfers
    • Arthrodesis
    • Muscle transfer

  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Pages 284-286

  • Brand’s operation
  • Fowler’s operation

1 - Medial femoral condyle

2 - Intercondylar eminence

3 - Lateral femoral condyle

4 - Neck of fibula

[[figure-2]]

Common peroneal nerve injury:

Anatomy:
  • The terminal branch of the sciatic nerve arises from the popliteal fossa.
  • Root value: L4,L5,S1 & S2.
  • Hooks around the neck of the fibula.
  • Terminates by dividing into Superficial peroneal nerve & Deep peroneal nerve

Muscles supplied:
  • Superficial peroneal nerve: Peroneus longus & brevis (foot eversion)
  • Deep peroneal nerve: Peroneus tertius, Tibialis anterior, Extensor digitorum, Extensor hallucis longus.

Cutaneous supply of foot:

[[figure-3]]

Common peroneal nerve injury:

Causes
  • Most common: Neck of fibula fracture (Option D)
  • Posterior dislocation of the hip
  • Fracture lateral tibial condyle

Clinical features
  • Foot drop (inability to evert)
  • High stepping gait

Treatment
  • Conservative (mainstay): Foot drop splint

[[figure-4]]

  • Surgical (tendon transfer) - only done >12 months of no recovery:
    • Barr’s technique
    • Ober’s technique

  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Pages 300-301

question:
A 40-year-old male following RTA presented with a deformity of the lower limb. The clinician prescribed him a splint as shown below.

What is the likely site of injury in this patient based on the markings in this X-ray?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment of the leg, including the gastrocnemius and soleus, which form the bulk of the calf, as well as the flexors of the ankle and toes.
  • Injury to the tibial nerve results in loss of plantarflexion and toe flexion, loss of sensation over the sole, and over time leads to denervation atrophy of the calf and foot, producing isolated calf wasting.
  • Because both the long flexors and intrinsic foot muscles are affected, marked clawing is usually minimal.
  • Chronic denervation also predisposes to pressure ulcers on the sole.
  • The nerve passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum and divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves, explaining why distal lesions around the ankle can selectively affect plantar function and lead to calf and foot atrophy.

Femoral nerve (Option A): Injury causes wasting of the quadriceps (anterior thigh) with weak knee extension and reduced patellar reflex; it does not cause calf wasting.

Sciatic nerve (Option B): A high lesion causes wasting of the hamstrings and all muscles below the knee, resulting in global leg wasting, not isolated calf wasting.

Common peroneal nerve (Option C): Supplies the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg; injury leads to foot drop and wasting of pretibial muscles, while the posterior calf muscles are spared.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 302
question: Isolated calf wasting is most likely to be seen in injury to which nerve?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Anterior shoulder dislocation typically occurs due to a combination of abduction, extension, and external rotation of the arm and is the most common type of shoulder dislocation.
  • The axillary nerve is the most frequently injured nerve in this condition because it winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and passes close to the inferior aspect of the glenohumeral joint, making it vulnerable to traction or compression during dislocation.
  • Injury to the axillary nerve results in weakness of shoulder abduction due to deltoid paralysis and sensory loss over the “regimental badge” area (lateral aspect of the shoulder).
  • Clinically, the shoulder often appears “squared off”, and associated bony or labral injuries such as Hill-Sachs deformity or Bankart lesion should be looked for on imaging.

Musculocutaneous nerve (Option A): Rarely injured in simple anterior dislocations; more often affected in high-energy trauma or surgical procedures around the shoulder.

Suprascapular nerve (Option C): More commonly involved in chronic compression or traction injuries (e.g., at the suprascapular notch) rather than acute shoulder dislocation.

Radial nerve (Option D): Classically injured in mid-shaft humeral fractures or compression neuropathies, not as the primary nerve in anterior shoulder dislocation.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 294
question: Which nerve is most commonly injured in an anterior shoulder dislocation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shows a baby with Erb’s palsy, and the deformity shown is “Waiter’s tip deformity”.
  • Erb’s palsy is caused by an injury to the upper brachial plexus (C5-C6), most commonly due to traction between the head and shoulder (e.g., shoulder dystocia during childbirth or trauma in adults).
  • The muscles supplied predominantly by C5-C6 roots - deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps, and brachialis are paralysed.
  • As a result, the limb assumes the characteristic “waiter’s tip” posture: the arm is adducted and medially (internally) rotated, the elbow is extended, the forearm is pronated, and the wrist is often flexed.
  • This posture reflects loss of shoulder abduction and external rotation, elbow flexion, and forearm supination.
  • There is typically sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the arm and forearm (C5-C6 dermatomes), and the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are reduced or absent.

Wrist drop (Option A): Caused by radial nerve palsy; presents with inability to extend the wrist and fingers, not the posture seen in Erb’s palsy.

Claw hand (Option C): Seen in ulnar nerve injury or Klumpke’s palsy (C8-T1); involves hyperextension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints, a different brachial plexus level.

Benediction hand (Option D): Seen in high median nerve injury when attempting to make a fist; the index and middle fingers remain extended due to paralysis of their flexors.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 290
question: Identify the characteristic deformity shown in the image

correctAnswer: C. Claw hand and Horner syndrome
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Klumpke’s paralysis results from injury to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1), most commonly due to excessive upward traction on the arm (e.g., during a difficult delivery or when a person grasps an object while falling).

  • The hallmark motor deficit is paralysis of the intrinsic muscles of the hand (interossei and lumbricals), leading to the characteristic claw hand deformity with hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints.
  • If the T1 root is involved proximally, the adjacent sympathetic fibers may be damaged, producing Horner’s syndrome (ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis) on the affected side.
  • Additional findings include weakness of finger and wrist flexion and sensory loss along the medial aspect of the forearm and hand (C8-T1 dermatomes).

Waiter’s tip deformity (Option A): Characteristic of Erb’s palsy (C5-C6) with loss of shoulder abduction and external rotation, not a lower trunk lesion.

Wrist drop (Option B): Due to radial nerve palsy, typically from mid-shaft humeral fractures or compression neuropathy.

Winged scapula (Option D): Caused by long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) injury affecting the serratus anterior, not by C8-T1 lesions.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 290

options.text: Waiter's tip deformity and loss of shoulder abduction
Wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand
Winged scapula and weakness of arm elevation

question: Klumpke's paralysis (C8‑T1 injury) is characterised by:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the biceps brachii and brachialis, the primary flexors of the elbow, and continues distally as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which provides sensation over the lateral forearm.
  • Injury to this nerve therefore produces the characteristic combination of weak elbow flexion and sensory loss over the lateral forearm.
  • Although the axillary nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in anterior shoulder dislocations, the musculocutaneous nerve can also be stretched or compressed.
  • The clinical pattern of elbow flexion weakness + lateral forearm sensory loss specifically localizes the lesion to the musculocutaneous nerve.

Axillary nerve (Option A): Causes deltoid paralysis with weakness of shoulder abduction and sensory loss over the “regimental badge” area of the shoulder, not over the forearm or affecting elbow flexion.

Radial nerve (Option C): Injury leads to wrist and finger extension weakness (wrist drop) and sensory loss over the posterior arm/forearm and dorsum of the hand, not the lateral forearm.

Median nerve (Option D): Typically causes thenar weakness and sensory loss over the palmar aspect of the lateral 3½ fingers; it does not produce this pattern of elbow flexion weakness with lateral forearm sensory loss.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6973755/
question: After an anterior shoulder dislocation, a patient has weakness of elbow flexion and sensory loss over the lateral forearm. Which nerve is injured?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has carpal tunnel syndrome, caused by compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum.

  • The image demonstrates thenar eminence wasting, indicating chronic median nerve compression.

[[figure-1]]

  • The diagnosis is supported by the combination of:
    • Nocturnal paresthesia involving the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger (median nerve sensory distribution)
    • Positive Tinel sign, in which percussion over the carpal tunnel reproduces paresthesia
    • Thenar muscle weakness and wasting, resulting in impaired thumb opposition and abduction, reduced pinch strength, and difficulty gripping objects
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome is the most common entrapment neuropathy of the upper limb.
  • It commonly occurs in individuals with repetitive wrist movements, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis, and obesity.

Ulnar nerve (Option A): Ulnar neuropathy causes sensory loss over the little finger and medial half of the ring finger with weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles, producing an ulnar claw hand rather than thenar wasting.

Radial nerve (Option B): Radial nerve palsy presents with wrist drop due to paralysis of the wrist extensors and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand. It does not cause nocturnal paresthesia or thenar muscle wasting.

Musculocutaneous nerve (Option D): This nerve supplies the anterior compartment of the arm and provides sensation over the lateral forearm. It has no motor or sensory distribution in the hand.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 297-303
question: A 48-year-old man presents with numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, particularly at night. He also reports weakness while gripping objects. On examination, tapping over the volar aspect of the wrist reproduces tingling in these fingers. The image is shown below.Which nerve is most likely involved in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Tardy ulnar nerve palsy is a delayed-onset ulnar neuropathy that develops years after an elbow injury, most commonly following a childhood fracture of the lateral condyle of the humerus that heals with non-union or malunion, leading to cubitus valgus (increased carrying angle).
  • In cubitus valgus, the ulnar nerve is chronically stretched and subjected to friction as it passes behind the medial epicondyle, resulting in progressive nerve damage over time.
  • The term “tardy” reflects the long latency period, often many years between the initial injury and the onset of symptoms.
  • Clinically, patients develop sensory loss in the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger, followed by weakness and wasting of intrinsic hand muscles, producing an ulnar claw hand.

Cubitus varus (Option A): An inward angulation of the elbow (commonly after supracondylar fractures). It does not typically cause chronic stretching of the ulnar nerve and is not the classic cause of tardy ulnar nerve palsy.

Gunstock deformity (Option C): This is another term for cubitus varus. Like cubitus varus, it is not associated with the chronic traction mechanism responsible for tardy ulnar nerve palsy.

Carrying angle reduction (Option D): A reduced carrying angle shifts the elbow toward a varus alignment. Tardy ulnar nerve palsy is associated with an increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus), not a decreased one.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 386
question: "Tardy ulnar nerve palsy" is most commonly associated with which elbow deformity?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A Monteggia fracture-dislocation consists of a fracture of the proximal ulna with dislocation of the radial head.
  • The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN), a motor branch of the radial nerve, winds around the neck of the radius and passes through the supinator, making it vulnerable to stretch or compression in this injury.
  • Injury to the PIN produces finger drop due to loss of extension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and weakness of thumb extension.
  • Sensation remains intact because the PIN is a purely motor nerve.
  • Wrist extension is preserved but radially deviated because extensor carpi radialis longus (and often brevis) are innervated proximal to the lesion, while extensor carpi ulnaris (PIN-supplied) is paralysed.
  • Most PIN palsies associated with Monteggia lesions are neuropraxias and often recover after urgent reduction of the radial head.
  • Persistent deficits or suspected entrapment may require surgical exploration, especially if open reduction and internal fixation is performed.

Radial nerve proper (Option A): Injury to the main radial nerve (e.g., in mid-shaft humeral fractures) causes wrist drop along with finger drop and sensory loss. This patient can extend the wrist, ruling this out.

Anterior interosseous nerve (Option C): A branch of the median nerve supplying deep flexors; injury causes inability to make the “OK sign” (pinch deformity), not loss of finger extension.

Median nerve (Option D): Causes sensory loss in the radial 3½ digits and weakness of thumb opposition/flexion; it does not supply the finger extensors at the MCP joints.



Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 297, 298, 305, 306
  • https://casereports.bmj.com/content/2018/bcr-2018-226254
question: A patient with a Monteggia fracture‑dislocation presents with the inability to extend the metacarpophalangeal joints but can extend the wrist (with radial deviation). Which nerve is injured?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The sciatic nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in total hip arthroplasty (THA), particularly when the posterior approach is used.
  • The nerve lies posterior to the hip joint, close to the posterior capsule and short external rotators, making it vulnerable to direct trauma, retractor pressure, traction, heat from bone cement, or postoperative hematoma.
  • A major risk factor is excessive limb lengthening, which can overstretch the sciatic nerve, especially its peroneal (fibular) division, leading to neuropraxia or more severe palsy.
  • Clinically, injury often presents as foot drop with or without sensory loss in the leg and foot.

Femoral nerve (Option A): Located anterior to the hip joint and more commonly at risk during anterior or anterolateral approaches or from misplaced anterior retractors, not the posterior approach.

Obturator nerve (Option C): Runs medially through the obturator foramen and is rarely injured in routine THA, except in cases of medial acetabular wall penetration or complex revision surgery.

Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (Option D): A pure sensory nerve commonly affected in the direct anterior approach, causing meralgia paresthetica; it is unlikely to be injured in the posterior approach.



Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 299, 300
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5705876/
question: Which nerve is most commonly injured during total hip arthroplasty via a posterior approach?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The test demonstrated is Froment’s sign, used to assess ulnar nerve integrity, specifically the function of the adductor pollicis muscle, which is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
  • In this test, the patient is asked to grasp a paper between the thumb and index finger. Normally, the adductor pollicis maintains adduction of the thumb.
  • In ulnar nerve palsy, the patient compensates by flexing the interphalangeal joint of the thumb using the flexor pollicis longus (median nerve), resulting in a positive Froment’s sign.
  • A positive Froment’s sign is therefore indicative of ulnar nerve dysfunction, commonly seen in cubital tunnel syndrome or medial elbow trauma.

Median nerve (Option A) supplies most of the forearm flexors and thenar muscles, including opponens pollicis. Injury leads to loss of thumb opposition and "ape thumb" deformity. Froment’s sign specifically tests ulnar nerve-mediated adduction, not median nerve function.

Radial nerve (Option B) primarily supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm. Injury leads to wrist drop and inability to extend the wrist and fingers. It does not affect pinch grip between thumb and index finger, and is not assessed by Froment’s test.

Musculocutaneous nerve (Option D) supplies the anterior compartment of the arm (biceps, brachialis). Injury results in weakness of elbow flexion and reduced supination. It has no role in intrinsic hand muscle function and is not involved in Froment’s sign.



Reference:

Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th Edition, Page 3697
question: A 34-year-old man presents with weakness of grip and difficulty performing fine motor tasks of the hand following a laceration near the medial aspect of the elbow. The clinical test demonstrated in the video is performed. Failure to maintain grip in this test suggests injury to which nerve?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Radial nerve

Explanation:

The X-ray shows a spiral fracture of the midshaft humerus. This type of fracture is notoriously associated with injury to the radial nerve, which runs in close anatomical proximity to the bone at this specific location.

  • Anatomical Proximity: The radial nerve courses through the spiral groove (or radial groove) on the posterior aspect of the humerus. This close relationship makes it highly vulnerable to trauma during a fracture of the midshaft.
  • Clinical Presentation: An injury to the radial nerve typically presents with wrist drop, which is the inability to extend the wrist and fingers. This is a result of the nerve's innervation of the extensor muscles of the forearm. The incidence of radial nerve palsy in these fractures is approximately 10-20%.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Median nerve (Option A) is located more medially in the arm and is rarely injured in a midshaft humeral fracture.

Ulnar nerve (Option C) runs along the medial epicondyle of the humerus and is most commonly injured in fractures of that region, not the midshaft.

Axillary nerve (Option D) is located more proximally, around the surgical neck of the humerus, and is most often injured in proximal humeral fractures or shoulder dislocations.



Reference:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop and finger drop due to loss of wrist and finger extensors.

Radial nerve management:

Type of Injury
  • Treatment

Open Injuries
  • Immediate exploration and nerve repair or grafting

Closed Injuries
  • Wait 12 weeks for recovery before exploring
  • Use EMG if no improvement; if denervation is detected, perform nerve exploration and repair or grafting

Fractures of Humerus
  • Assess for nerve injury on admission
  • If the injury appears post-manipulation or internal fixation, explore and repair or graft immediately

Recovery Management
  • Perform passive hand movements
  • Splint the wrist in extension-cock up splint:

Long-term Disability
  • Tendon transfers: pronator teres to short radial extensor, flexor carpi radialis or ulnaris to finger extensors, palmaris longus to thumb abductor

Median nerve (Option B): Median nerve injury can lead to Carpal tunnel syndrome. Rest + Analgesics are the preferred management.


Ulnar nerve (Option C): Knuckle bender splint is used in the management of ulnar nerve injury.

[[figure-2]]

Volkmann's ischemic contracture (Option D): Volkman splint or Turn buckle splint is used in the management.

[[figure-3]]

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 295-296.
question: In which of the following nerve injuries is the instrument shown below used?

correctAnswer: D. Carpal tunnel syndrome, Durkan's test
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Tingling and numbness of fingers, with symptoms worsening at night is suggestive of Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). The most reliable clinical test to diagnose CTS is the Durkan test.

[[figure-1]]

Carpal tunnel syndrome:

Definition
  • Compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel in the wrist

Symptoms
  • Numbness, tingling in thumb, index, and middle fingers
  • Pain in hand and wrist, Weakness in grip
  • Symptoms often worse at night and improve during the day.
  • Advanced cases may lead to hand weakness, clumsiness, and muscle atrophy.

Structures Affected
  • Median Nerve: Compressed within the carpal tunnel, leading to symptoms and signs.
  • Flexor Tendons: The nine flexor tendons passing through the carpal tunnel can become inflamed, further compressing the median nerve.

Structures Spared
  • Thenar Eminence: Sensory loss generally spares this area because its nerve (palmar sensory cutaneous nerve) bypasses the carpal tunnel.

Clinical Signs
  • Weakness: Notable weakness in thumb abduction and opposition.
  • Atrophy: Possible atrophy of the thenar eminence in advanced cases.
  • Sensory Loss: Loss typically affects the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the fourth digit).

Causes
  • Idiopathic- commonest cause
  • Inflammatory causes- Rheumatoid arthritis, wrist osteoarthritis
  • Post-traumatic causes- Bone thickening after a Colles' fracture
  • Endocrine causes- Myxoedema, Acromegaly

Diagnostic Tests
  • Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS) - primary diagnostic test
  • Electromyography (EMG)
  • Phalen Test: Positive if pain/paresthesias arise during wrist flexion.

[[figure-2]]

  • Tinel Test: Positive if tapping over the carpal tunnel elicits symptoms.
  • Durkan test: Direct compression on Median nerve for 30 seconds. More specific than the Phalen/Tinel test.

Treatment
  • Conservative: Wrist splinting, NSAIDs, activity modification
  • Corticosteroid injections
  • Surgical: Carpal tunnel release (for severe or refractory cases)

Guyon’s canal syndrome and Froment’s test (Option A):

  • Refers to involvement of the Ulnar side of the wrist leading to compression of Ulnar nerve.
  • Froment’s test: Used to test adductor pollicis muscle (supplied by Ulnar nerve).


Reference:

Campbell’s Operative Orthopedics 14th Edition pages 3697,3857-3859.

Radial nerve management:

Type of Injury
  • Treatment

Open Injuries

Closed Injuries
  • Wait 12 weeks for recovery before exploring
  • Use EMG if no improvement; if denervation is detected, perform nerve exploration and repair or grafting

Fractures of Humerus
  • Assess for nerve injury on admission
  • If the injury appears post-manipulation or internal fixation, explore and repair or graft immediately

Recovery Management

Long-term Disability
  • Tendon transfers: pronator teres to short radial extensor, flexor carpi radialis or ulnaris to finger extensors, palmaris longus to thumb abductor

Incorrect Options:

Wrist splint (Option A): Wrist splints are widely used during post operative and post reduction period to reduce the pain and promote proper healing. The two conditions where a wrist splint is indicated are carpal tunnel syndrome and osteoarthritis (OA).

Knuckle bender splint (Option C): This splint is used to flex metacarpophalangeal (MCP) in cases of Ulnar nerve injury.

Dynamic finger splint (Option D): This splint is spring loaded and is used to provide stretch to those joints with reduced range of motion due to immobilization. It is done mainly after tendon and ligament injury, surgical repair etc.

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 295-296.

Clinical tests for Median nerve:

Test

Muscle tested and action

Pen test:
  • Muscle: Abductor pollicis brevis
  • Action: Abduction of thumb

Oschner clasp test:
  • Muscle: Flexor digitorum superficialis & flexor digitorum profundus

  • If not recovered, nerve repair is done by

Froment’s sign (Option A):

Benediction sign (Option C):

  • Patient when asked to make a fist, his/her middle and index fingers are extended. Hand of benediction (Preacher's hand) indicates clinical sign of peripheral neuropathy. It is specifically indicative of peripheral neuropathy affecting the muscles of the hand.

The Seddon classification is a system used to categorize peripheral nerve injuries based on the degree of damage to the nerve and its components.

Type

Description

Prognosis

Neurapraxia

(Grade I)
  • Temporary conduction block, myelin damage only.
  • No neuroma and no degeneration.
  • Recovery is complete within 6 weeks.

Axonotmesis

(Grade II)
  • Axonal damage, connective tissue intact.
  • Neuroma in continuity.
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Recovery can take up to months
  • Complete recovery may not occur.
  • Motor march present

Neurotmesis

(Grade III)
  • Complete nerve disruption.
  • End or side neuroma.
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Spontaneous recovery never occurs.
  • Repair is required (poor recovery)

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 281

Partial claw hand:
  • Clawing: Hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion of interphalangeal joints.
  • Clawing is seen in 2 medial fingers only.
  • Seen in pure ulnar nerve injury.
  • Also known as the true claw hand.

Complete claw hand:
  • Clawing of all 4 fingers.
  • Seen in combined median + ulnar nerve palsy

Tardy ulnar nerve palsy:
  • Slow-onset (over years) ulnar nerve palsy.
  • Seen with cubitus valgus deformity seen in lateral epicondyle humerus fracture.

Other deformities:
  • Wasting of hypothenar muscles & intrinsic muscles of the hand.
  • Hollow inter-metacarpal spaces in hand.

[[figure-1]]

Ulnar paradox:

  • The higher the lesion, the less severe the deformity.
  • Reason: Long finger flexors are paralyzed and loss of finger flexion makes the deformity less obvious.

Treatment of Ulnar claw hand:

Static procedure (removal)
  • Zancolli Lasso procedure

Dynamic procedures (tendon transfer)
  • Modified Bunnel technique
  • Brand’s operation
  • Fowler’s operation

Radial Nerve (Option B) palsy causes wrist drop due to paralysis of the extensor carpi radialis longus and extensor carpi radialis brevis. Compression of the radial nerve in the radial groove while putting a hand on a chair/clutch causes Saturday night/crutch palsy.

Median Nerve (Option C) palsy causes carpal tunnel syndrome (Compression neuropathy). Paralysis of opponens pollicis muscle causes ‘Ape thumb deformity’. Paralysis of the flexor digitorum superficialis and lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus of the index finger causes ‘Pointing index’.

Posterior Interosseous Nerve (Option D) injury causes loss of finger extension called finger drop. There is no sensory loss. The injury occurs at the head of the radius.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 296-297

Campbell textbook of orthopedics, 14th edition - Page No. 3306-3308

question: What condition is caused by nerve injury?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: C) Axonotmesis

Explanation:

  • The intact outer sheath and damaged inner axon are known as axonotmesis.
  • Tinel’s sign is positive and progressive. It is an axonal breakdown.
  • Recovery is not complete.
  • An injury to the peripheral nerve of one of the extremities of the body. The axons and their myelin sheath are damaged, but the endoneurium, perineurium and epineurium remain intact is defined as axonotmesis.

The Seddon classification is a system used to categorize peripheral nerve injuries based on the degree of damage to the nerve and its components.

Type

Description

Prognosis

Neurapraxia

(Grade I) (Option A)
  • Temporary conduction block, myelin damage only.
  • No neuroma and no degeneration.
  • Recovery is complete within 6 weeks.

Axonotmesis

(Grade II) (Option B)
  • Axonal damage, connective tissue intact.
  • Neuroma in continuity.
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Recovery can take up to months
  • Complete recovery may not occur.
  • Motor march present

Neurotmesis

(Grade III) (Option D)
  • Complete nerve disruption.
  • End or side neuroma.
  • Degeneration: Proximally+distally.
  • Spontaneous recovery never occurs.
  • Repair is required (poor recovery)

[[figure-1]]

Axonopraxia (Option B) There is a partial axonal disruption with no significant damage to the surrounding nerve structure.



Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 281
  • Neurapraxia

question: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling on an outstretched hand. X-ray shows an extension–type supracondylar fracture of the humerus. On examination, he is unable to make an “OK” sign with his thumb and index finger. Which structure is most likely injured?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Neuropraxia is characterised by a physiological conduction block without structural disruption of the axon or surrounding connective tissue.

  • It is the mildest form of peripheral nerve injury.
  • Commonly caused by compression or mild traction injury.
  • There is a temporary interruption of nerve conduction without structural damage.
  • Features:
    • Physiological conduction block occurs.
    • The axon remains intact.
    • No Wallerian degeneration occurs.
  • Clinical manifestations:
    • Temporary motor weakness and sensory loss may occur.
    • Recovery is usually complete within days to weeks.
  • Examples:
    • Saturday night palsy
    • Transient nerve compression injuries.

Axonal disruption (Option B) occurs in axonotmesis and neurotmesis, associated with Wallerian degeneration distal to injury

Nerve trunk damage (Option C): Severe injury involving the entire nerve trunk is seen in neurotmesis, and recovery is poor without surgical repair

Perineurium damage (Option D): Damage to the perineurium suggests more severe nerve injury than neuropraxia and is associated with axonotmesis or neurotmesis.



Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 281.
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560501/
question: Which of the following is the characteristic feature of neuropraxia?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle in the cubital tunnel. An elbow dislocation (especially posterolateral) or subsequent improper healing (e.g., valgus deformity, fibrosis) can compress or stretch the ulnar nerve, causing tingling in the medial palm, 4th and 5th fingers (ulnar distribution).

Incorrect Options:

  • Median nerve (Option A) is anterior in the elbow and less commonly injured in elbow dislocations; its sensory deficit affects the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger (not primarily the palm tingling described).
  • Radial nerve (Option C) is more often injured in humeral shaft fractures; sensory loss involves the dorsum of the hand, not palmar tingling.
  • Axillary nerve (Option D) is associated with shoulder dislocations, not elbow injuries.

Simple Bone Cyst (SBC) / Unicameral bone cyst

  • Definition: Unilocular, fluid-filled bone cavity lined by fibrous membrane

  • Age/Sex: <20 years; M > F (2:1)

  • Location: Metaphysis near physis; common in proximal humerus, femur, tibia

  • Presentation: Often asymptomatic; may present with pathological fracture

  • Types:

    • Active: Near growth plate

    • Latent: Away from growth plate

  • X-ray: Central, well-defined metaphyseal lytic lesion; cortical thinning

    • Fallen leaf sign – bone fragment in cavity

    • Trap-door sign – hinged fragment at cortex

  • MRI: Homogeneous fluid cavity

  • Histology: Fibrous lining, giant cells, reactive bone

  • Treatment: Steroid injection (active); curettage + bone grafting

question: Which of the following is the cause of the indicated arrow?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The X-ray demonstrates periosteal elevation (periosteal reaction), which occurs when the periosteum is lifted from the cortex in response to an underlying pathological process.

  • It is a nonspecific radiological finding and may be seen in a variety of conditions, including nutritional disorders (scurvy), infections (syphilis), and bone tumors such as osteosarcoma.
  • The pattern of periosteal reaction helps narrow the differential diagnosis.
  • While Codman's triangle is a type of aggressive periosteal reaction classically seen in osteosarcoma, simple periosteal elevation can occur in many benign and malignant conditions.

Other important causes of periosteal reaction include:

  • Trauma: Fractures, stress (march) fractures, and subperiosteal hematoma.
  • Infections: Acute osteomyelitis, Brodie abscess, tuberculosis, and congenital or acquired syphilis.
  • Neoplasms: Osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, osteoid osteoma, and metastatic bone disease.
  • Metabolic and nutritional disorders: Scurvy, rickets, and hypervitaminosis A.
  • Systemic conditions: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, sickle cell disease, and leukemia.


Reference:

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/347426599

question: A 70-year-old man comes to the clinic for a routine check-up. During the visit, he shared his family history of bone tumors, mentioning that several relatives have passed away from various types of bone cancers. Concerned about his own risk, he asks the doctor which type of bone malignancy he should be most vigilant about.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient is 70 years old, making multiple myeloma the most likely diagnosis, as it is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in adults over 40 years of age.

  • It is a malignancy of clonal plasma cells arising in the bone marrow and commonly involves the vertebrae, skull, ribs, pelvis, and proximal long bones.
  • Patients typically present with bone pain, pathological fractures, anemia, hypercalcemia, and renal impairment.
  • Radiographs classically show multiple punched-out lytic lesions or diffuse osteopenia.

Osteochondroma (Option A): A benign bone tumor that typically presents during childhood and adolescence.

Osteoclastoma (Option B): A locally aggressive benign tumor that usually occurs in skeletally mature adults between 20 and 40 years of age.

Ewing sarcoma (Option C): A high-grade malignant bone tumor that primarily affects children and adolescents, most commonly between 10 and 20 years of age.

question: A 20-year-old woman presents with a one-year history of progressively worsening thigh pain, initially accompanied by intermittent fevers and malaise. Recently, her pain has intensified to the point of bedridden status. She develops acute confusion and altered consciousness, with laboratory tests revealing severe hypercalcemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase. An X-ray is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The radiograph demonstrates an aggressive diaphyseal lesion of the femur with a lamellated ("onion-skin" or "onion-peel") periosteal reaction, which is characteristic of Ewing sarcoma.

  • Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant small round blue cell tumor that predominantly affects children and adolescents (10-20 years).
  • It most commonly arises in the diaphysis of long bones, especially the femur, tibia, and humerus, and may also involve flat bones such as the pelvis.
  • Patients typically present with localised pain, swelling, tenderness, and occasionally pathological fractures.
  • Constitutional symptoms such as fever, malaise, weight loss, leukocytosis, and elevated ESR may occur, often leading to confusion with osteomyelitis.
  • Radiographic Features
    • Diaphyseal permeative ("moth-eaten") lytic lesion
    • Wide zone of transition
    • Lamellated ("onion-skin" or "onion-peel") periosteal reaction
    • Cortical destruction with an associated soft-tissue mass

[[figure-1]]

  • Histopathology
    • Composed of uniform small round blue cells
    • Characteristic t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation producing the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion gene

[[figure-2]]

Osteosarcoma (Option A): Typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones, especially around the knee (distal femur and proximal tibia). Radiographs classically show cloud-like osteoid matrix, Codman triangle, and sunburst periosteal reaction rather than an onion-skin appearance.

Multiple myeloma (Option C): Usually affects older adults (>50 years) and presents with multiple punched-out lytic lesions, anemia, renal dysfunction, and hypercalcemia. It is exceedingly rare in adolescents.

Osteoclastoma (Option D): Giant cell tumor typically occurs in skeletally mature adults (20-40 years) and involves the epiphysis extending into the metaphysis, producing an eccentric expansile "soap-bubble" lytic lesion rather than a diaphyseal lesion.



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 213-217
  2. Textbook of Orthopaedics, John Ebnezar, 5th Edition, Pages 612-615
  3. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10781019/
question: A 15-year-old boy presents with progressively worsening pain and swelling over the left thigh for the past 3 months, associated with intermittent fever and malaise. On examination, there is localised tenderness over the femoral shaft. The radiograph is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Sunburst appearance in long bones
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Findings suggest multiple myeloma. All options are typical except sunburst appearance, which is seen in osteosarcoma.

Multiple myeloma:

  • It is the most common primary malignant bone tumor.
  • It is the malignant proliferation of plasma cells of the B-cell lineage within the bone marrow.
  • Common age group: Around 70 years of age.
  • Men > Female.

Clinical manifestations:

Common symptoms: severe spine pain, pathological fractures, local tenderness, fatigue, weight loss, and neurological signs.
Complications: anemia, hypercalcemia, hyperviscosity, immunosuppression, renal dysfunction.

Investigations:

  • Skeletal survey to screen for bone lesions, and assess tumor burden and fracture risk: X-rays of the spine, skull, pelvis, ribs/sternum, and the humerus/femurs.
  • Multiple punched-out lesions in the skull and other flat bones. In the skull, it may cause a ‘pepper-pot’ appearance. (Options A & B ruled out)


  • Pathological wedge collapse of the vertebra (Common in the thoracic spine). (Option C ruled out)

A. A lateral X-ray of the lumbar spine shows diffuse osteopenia and a pathologic compression fracture of the L1 vertebral body (arrow).

B. A midsagittal T2-weighted MRI taken several months later shows extensive marrow infiltration and compression fractures of many vertebral bodies.

  • CT > X-ray for fractures, lytic lesions, and soft-tissue masses

  • Urine: Bence Jones proteins

  • Serum electrophoresis: M-spike (gamma region)

  • Biopsy: Iliac crest or CT-guided vertebral biopsy

Treatment:

  • Treatment of choice: Autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT).
  • Bisphosphonates to control hypercalcemia.
  • In transplant-ineligible patients:
    • Bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (VRd).
    • Daratumumab, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (DRd).



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 214, 217, 206
  2. Multiple Myeloma - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)
question: A 58-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of worsening back pain, fatigue, and significant weight loss. He also reports frequent headaches, difficulty concentrating, and numbness in his legs. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the lumbar spine and decreased sensation in the lower extremities. Laboratory investigations show normocytic anemia, hypercalcemia, and elevated serum creatinine. Urinalysis reveals the presence of Bence Jones proteins. A skeletal survey is done. Which of the following is NOT a typical radiological feature of the patient’s most likely condition?

correctAnswer: B. Bone-to-bone metastasis is not common.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical picture and onion peel appearance in the proximal part of the shaft of the left humerus on the X-ray are consistent with a diagnosis of Ewing’s sarcoma.
  • Bone-to-bone metastasis is very common, making metastasis a frequent and challenging complication.

Ewing's sarcoma

  • Highly malignant tumor. (Option A ruled out)
  • Cell of origin: Mesenchymal stem cells in the bone marrow.
  • Age group: 10-20 years of age.
  • Males > Females. (Option D ruled out)
  • Common site: Diaphysis of the long bone. Femur > tibia > humerus > fibula.

Histopathology:The tumor cells surround a central clear area, forming a pseudo-rosette.

Clinical manifestations:

  • The earliest symptom is pain.
  • Later symptoms are swelling and low-grade fever.
  • Swelling is usually located in the diaphysis and has features of a malignant swelling.
  • Very poor prognosis.
  • Bone-to-bone metastasis is very common. (Option B)

X-ray findings:

  • Onion-peel appearance- new bone formation in layers.

[[figure-1]]

Treatment

Combined therapy:

  • Radiotherapy: Highly radio-sensitive tumor so melts quickly but has recurrence (Option C ruled out)
  • Wide surgical excision
  • Chemotherapy.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 213, 214

Explanation: Soap bubble appearance is the characteristic radiological finding of giant cell tumors. It presents as a lytic lesion with multiple internal septations, giving it a soap bubble appearance. It is usually located in the epiphysis of long bones, such as the distal femur.

X-ray findings in Giant cell tumors (GCTs):

  • Eccentric location, often subchondral.
  • Expansion of the overlying cortex.
  • The cortex may be thinned out.
  • Lobulated lytic lesions with narrow zones of transition produce a soap bubble appearance. (Option C)

[[figure-1]]

Sun-rays appearance (Option A) seen in osteosarcoma.

Onion peel appearance (Option B)is associated with Ewing's sarcoma

Pepper pot appearance (Option D) is seen in multiple myeloma.

Osteoclastoma/ Giant Cell Tumor

  • Benign but locally aggressive tumor of bone. (Option B)

question: A 32-year-old woman presents with progressive and persistent vague pain and swelling around her right knee for the past 3 months. On physical examination, there is swelling around the distal femur with tenderness. Histopathology shows multinucleated giant cells and spindle-shaped mononuclear stromal cells. Which of the following statements is true regarding the nature of the tumor in this patient?

correctAnswer: B. It is benign but can behave aggressively locally
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and histopathology are characteristic of a Giant Cell Tumour (GCT) of bone (Osteoclastoma).

  • It is classified as an intermediate (locally aggressive), rarely metastasising tumour and is traditionally described as benign but locally aggressive because it can cause extensive bone destruction, cortical breach, pathological fractures, and local recurrence.

Characteristic features include:

  • Peak incidence: 20-40 years (Option D)
  • Slight female predominance
  • Most commonly affects the epiphysis of long bones (Option A) after closure of the growth plate
  • Common sites:
    • Distal femur (most common)
    • Proximal tibia
    • Distal radius
    • Sacrum
  • Histology:
    • Numerous osteoclast-type multinucleated giant cells
    • Mononuclear spindle-shaped stromal cells, which constitute the neoplastic component

[[figure-1]]

  • Radiographs typically show an eccentric expansile lytic epiphyseal lesion with a characteristic "soap-bubble" appearance.

[[figure-2]]

  • Although usually benign, local recurrence is relatively common, and pulmonary metastases occur rarely (approximately 1-5%).
  • Malignant transformation is uncommon.

It most frequently metastasises to regional lymph nodes (Option C): Metastasis is uncommon. When it occurs, the lungs are the most common site; regional lymph node involvement is rare.



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 198

question: A 32-year-old woman presents with progressive vague pain and swelling around the right knee for the past 3 months. Examination reveals tenderness and swelling over the distal femur. Histopathology demonstrates numerous multinucleated giant cells scattered among spindle-shaped mononuclear stromal cells. Which of the following statements regarding this tumor is true?

correctAnswer: C. It is a result of the tumor breaking through the periosteum, lifting it off the bone
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The triangular shadow seen on the X-ray is Codman’s triangle. It results from rapid tumor growth in osteosarcoma, which lifts the periosteum off the bone.

X-ray findings of osteosarcoma:

  • Area of irregular destruction in the metaphysis. The cortex overlying the lesion is eroded.
  • Sun-ray appearance (aggressive periostitis): As the tumor grows into the overlying soft tissues new bone is laid down centrifugally along the blood vessels within the tumor. (Option A ruled out)

[[figure-1]]

  • Codman's triangle: Elevation of periosteum by the growing tumor in the form of a triangle. (Option C)

[[figure-2]]

It represents tumor calcification within the bone (Option B): Calcifications in osteosarcoma typically occur in the osteoid matrix produced by the tumor, but Codman’s triangle is related to periosteal elevation, not tumor calcification.

It indicates early metastasis to the nearby soft tissue (Option D): Osteosarcoma can spread to soft tissues, but Codman’s triangle is related to periosteal elevation rather than distant spread or metastasis.





Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 206
  2. Osteosarcoma - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)

question:
A 17-year-old boy presents to orthopedics OPD with mild fever and intermittent thigh pain for the past several months, particularly at night. There is no history of fever and weight loss. On physical exam, there is swelling and tenderness over the distal femur. An X-ray image is shown below.

Which of the following best explains the radiological finding in osteosarcoma that is marked with an arrow in the above image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the patient's demographics, clinical manifestations, and X-ray showing a sunburst appearance, the most probable diagnosis is osteosarcoma.
  • It most commonly originates in the metaphysis of long bones.

Osteogenic Sarcoma (Osteosarcoma):

  • The most common primary malignant bone tumor of non-hematopoietic origin/ solid malignant bone tumor.
  • Age group: Bimodal age distribution peaking in adolescence (10–14 years) and again in the seventh decade.
  • Gender: Male>> Female

Pathology:

  • Origin: It arises from mesenchymal cells.
  • Common site: From the metaphysis or meta-diaphysis. (Option C)
  • All osteosarcomas are aggressive and metastasize widely through the hematogenous route, typically to the lungs.
  • Despite its aggressiveness, it seldom penetrates the epiphyseal plate. (Option D ruled out)

Histopathology:

  • Anaplastic mesenchymal parenchyma with tumor cells surrounded by osteoid.

Clinical manifestation:

  • Increasing pain/swelling, worse at night

  • Rare pathological fractures

  • Exam: warm, tender, ill-defined swelling with shiny skin, visible veins

  • Limited joint movement; possible neurovascular compression

  • Reactive lymphadenopathy

  • Associated syndromes: Li-Fraumeni, hereditary retinoblastoma, Rothmund–Thomson

Hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow (Option A) are more commonly associated with multiple myeloma.

Ewing sarcoma commonly originates in the diaphysis of long bones(Option B)

Explanation:

An expansile, lytic lesion often characterizes an aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC), and its FNA typically yields a bloody aspirate due to the cystic, vascular nature of the lesion. Hemosiderin-laden macrophages are commonly seen due to prior hemorrhage within the cyst.

Giant cell tumor (GCT) (Option A) can also present as an expansile lytic lesion, but it usually involves the epiphysis without such a significant cystic, vascular component or bloody aspirate on FNA.

Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC)

Giant Cell Tumor (GCT)

Age

Primarily affects children and teenagers

Most common in young adults (15-35 years)

Gender

Equal distribution between males and females

More common in females (Female: Male ratio 1.5:1)

Location

Metaphyses of long bones (femur, tibia, humerus), spine

Epiphyses of long bones (lower end of femur, upper end of tibia)

Symptoms

Pain and swelling; spinal lesions may cause neurological issues

Swelling without pain; late stages show joint limitation and pathological fracture

Histology

FNAC: Hemosiderin +

Blood-filled cystic spaces separated by fibrous septae

FNAC: No hemosiderin

Abundant giant cells with multiple nuclei (>150), spindle cells indicating malignancy

Radiology

Osteolytic lesion, multiple septations and fluid-fluid levels on MRI

Thin septa with soap-bubble appearance on X-ray, cortex thin and expanded, no periosteal reaction

Treatment

Curettage, debridement, and in some cases radiation (cautiously)

question: A 22-year-old male presents with pain and swelling over the distal radius. X-ray shows an expansile lytic lesion in the epiphysis extending to the metaphysis. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) reveals a bloody aspirate with hemosiderin-laden macrophages. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign, expansile, osteolytic lesion that commonly affects metaphysis of long bones in adolescents.

Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC)

A benign, expansile bone lesion composed of blood-filled cystic spaces.

Epidemiology

Primarily affects children and teenagers (10 to 30 years).

Males > Females

Location

Metaphyses of long bones (femur, tibia, humerus).

Located subperiosteally.

Presentation

Pain and Swelling.

Radiological Features

X-ray: Radiolucent area situated at the metaphysis.

Osteolytic, poorly defined lesion elevating and eroding the cortex.

MRI: Multiple intralesional septations and fluid levels.

Angiography: Persistence of contrast and a blush of flow within the lesion.

Histology

Composed of blood-filled cystic spaces separated by fibrous septae.

In chronic cases, the septae may contain woven bone.

Treatment

Surgery: Curettage and bone grafting


Giant cell tumor (Option A): It usually occurs in adults near the ends of long bones, show a lytic lesion without fluid levels, and often extend into the subchondral bone.

Osteosarcoma (Option B): It is a malignant bone tumor that presents with aggressive, mixed lytic-sclerotic lesions and periosteal reactions like Codman's triangle or sunburst appearance.

Osteoid osteoma (Option D): It is a small, benign lesion typically causing nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs, and appears as a small nidus surrounded by sclerosis on imaging.



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 201, 202, 198, 205, 206, 196.

question: A 15-year-old female presents with a gradually enlarging, painful swelling over the distal femur. On examination, the swelling is tender and firm. X-ray shows an expansile, lytic lesion with multiple fluid levels in the metaphysis. The most likely diagnosis is:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given scenario with a history of a slowly growing, painless swelling on the forehead and a CT scan showing a dense, well-circumscribed, bony lesion in the frontal sinus is suggestive of Ivory osteoma.

Ivory Osteoma / Compact Osteoma:

It is a painless condition affecting membranous bones or soft tissues.

Two Types

  • Homoplastic: arises purely from bone
  • Heteroplastic: arises from soft tissues

Most common site: The outer surface of the Skull (especially in front of the frontal sinus)

Presentations:

  • Cosmetic problems
  • Mucocele.
  • It can become a space-occupying lesion (if the inner table of the skull is involved) and can predispose to epilepsy.

[[figure-1]]

Treatment: Excision

question: A 35-year-old male presents with a history of a slowly growing, painless swelling on the forehead for the past 3 years. On examination, a hard, immobile mass is palpated. A CT scan shows a dense, well-circumscribed, bony lesion in the frontal sinus. The most likely diagnosis is:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient presenting with persistent pain, relieved by NSAIDs and an X-ray showing a characteristic lesion with a sclerotic margin and radiolucent nidus, points towards an Osteoid Osteoma.

Osteoid Osteoma

Demographics
  • Sex: Males > Females
  • Age: Young patients, but rare under 5 years and over 30.

Location
  • The diaphysis of long bones, especially the proximal tibia, and femur.
  • It can also occur in the spine, particularly the posterior arches.

Pathophysiology

The nidus releases prostaglandins which cause the characteristic pain that relieves on taking NSAIDs

Symptoms
  • Characterized by pain, often worse at night (Night crises), and relieved by NSAIDs (Therapeutic test).
  • When near joints, it may cause stiffness and effusion.
  • In the spine, it can lead to muscle spasms and scoliosis.

Radiology

X-Ray:

  • Dense sclerosis with a small, rounded area of osteolysis, often obscured by the surrounding sclerosis.
  • The characteristic lesion is less than 1.5 cm in diameter with a sclerotic margin and radiolucent nidus.

[[figure-1]]

Isotope bone scans (Best investigation) are positive

Histology
  • Consists of a mesh of woven bone, osteoblastic rimming, osteoclasts, and dilated capillaries.
  • The mature osteoid forms the nidus, surrounded by dense, reactive bone and soft tissue with inflammatory changes.

[[figure-2]]

Treatment
  • CT-guided radiofrequency ablation.
  • Surgical excision of the nidus (gold standard)



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 196, 213, 214
  2. Textbook of Orthopedics- John Ebnezar, 5th Edition, Page 603.
question: A 16-year-old boy presents with persistent pain in his right leg, which is worse at night and relieved by ibuprofen. Physical examination is unremarkable, with no swelling or warmth over the affected area. An X-ray of the right leg is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A teenager presenting with mild intermittent pain and an Xray showing an eccentric, lytic lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis without periosteal reaction, with a biopsy showing stellate cells in a myxoid background is suggestive of Chondromyxoid Fibroma.

Chondromyxoid Fibroma

Demographics

Sex: Slightly more common in males.

Age: Teenagers and young adults (2nd and 3rd decade of life).

Location

Metaphyses of long bones,

particularly the proximal tibia and pelvis.

Presentation

Slow-growing swelling with pain

Radiology

X-ray:

Small, metaphyseal, eccentric lytic lesions, lying parallel to the bone's long axis.

The cortex is expanded, thin, and interrupted. Medullary margins are scalloped and sclerosed.

It erupts through the cortex with minimal periosteal or soft tissue reaction.

[[figure-1]]

Histology

Stellate cells on a myxoid background. Mitotic figures are rare, though cellular atypia may occur.

Treatment

Small tumors: Local excision and bone grafting

large tumors: Wide en bloc excision

question: A 19-year-old male presents with mild, intermittent knee pain for 6 months. X-ray shows an eccentric, lytic lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis without periosteal reaction. Biopsy reveals stellate cells in a myxoid background. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. The tumor occurs commonly at the epiphysis of long bones.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This case points towards a diagnosis of Chondroblastoma.
  • Recurrence of chondroblastoma is observed in about 10% of cases, indicating the need for careful monitoring.

Chondroblastoma

  • Type: Benign but potentially aggressive bone tumor
  • Commonly Affected Age Group: Primarily affects children and adolescents (Option A ruled out)
  • Gender: More prevalent in males than females (Option D ruled out)

Clinical Presentation

  • Main Symptom: Localized pain
  • Additional Symptoms: Joint effusion and stiffness, especially near joints

Location

  • Typical Sites:
    • Epiphyses of long bones (especially around the knee) (Option B)

Radiographic Features

  • Appearance: Well-defined round/oval lytic lesions

  • Size: 1–7 cm

  • Cortical Expansion: Possible without breach

  • MRI: Homogeneous high-signal lesions

[[figure-1]]

  • Pathognomonic Features:
    • "Chicken-wire" calcification

[[figure-2]]

Recurrence

  • Approximately 10% chance of recurrence (Option B ruled out)

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 195
