question: A 15-year-old male presents with localized pain and joint stiffness around the knee. Radiographic examination reveals a well-defined lytic lesion in the epiphysis of a long bone. Histological analysis shows a "wet-sawdust" appearance and "chicken-wire" calcification. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Serial X-rays for monitoring are appropriate for asymptomatic chondromas, as they typically stop growing after skeletal maturity.

Chondroma: Summary of X-ray Findings and Treatment

X-ray Findings

  • Chondromas present as:
    • Well-defined, radiolucent lesions
    • Surrounded by a thin border of reactive sclerosis
  • Typically located centrally in the bone with:
    • Rounded, lobulated edges
  • Internal characteristics:
    • "Popcorn-like," "glandular," or "ring-like" opacities indicating calcification

[[figure-1]]

  • Rarely exceed 6 cm in diameter

[[figure-2]]

Treatment

  • Asymptomatic Chondromas: No treatment required : (Option D ruled out)
  • Symptomatic Chondromas: Treatment options include:
    • Curettage: (Option A ruled out)
      • Scraping out tumor tissue from the bone
      • Recommended for symptomatic lesions in the hand or in cases of pathological fractures
    • Serial X-rays: (Option B- more appropriate)
      • Monitor size changes post-skeletal maturity
      • Growth after maturity may indicate malignant transformation, necessitating further evaluation and treatment

Immediate surgical excision (Option C): Not necessary since the lesion is asymptomatic and likely benign.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 192- 194
question: A 25-year-old patient presents with a well-defined, radiolucent lesion in the distal phalanx of the hand. Radiographic findings reveal rounded, lobulated edges with characteristic "popcorn-like" opacities. The lesion measures 4 cm in diameter and is asymptomatic. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate management for this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Surgical excision of all chondromas is the standard treatment to prevent malignant transformation.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • It is a case of Multiple Enchondromatosis associated with hemangiomas, Maffucci syndrome.
  • Surgical excision may be indicated for symptomatic chondromas or those showing signs of malignant transformation
  • It is not necessary to excise all chondromas as a preventive measure.

Multiple Enchondromatosis

  • Definition: Condition characterized by numerous benign cartilaginous tumors (chondromas).
  • Associated Conditions:
    • Ollier's disease- only enchondromas
    • Maffucci syndrome- enchondromas + hemangiomas

[[figure-1]]

Higher risk of malignant transformation (Option A):

  • Ollier disease: ~20–30% risk of chondrosarcoma.

  • Maffucci syndrome: >50% risk.

Bone expansion & cortical thinning (Option B):

  • Enchondromas grow inside bone → expand medullary cavity → thin cortex → predispose to fractures.

Increased risk of extra-skeletal malignancies (Option D):

  • Especially in Maffucci syndrome:

    • CNS tumors

    • Pancreatic cancer

    • Ovarian tumors

    • Soft-tissue sarcomas



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 193, 194

question: An X-ray image shows multiple large chondromas in the hands and feet of a 28-year-old female patient. Based on this radiological finding, which of the following statements is false regarding her condition?

correctAnswer: B. Most chondromas are symptomatic and present with pain or fractures.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Most chondromas are asymptomatic and are often discovered incidentally rather than presenting with pain or fractures.

Clinical Features

Aspect

Details

Location

Predominantly found in tubular bones of the hand. (Option C ruled out)

Other common sites include the femur and humerus.

Symptoms

Mostly asymptomatic; often discovered via radiography.

May cause pain or pathological fractures in some cases.

Growth

Generally slow-growing, ceasing post-skeletal maturity. (Option A ruled out)

Malignant Transformation

Typically benign, but differentiation from low-grade chondrosarcoma (grade 1) is challenging.

Indicators of chondrosarcoma include:

Increased cellularity

Enlarged nuclei

Presence of multiple double-nucleated cells

Infiltration into marrow spaces and haversian system

Serial X-rays are useful for monitoring potential malignancy; growth post-skeletal maturity may signal transformation. (Option D ruled out)

[[figure-1]]

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 192- 194

Osteochondroma: X-ray, Treatment, and Complications

X-ray Appearance

  • Bony outgrowth with sharp edges

  • Continuity with widened host bone cortex

  • Thin cortex, cancellous inside

  • Pedunculated or sessile; pedunculated grows toward diaphysis

question: A 25-year-old male presents with a bony swelling near his knee. He denies pain or any recent trauma. X-ray shows a pedunculated bony outgrowth growing away from the joint, with a thin outer cortex and cancellous structure. What is the next step in management?

correctAnswer: B. Cortical flaring into the lesion
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The characteristic radiographic feature of osteochondroma is the flaring of the host bone's cortex into the osteochondroma, indicating a benign growth.

Osteochondroma:

  • Benign cartilaginous neoplasms arising from physeal cartilage beneath the periosteum

Clinical Presentation

  • Typically a painless mass

  • May cause bursa formation or activity-related discomfort

  • Rarely: nerve pain or fracture-related pain

Types of Osteochondromas and Malignant Transformation

Type

Characteristics

Risk of Malignant Transformation

Solitary Osteochondroma

Low risk (~1%). Difficult to determine exact incidence.

~1%

Multiple Osteochondromas (MO)

Higher risk (~4%). Autosomal dominant disorder with EXT1 or EXT2 gene mutations in 90% of cases.

~4%
  • Factors affecting malignant transformation:
    • Larger lesions with thicker cartilage caps (especially >1.5 cm).
    • More common in trunk lesions, and rare in extremities.
    • Suspicious changes in size or pain after skeletal maturity in MO patients.

Radiographic Appearance

  • Bony protuberance with well-defined borders.
  • Key radiographic features:
    • Cortex flaring into the osteochondroma. (Option B)
    • Thin outer cortex with inner cancellous structure.
    • Pedunculated (cauliflower-like summit) or broad sessile base.
    • Pedunculated lesions point away from the joint toward the diaphysis.



  • MRI findings:
    • Cartilaginous cap thickness, generally thicker in children and thins with age.

Note: Tumor appears small in radiograph and large when palpated because of the cartilage cap.

question: A 14-year-old male presents with a painless, hard mass near his proximal humerus. Imaging reveals a bony protuberance with a well-defined cortex that flares into the lesion. Which of the following radiographic features is most indicative of osteochondroma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Adamantinoma is a rare, low-grade malignant bone tumour of epithelial origin.
  • It shows a strong predilection for the tibia, especially the anterior cortex of the diaphysis, which is involved in approximately 70-90% of cases.
  • It is a slow-growing primary malignant bone tumour that typically affects young adults.
  • Histologically, it is a biphasic tumour composed of epithelial cells within an osteofibrous stroma.
  • Clinically, patients usually present with dull aching pain and localized swelling, and occasionally with a pathological fracture.
  • Radiographically, it classically appears as a multiloculated lytic, cortical-based lesion in the tibial diaphysis with cortical expansion, sometimes giving a soap-bubble-like appearance.
  • Although indolent, adamantinoma is locally aggressive and can metastasize, most commonly to the lungs.
  • The treatment of choice is wide surgical resection, as the tumour is generally resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
  • Long-term follow-up is essential due to the risk of local recurrence and late metastasis.

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 219

question:
A 60-year-old man with renal cell carcinoma presents with arm pain. His X-ray is as shown. The risk of pathological fracture is assessed using the Mirel's scoring system.

Which of the following parameters is not included in Mirel's scoring system?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is classically associated with purely osteolytic, aggressive, and expansile bone metastases.
  • Unlike many other malignancies, RCC metastases do not induce new bone formation, resulting in rapid skeletal destruction.
  • This osteolysis is mediated by tumour-induced activation of osteoclasts through factors such as RANKL and PTHrP, which promote bone resorption and suppress osteoblastic activity.
  • On imaging, RCC metastases appear as lucent, destructive lesions without a sclerotic rim, often described as punched-out or expansile lytic lesions.
  • They are also characteristically hypervascular, which explains the high risk of severe bleeding during biopsy or surgical stabilisation.
  • The purely lytic nature leads to cortical thinning, predisposing to pathological fractures, severe pain, and spinal cord compression.
  • Extensive bone destruction can also result in malignancy-associated hypercalcemia.

Types of bony metastasis:

Type of Metastasis

Primary Tumours (Common Associations)

Osteolytic (bone destruction)

Renal cell carcinoma, Lung cancer, Thyroid carcinoma, Multiple myeloma

Osteoblastic (sclerotic)

Prostate carcinoma (classical), Carcinoid tumour

Mixed (lytic + blastic)

Breast carcinoma (most common), GI malignancies

Intertrabecular (invisible on X-ray early)

Leukaemia, Lymphoma

Expansile / Hypervascular lytic

Renal cell carcinoma, Thyroid carcinoma

Prostate adenocarcinoma (Option A): Classically produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases, appearing as dense, sclerotic lesions on imaging rather than lytic defects.

Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (Option B): Thyroid cancer metastases may be lytic or mixed, but medullary carcinoma is not the classic tumour associated with purely osteolytic bone metastases compared with RCC.

Breast carcinoma (Option C): Most commonly produces mixed lytic and blastic bone metastases; although lytic lesions can occur, breast cancer is not characteristically purely osteolytic.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 221
question: Which of the following primary malignancies typically produces purely osteolytic bone metastases?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Glioblastoma is a WHO grade 4 astrocytoma and the most common malignant primary brain tumour in adults.
  • Although it is highly aggressive locally, it is rare for glioblastoma to metastasise outside the central nervous system, including to bone.
  • Extracranial metastasis occurs in <2% of cases.
  • This rarity is attributed to several factors, including the blood-brain barrier, the absence of conventional lymphatic drainage in the brain, and the tumour’s tendency for rapid local invasion rather than hematogenous spread.

Lung carcinoma (Option A): One of the most common primary tumours to metastasise to bone, typically producing osteolytic lesions and frequently causing pathological fractures.

Prostate adenocarcinoma (Option B): A classic bone-seeking tumour that characteristically produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) metastases, especially in the axial skeleton (spine, pelvis, ribs).

Renal cell carcinoma (Option C): Well known for causing highly vascular, expansile osteolytic bone metastases, often associated with a significant risk of bleeding during surgical procedures.



Reference:

Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th Edition, Page 1028
question: Which of the following primary tumours is least likely to metastasise to bone?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The “winking owl” sign is a classic radiographic finding seen on an anteroposterior (AP) view of the spine.
  • The pedicles form the two “eyes” of the owl on this view.
  • When one pedicle is destroyed or absent, the vertebra appears to have only one visible “eye,” creating the appearance of a winking owl.

[[figure-1]]

  • The most common cause of this finding is osteolytic metastatic disease (classically from lung, breast, kidney, or thyroid carcinoma), as the pedicle is a frequent site of tumour involvement due to its rich vascular supply.
  • Other less common causes include primary bone tumours, infection (e.g., tuberculosis), or congenital absence of a pedicle.
  • On plain radiographs, a pedicle usually becomes invisible only after significant bone destruction (≈30-50%), so this sign indicates substantial local disease.
  • Unlike osteoporosis, which typically causes vertebral body compression, isolated pedicle destruction strongly suggests an infiltrative process such as malignancy.

Vertebral body (Option A): Destruction typically leads to loss of vertebral height or compression fracture, not the “winking owl” appearance.

Spinous process (Option B): This is a midline posterior structure and does not form the lateral “eye” shadows on an AP view.

Transverse process (Option C): These are more laterally placed projections and do not contribute to the characteristic “owl face” silhouette.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3302920/

question: Which genetic abnormality is characteristic of synovial sarcoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Chordoma is a rare, slow-growing but locally aggressive malignant tumour derived from remnants of the notochord.
  • It most commonly arises at the ends of the axial skeleton, with the sacrum being the most frequent site (≈50% of cases), followed by the clivus and the mobile spine.
  • On imaging, it typically appears as a midline, destructive lytic lesion with bone expansion and a prominent soft-tissue component.
  • Chordomas often show internal calcifications or bone fragments from bone destruction and do not produce osteoid.
  • Histologically, they are characterised by physaliphorous cells - large, vacuolated, mucin-rich cells.

[[figure-1]]

  • Although slow-growing, chordomas are malignant, are locally aggressive, and can metastasise (most commonly to the lungs, liver, or bone) in advanced disease.
  • They are resistant to conventional chemotherapy and relatively radioresistant, making wide surgical resection the mainstay of treatment, sometimes combined with high-dose or proton-beam radiotherapy.

Chondrosarcoma (Option A): A malignant cartilage-producing tumour that most commonly involves the pelvis, proximal femur, and proximal humerus; although it can affect the spine, it is not the most common primary malignant tumour of the sacrum, unlike chordoma.

Osteosarcoma (Option B): The most common primary malignant bone tumour overall, typically arising in the metaphysis of long bones (e.g., distal femur, proximal tibia) in adolescents and young adults; primary involvement of the sacrum is rare.

Giant cell tumour (Option D): A locally aggressive but usually benign tumour that commonly affects the epiphysis of long bones and is the most common benign tumour of the sacrum; it typically shows a “soap-bubble” lytic appearance and is not classified as a malignant tumour in this context.



Reference:

Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th Edition, Page 1021
question: A destructive, lytic lesion is identified in the sacrum on imaging. Given that it is the most common primary malignant tumour of the sacrum, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Ewing sarcoma is a highly aggressive primary bone malignancy of children and young adults and is notable for its tendency to present with systemic inflammatory symptoms, sometimes mimicking osteomyelitis.
  • The presence of fever reflects a high inflammatory and tumour burden and is associated with more aggressive disease biology, making it a poor prognostic indicator.
  • Fever is often accompanied by elevated ESR and leukocytosis, both of which also correlate with worse outcomes.
  • In contrast, smaller tumour size and lower inflammatory markers are associated with better survival.
  • Prognosis in Ewing sarcoma is influenced by several factors, including tumour size, site, presence of metastasis, response to chemotherapy, and systemic symptoms such as fever.

Normal ESR (Option A): A normal ESR suggests a lower inflammatory burden. It is the elevated ESR, not normal ESR, that is associated with poorer prognosis.

Small tumour size (Option B): A large tumour volume is a major adverse prognostic factor in Ewing sarcoma. A small tumour (<5 cm) is associated with better resectability and a more favourable outcome.

Female gender (Option D): Epidemiologically, male sex is associated with slightly worse outcomes.



Reference:
  • Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th Edition, Pages 1018 - 1021
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559183/
question: Which of the following is considered an indicator of poor prognosis in a patient with Ewing sarcoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant bone tumour that most frequently involves the diaphysis (mid-shaft) of long bones.

  • It typically affects children and adolescents and commonly involves the femur, tibia, humerus, and also the pelvis.
  • A diaphyseal lesion in a young patient with an aggressive periosteal reaction (classically an “onion-skin” pattern) is a classic presentation of Ewing sarcoma.

[[figure-1]]

Epiphysis (Option A): The epiphysis is the end of the long bone near the joint. Primary tumours in this location are uncommon in children; chondroblastoma (in children/adolescents) and giant cell tumour (in skeletally mature patients) are the typical epiphyseal tumours.

Metaphysis (Option B): The metaphysis is the most common site for many primary bone tumours such as osteosarcoma and osteochondroma.

Apophysis (Option D): An apophysis is a secondary ossification centre that serves as a tendon or ligament attachment site (e.g., tibial tuberosity). It is typically involved in traction-related conditions (such as Osgood-Schlatter disease) rather than being a primary site for malignant small round blue cell tumours like Ewing sarcoma.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 213
question: In which part of a long bone is Ewing sarcoma most commonly located?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant small round blue cell tumour that primarily affects children and young adults and is characterised by a specific chromosomal translocation, most commonly t(11;22)(q24;q12) resulting in the EWS-FLI1 fusion gene.
  • Histologically, the tumour is composed of densely packed, uniform small round blue cells with scant cytoplasm and fine, evenly distributed chromatin.
  • A characteristic diagnostic feature is that the tumour cells show positivity for Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) staining.
  • This PAS positivity occurs because the cytoplasm contains abundant glycogen. Importantly, this staining is diastase-sensitive, meaning the PAS positivity disappears after treatment with diastase, confirming that the PAS-positive material is glycogen.
  • This helps in differentiating Ewing sarcoma from other small round blue cell tumours such as neuroblastoma, which is typically not glycogen-rich.
  • On immunohistochemistry, Ewing sarcoma cells usually show strong membranous CD99 (MIC2) positivity.
  • Anatomically, the tumour most commonly arises in the diaphysis of long bones (such as the femur) or in the pelvis, and classically shows an “onion-skin” periosteal reaction on radiographs.

Lipid droplets (Option A): Demonstrated by stains like Oil Red O or Sudan Black, not by PAS.

Melanin granules (Option B): Characteristic of melanoma and identified by pigments or Masson-Fontana stain, not by PAS in this context.

Mucin (Option D): Although mucin can be PAS-positive, it is typically mucicarmine or Alcian blue positive; in Ewing sarcoma, PAS positivity is specifically due to diastase-sensitive glycogen.



Reference:
  • https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15045938/
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3077725/
question: In Ewing sarcoma, tumour cells characteristically show positivity for Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) staining due to the presence of which substance?

correctAnswer: C. Mesenchymal stem cells in bone marrow
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Ewing sarcoma is a highly aggressive small round blue cell tumour of bone and soft tissue that primarily affects children and adolescents.

  • Current evidence supports its origin from primitive mesenchymal stem/progenitor cells of the bone marrow, which undergo characteristic chromosomal translocations leading to malignant transformation.
  • The hallmark genetic abnormality is:
    • t(11;22)(q24;q12) resulting in the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion gene
  • The resulting fusion protein acts as an aberrant transcription factor that blocks normal cellular differentiation and drives uncontrolled proliferation of primitive mesenchymal cells.

Characteristic features of Ewing sarcoma:

  • Peak incidence: 10-20 years
  • Common sites: Diaphysis of long bones (especially femur), pelvis, ribs
  • Histology: Uniform small round blue cells with glycogen-rich cytoplasm (PAS-positive)
  • Immunohistochemistry: Strong membranous CD99 (MIC2) positivity
  • Cytogenetics: EWSR1-FLI1 fusion is the most common molecular abnormality.

Osteoblasts (Option A): Osteoblasts are the cells of origin for osteosarcoma, a malignant bone-forming tumour characterised by the production of malignant osteoid.

Chondroblasts (Option B): Tumours arising from the cartilaginous lineage, such as chondrosarcoma, originate from chondrocytes or chondroblasts rather than mesenchymal progenitor cells.

Epithelial cells (Option D): Ewing sarcoma is a primary mesenchymal tumour and does not arise from epithelial tissue.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 213

options.text: Mesenchymal stem cells in bone marrow

question: Ewing sarcoma is a malignant bone tumour that arises from which of the following cell types?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Breast carcinoma is the most common primary tumour causing bone metastases overall, because it is highly prevalent and patients often survive long enough for skeletal spread to occur.
  • The axial skeleton (spine, pelvis, ribs, proximal femur) is most commonly involved. Metastases from breast cancer are usually osteolytic or mixed, leading to pathological fractures, bone pain, hypercalcaemia, and spinal cord compression.
  • The most common cancers that metastasise to bone are:
    • Breast
    • Prostate
    • Lung
  • Among these, prostate cancer has the highest predilection for bone and classically produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) metastases, while lung cancer frequently causes aggressive osteolytic metastases and often presents with early skeletal involvement.

Thyroid carcinoma (Option B): Can cause osteolytic, highly vascular bone metastases (often to skull and spine), but it is far less common than breast cancer as a source of skeletal metastasis.

Colorectal carcinoma (Option C): May metastasise to bone in advanced disease, but the liver and lungs are more common metastatic sites, and bone involvement is much less frequent than in breast cancer.

Pancreatic carcinoma (Option D): Rarely metastasises to bone; it more commonly spreads to the liver and peritoneum, making it an uncommon cause of skeletal metastases.



Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 220
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507911/
question: Which of the following is the most common primary tumour causing bone metastases?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A moth-eaten pattern of bone destruction indicates an aggressive lytic process and is classically seen in conditions such as multiple myeloma, metastases, lymphoma, and Ewing sarcoma.
  • Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell disorder that commonly involves the skeleton.
  • The most characteristic skull finding is multiple well-defined “punched-out” lytic lesions producing the classic “raindrop skull” appearance, although more aggressive disease can show ill-defined, permeative or moth-eaten destruction.

[[figure-1]]

  • Other common skeletal manifestations include diffuse osteopenia, pathological fractures (especially of the ribs, pelvis, and long bones), and vertebral body collapse (vertebra plana).
  • On MRI, multiple myeloma shows focal or diffuse low-signal intensity on T1-weighted images due to replacement of fatty marrow by tumour cells, sometimes described as a heterogeneous or “salt-and-pepper” marrow pattern.

Osteoid osteoma (Option A): A benign tumour characterised by a small radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis, classically causing nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs; it does not produce a moth-eaten destructive pattern.

Paget’s disease of bone (Option B): In the skull, the early lytic phase shows osteoporosis circumscripta, and the later phase shows a “cotton wool” appearance due to disorganised bone formation, not a ragged moth-eaten pattern.

Osteopetrosis (Option D): A sclerosing bone disorder with generalised increased bone density (“marble bone”) and obliteration of the medullary cavity, not lytic destruction.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6206383/
question: A skull X-ray shows a "moth-eaten" appearance of bone, characterised by poorly defined areas of destruction with ragged edges. Which of the following conditions is a classic cause of this radiographic finding?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most common presenting symptom of multiple myeloma is bone pain, especially in the back and ribs, due to lytic bone lesions caused by increased osteoclast activity and suppressed osteoblast function.
  • These lytic lesions also predispose to pathological fractures.
  • Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow that produces a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein), leading to marrow infiltration, bone destruction, immunosuppression, and organ damage.

Diagnostic Criteria of Multiple Myeloma:

Diagnosis requires BOTH:

  • Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥10% OR biopsy-proven plasmacytoma

AND

  • At least one myeloma-defining event:

A) CRAB Features:

  • C → Hypercalcemia (Ca >11 mg/dL)
  • R → Renal insufficiency (Creatinine >2 mg/dL)
  • A → Anaemia (Hb <10 g/dL)
  • B → Bone lesions (lytic lesions on imaging)

OR

B) Biomarkers of Malignancy:

  • ≥60% clonal plasma cells in bone marrow
  • Serum free light chain ratio ≥100
  • Focal lesion on MRI (>5 mm)

Fatigue (Option A): Common due to anaemia, but it is usually a secondary symptom and not the most frequent presenting complaint.

Hypercalcemia (Option B): A classic feature of multiple myeloma, but present in only about 20-30% of patients at diagnosis and is a complication of bone resorption rather than the most common symptom.

Peripheral neuropathy (Option D): Uncommon as a presenting feature of typical multiple myeloma; more often seen in POEMS syndrome, AL amyloidosis, or as a treatment-related adverse effect (e.g., bortezomib, thalidomide).



Reference:

Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th Edition, Page 1025
question: Which of the following is the most common symptom in patients with multiple myeloma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Osteosarcoma spreads primarily via the hematogenous route, and the lungs are both the earliest and the most common site of metastasis.
  • Pulmonary micrometastases are frequently present at diagnosis, even when not visible on plain radiographs, which is why a CT scan of the chest is mandatory for staging.
  • Although osteosarcoma can also metastasise to other bones and rarely to lymph nodes, these are less common than lung involvement.
  • The presence of metastasis at diagnosis is a major adverse prognostic factor and usually necessitates aggressive multi-agent chemotherapy combined with surgical resection of the primary tumour and, when feasible, pulmonary metastases.

Liver (Option A): An uncommon site of metastasis for osteosarcoma; more typical for gastrointestinal malignancies.

Regional lymph nodes (Option B): Sarcomas, including osteosarcoma, rarely spread via lymphatics; nodal metastasis is uncommon and usually indicates advanced disease.

Bones (Option C): Bone metastases and skip lesions can occur and carry a poor prognosis, but they are less common as the initial and predominant site of spread compared to the lungs.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8702962/
question: What is the earliest and most common site of metastasis in osteosarcoma?

correctAnswer: B. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy, ablative surgery (amputation), and adjuvant chemotherapy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Modern treatment of osteosarcoma is multimodal.
  • Limb-salvage surgery is the preferred option in most patients, but amputation (ablative surgery) is indicated when safe oncological margins cannot be achieved.
  • Standard management begins with multi-agent neoadjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., doxorubicin, cisplatin, ifosfamide, methotrexate) for about 8-12 weeks, followed by re-staging.
  • If the tumour is resectable with safe margins, wide resection and limb reconstruction are performed.
  • However, when attempted excision would compromise tumour-free margins (e.g., major neurovascular involvement), ablative surgery is required.
  • After surgery, the resected specimen is examined to assess margin status and tumour necrosis (≥90% necrosis indicates a good response).
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy is then continued or modified based on this response.
  • Because osteosarcoma is relatively radioresistant, radiotherapy is not a primary treatment modality and is reserved for unresectable disease or palliation.

Wide resection alone (Option A): Inadequate for high-grade osteosarcoma because micrometastases are usually present at diagnosis; survival is poor without chemotherapy.

Radiotherapy alone followed by limb-sparing surgery (Option C): Osteosarcoma is radioresistant; radiotherapy is not used as primary local treatment to enable limb salvage.

Adjuvant chemotherapy only after limb-sparing resection (Option D): Omitting neoadjuvant chemotherapy is suboptimal. Pre-operative chemotherapy is essential to treat micrometastases early and to assess histological tumour necrosis, a key prognostic factor.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 206, 208

options.text: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy, ablative surgery (amputation), and adjuvant chemotherapy
Radiotherapy alone followed by limb-sparing surgery
Adjuvant chemotherapy only after limb-sparing resection

question: A patient has osteosarcoma in which safe surgical margins cannot be achieved with limb-salvage surgery. According to standard management protocols, what is the recommended treatment approach?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The radiograph demonstrates a Codman triangle, an aggressive periosteal reaction produced when a rapidly growing lesion elevates the periosteum faster than new bone can be deposited.

  • Only the edges of the lifted periosteum ossify, producing the characteristic triangular area of subperiosteal new bone.

[[figure-1]]

  • A Codman triangle is classically associated with osteosarcoma, the most common primary malignant bone tumor.
  • Radiographic features of osteosarcoma include:
    • Mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion
    • Cloud-like (fluffy) osteoid matrix
    • Codman triangle
    • Cortical destruction with an associated ossified soft-tissue mass
    • Sunburst (sunray) periosteal reaction

[[figure-2]]

Onion-skin periosteal reaction (Option A): Characterised by multiple concentric layers of periosteal new bone and is classically associated with Ewing sarcoma, although it may also occur in osteomyelitis.

Soap-bubble lesion (Option C): Refers to an expansile, multiloculated lytic lesion, classically seen in giant cell tumor and occasionally in an aneurysmal bone cyst.

Central nidus with surrounding sclerosis (Option D): Characteristic radiographic appearance of osteoid osteoma, showing a small radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 206
question: Which of the following radiographic finding is shown here:

correctAnswer: B. Osteoid production by malignant stromal cells
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Osteosarcoma is defined by the direct production of osteoid (immature bone) by malignant tumour cells, which is the diagnostic hallmark.
  • The osteoid typically appears as eosinophilic, lace-like or delicate trabecular matrix intimately associated with malignant cells.
  • The tumour shows marked cellular pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, and high mitotic activity, reflecting its high-grade nature.
  • Growth is infiltrative, often destroying pre-existing bone and extending into surrounding soft tissues, and vascular invasion is common, explaining the frequent hematogenous metastasis to the lungs.
  • Depending on the subtype, areas of cartilage (chondroblastic) or fibrous tissue (fibroblastic) may be present, but malignant osteoid must be identified to make the diagnosis.

[[figure-1]]

Cartilaginous matrix production (Option A): This is the hallmark of chondrosarcoma. Although chondroblastic osteosarcoma may contain cartilage, the presence of malignant osteoid is what defines osteosarcoma.

Small round blue cells (Option C): Characteristic of Ewing sarcoma and some lymphomas, not of osteosarcoma, which shows malignant osteoid rather than a small round cell pattern.

[[figure-2]]

Multinucleated giant cells (Option D): The defining feature of giant cell tumour of bone (osteoclastoma). While occasional giant cells may be seen in osteosarcoma, they are not the diagnostic hallmark.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 206

options.text: Cartilaginous matrix production by tumour cells
Osteoid production by malignant stromal cells

question: The histopathological hallmark of osteosarcoma is:

correctAnswer: C. MRI of the involved bone
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI of the involved bone is the gold standard for local staging in osteosarcoma.
  • It accurately defines the intramedullary extent of the tumour, soft-tissue extension, epiphyseal and joint involvement, and the relationship to major neurovascular structures, all of which are critical for surgical planning (limb salvage versus amputation and margin selection).
  • MRI is also the best modality for detecting skip lesions within the same bone and for planning the biopsy tract, which must be excised en bloc during definitive surgery.

Plain radiography (Option A): Useful as an initial investigation to show features such as sunburst periosteal reaction or Codman triangle, but cannot accurately assess marrow or soft-tissue extent, so it is insufficient for surgical planning.

CT scan of the chest (Option B): Essential for metastatic staging because the lungs are the most common site of spread, but it does not assess the local extent of the primary bone tumour.

Bone scintigraphy (Option D): Useful for detecting skip lesions or distant skeletal metastases, but it lacks anatomical detail and is not suitable for defining surgical margins.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 206
question: Which imaging modality is most essential for local staging and surgical planning in osteosarcoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Osteosarcoma is a highly malignant primary bone tumour defined by direct production of osteoid by malignant cells.
  • It can be markedly hypervascular, and in particular, the telangiectatic variant may present as a pulsatile mass with an audible bruit, reflecting its rich blood supply.
  • The tumour most commonly arises in the metaphysis of long bones, especially around the knee (distal femur, proximal tibia) and the proximal humerus.
  • Classic radiographic features include a sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman’s triangle.
  • It spreads hematogenously, most often to the lungs, and standard treatment involves multi-agent chemotherapy combined with surgical resection.

Pulsatile Tumours in the Body:

  • Osteosarcoma (bone)
  • Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC)
  • Giant cell tumour (occasionally hypervascular)
  • Glomus tumour (subungual, very painful & vascular)
  • Carotid body tumour (paraganglioma)
  • Glomangioma / hemangioma
  • Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) (tumour-like vascular lesions)
  • Renal cell carcinoma metastasis (highly vascular)
  • Thyroid carcinoma (especially follicular) metastasis

Osteochondroma (Option A): A benign cartilage-capped exostosis that is slow-growing and non-vascular; it does not present as a pulsatile mass.

Chondrosarcoma (Option C): A malignant cartilage-producing tumour, often large and destructive, but not classically hypervascular or pulsatile.

Ewing sarcoma (Option D): A highly aggressive diaphyseal tumour of children and adolescents, typically showing an “onion-skin” periosteal reaction; it is not classically described as a pulsatile mass.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3671797/

Osteosarcoma is a primary malignant bone tumour defined by direct production of osteoid by malignant cells.

question: Which primary bone tumour is considered radioresistant, making surgery the mainstay of treatment?

explanationHtml:
Osteosarcoma is a common primary bone tumor that often presents in adolescents and young adults with localized pain that worsens over time. It is typically seen in the metaphysis of long bones, and the X-ray findings often show a characteristic "sunburst" pattern or Codman's triangle.



Osteogenic Sarcoma (Osteosarcoma):

  • Most common primary malignant bone tumor of non-hematopoietic origin/ solid malignant bone tumor.
  • Age group: Bimodal age distribution peaking in adolescence (10–14 years) and again in the seventh decade.
  • Gender: Males >> Female

Pathology:

  • Origin: It arises from mesenchymal cells.
  • Common site: From the metaphysis or meta-diaphysis.
  • Order of frequency: Lower-end of the femur > upper-end of the tibia > upper-end of the humerus.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • All osteosarcomas are aggressive and metastasize widely through the hematogenous route, typically to the lungs.
  • Despite its aggressiveness, it seldom penetrates the epiphyseal plate.

Histopathology: Anaplastic mesenchymal parenchyma with tumor cells surrounded by osteoid.

Clinical manifestation:

  • Worsening pain and swelling, particularly night pain.
  • Pathological fracture is rare.
  • On examination:
    • Shiny skin with prominent veins over swelling.
    • Poorly defined, warm, and tender swelling.
    • Adjacent joint movement may be limited due to swelling.
    • The tumor may compress neurovascular structures, causing symptoms.
    • Usually reactive enlargement of regional lymph nodes.
  • Associated syndromes with osteosarcoma development:
    • Li–Fraumeni (p53 tumor suppressor gene mutation)
    • Hereditary retinoblastoma syndromes
    • Rothmund–Thomson syndrome

X-ray findings of osteosarcoma:

  • Area of irregular destruction in the metaphysis. The cortex overlying the lesion is eroded.

Sun-ray appearance (aggressive periostitis): As the tumor grows into the overlying soft tissues new bone is laid down centrifugally along the blood vessels within the tumor.

[[figure-3]]

  • Codman's triangle: Elevation of periosteum by the growing tumor in the form of a triangle. (Option C)

  • [[figure-4]]

CT scan is primarily used to assist with biopsy and disease staging.

Treatment

Combination of therapy:

  • Surgical amputation is the treatment of choice- complete removal of the tumor must be ensured. Limb-salvage procedures have become possible and popular.
  • Radiotherapy
  • Chemotherapy
    • Doxorubicin
    • Cisplatin
    • Ifosfamide
    • Methotrexate
  • Follow-up: Every 6-8 weeks. Evidence of recurrence of the primary tumor or appearance of the secondary (usually in the chest) is diagnosed early and treated.





Option B: Ewing sarcoma

  • Typically occurs in children and adolescents.
  • More common in the diaphysis of long bones (e.g., femur, pelvis).
  • X-ray shows an onion-skin (lamellated) periosteal reaction and moth-eaten appearance due to aggressive bone destruction.
  • Associated with t(11;22) translocation.

Option C: Chondrosarcoma

  • More common in older adults (>40 years).
  • Arises in the pelvis, femur, or proximal humerus.
  • X-ray shows a rings and arcs (popcorn) calcification pattern due to cartilaginous matrix production.

Option D: Gout

  • A metabolic disorder causing monosodium urate crystal deposition.
  • Typically affects the 1st metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) but can involve other joints.

X-ray findings include punched-out erosions with overhanging edges (rat-bite lesions), not the characteristic periosteal reactions seen in osteosarcoma.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 206

question: A 20-year-old male patient presented with localized pain, which is gradual in onset and worsened over time. X-ray showed the following finding. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Enchondromas are benign hyaline cartilage tumors of unknown etiology occurring in bones of endochondral origin.
  • Although they can develop in other bones as well, these tumors are most frequently found in the tiny bones of the hands and feet.
  • When multiple enchondromas manifest in a unilateral pattern, the ailment is known as Ollier's disease.
  • In the given X-ray growth of some benign tumors made of cartilage tissue near the tiny bones of the hand is observed.

Multiple Enchondromatosis

  • Definition: Condition characterized by numerous benign cartilaginous tumors (chondromas).
  • Associated Conditions:
    • Ollier's disease- only enchondromas
    • Maffucci syndrome- enchondromas + hemangiomas

[[figure-1]]

Ollier's Disease

Feature

Details

Usually diagnosed in childhood

Most chondromas found in phalangeal bones

Common findings:

  • Swelling of fingers/toes

question: Identify the following condition

explanationHtml:
• The tibia is the most common site for adamantinoma, particularly the anterior metaphysis or diaphysis. This predilection is due to the close proximity of the tibia's enchondral bone to the skin, which supports the embryological displacement theory.

Adamantinoma

About
  • Rare, low-grade malignant bone tumors of uncertain histogenesis
  • Commonly affects the anterior metaphysis and diaphysis tibia, close to the skin surface.
  • Immunohistochemical studies suggest epithelial origin.
  • Commonly affects individuals aged 20-40 years.

Histopathology
  • Macroscopic: Well-defined, lobulated cortical tumors with yellowish-gray appearance and possible cystic spaces.
  • Microscopic: Biphasic composition (epithelial and osteofibrous components) with basaloid, tubular, spindle-cell, squamous, and osteofibrous dysplasia-like patterns.
  • Immunohistochemistry:
    • Epithelial cells: Positive for keratin, EMA, vimentin, p63, podoplanin.
    • Fibrous component: Positive for vimentin.
    • Expression of EGF, EGFR (epithelial), FGF2, FGFR1 (both components).

Clinical Features
  • Prolonged clinical course with slow-growing swelling, possible pain, bone deformities, or pathological fractures (~23%).
  • Rarely involves neurological deficits when the spine is affected.
  • Metastases commonly involve lungs, lymph nodes, or spine.

Evaluation
  • X-ray: Well-circumscribed, multilobulated, osteolytic cortical tumor with a "soap-bubble" appearance.
  • CT Scan: Assesses soft tissue extension and cortical involvement.
  • MRI: Locoregional staging; visualizes tumor margins, cortical involvement, and soft tissue extension.

Treatment
  • Wide Resection: En bloc removal with wide margins preferred.
  • Metastasectomy: First-line for pulmonary recurrences.

Radius (Option A): Although adamantinoma can rarely occur in the radius, it is an atypical site. The tibia remains the most frequently affected bone.

Humerus (Option B): Adamantinoma seldom affects the humerus. It primarily involves long bones of the lower limb, with the tibia being the most common.

Femur (Option C) can be involved in rare cases, but it is far less commonly affected than the tibia.



Reference:

Adamantinoma - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

Description

  • It commonly arises from epiphysis.
  • MC Age: 20 and 45 years of age.

Sites affected

Malignancy
  • Malignant transformation in <1% of cases.
  • Lungs are the most common site for metastases.

Clinical features

  • Pathological fracture.

Radiology

[[figure-2]]

Management
  • Extended curettage with Bone grafting

Incorrect Options:

Osteosarcoma (Option A): Sunburst appearance on X-ray, seen in children. Biopsy shows cellular pleomorphism, osteoid formation with increased mitotic activity.

Ewing’s Sarcoma (Option B): Associated with fever, Onion peel appearance on x-ray. Small round blue cells, homer-wright rosettes are seen on biopsy.

question: What is the probable diagnosis for a 30-year-old female who presents with a tumor located at the knee joint, as shown in the provided biopsy-image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the demographics of the patient, clinical manifestation, and X-ray showing sunburst appearance, the most probable diagnosis is osteosarcoma. It most commonly originates in the metaphysis of long bones.

Osteogenic Sarcoma (Osteosarcoma):

  • Most common primary malignant bone tumor of non-hematopoietic origin/ solid malignant bone tumor.
  • Age group: Bimodal age distribution peaking in adolescence (10–14 years) and again in the seventh decade.
  • Gender: Males >> Female

Pathology:

  • Origin: It arises from mesenchymal cells.
  • Common site: From the metaphysis or meta-diaphysis
  • Order of frequency: Lower-end of the femur > upper-end of the tibia > upper-end of the humerus.
Types base on Clinical Setting

Primary osteosarcoma

  • No known pre-malignant conditions related to it.
  • Age group: 15-25 years

Secondary osteosarcoma

  • Pre-malignant conditions are often associated with it.
  • Paget's disease, multiple enchondromatosis, fibrous dysplasia, irradiation to bones, multiple osteochondroma.
  • Older age group

[[figure-1]]

  • All osteosarcomas are aggressive and metastasize widely through the hematogenous route, typically to the lungs.
  • Despite its aggressiveness, it seldom penetrates the epiphyseal plate.

Histopathology: Anaplastic mesenchymal parenchyma with tumor cells surrounded by osteoid.

Clinical manifestation:

  • Worsening pain and swelling, particularly night pain.
  • Pathological fracture is rare.
  • On examination:
    • Shiny skin with prominent veins over swelling.
    • Poorly defined, warm, and tender swelling.
    • Adjacent joint movement may be limited due to swelling.
    • The tumor may compress neurovascular structures, causing symptoms.
    • Usually reactive enlargement of regional lymph nodes.
  • Associated syndromes with osteosarcoma development:
    • Li–Fraumeni (p53 tumor suppressor gene mutation)
    • Hereditary retinoblastoma syndromes
    • Rothmund–Thomson syndrome

X-ray findings of osteosarcoma:

  • Area of irregular destruction in the metaphysis. The cortex overlying the lesion is eroded.
  • Sun-ray appearance (aggressive periostitis): As the tumor grows into the overlying soft tissues new bone is laid down centrifugally along the blood vessels within the tumor.

[[figure-2]]

  • Codman's triangle: Elevation of periosteum by the growing tumor in the form of a triangle.

[[figure-3]]

CT scan is primarily used to assist with biopsy and disease staging.

Incorrect Options:

Giant Cell Tumor (Option A):

  • Benign but aggressive tumor, typically affecting older adolescents/adults.
  • Seen in the epiphysis, not typically with the "sunburst" appearance.
  • Usually localized, not extending aggressively like osteosarcoma.

Chondroblastoma (Option B):

  • Benign tumor, usually in the epiphysis of long bones.
  • Common in adolescents but lacks aggressive features like periosteal reactions seen in osteosarcoma.

Osteoid Osteoma (Option C):

  • Benign tumor causing localized pain, often relieved by NSAIDs.
  • Small lesion with central nidus and sclerosis, no aggressive periosteal reaction.


Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 205, 206, 213, 214
  2. Osteosarcoma - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)

question: A 28-year old male with gradual progressive swelling around his wrist joint for 3 months. Image of the swelling on the x-ray film is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Condition

Features and Findings

Treatment

Osteosarcoma

[[figure-1]]
  • A malignant bone tumor, commonly affecting the metaphyses of long bones (e.g., femur, tibia).
  • It most frequently occurs in adolescents and young adults. Symptoms include pain, swelling, and sometimes a palpable mass.
  • X-rays typically show a sunburst appearance with mixed lytic and sclerotic areas.
  • Surgical resection (amputation or limb-sparing surgery), followed by chemotherapy.
  • Radiation therapy is rarely used.

Simple Bone Cyst

[[figure-2]]
  • A benign, fluid-filled cyst, often occurring in the proximal humerus or femur.
  • It is typically asymptomatic
  • On X-ray, it appears as a well-defined, cystic lesion with a thin cortical rim.
  • Often occurs in children and adolescents.
  • Aspiration and steroid injection, or curettage with bone grafting if recurrent fractures occur.
  • Surgical intervention is usually necessary if there is risk of fracture.

Giant Cell Tumor

[[figure-3]]
  • A benign, locally aggressive tumor that typically occurs in the epiphysis of long bones (e.g., distal femur, proximal tibia).
  • It is most common in young adults.
  • Symptoms include pain, swelling, and sometimes joint dysfunction.
  • X-rays show a lytic lesion with a "soap bubble" appearance.
  • Curettage with bone grafting or chemical adjuvants (e.g., phenol). Wide resection for larger or more aggressive tumors..

Osteoid Osteoma

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]
  • A benign bone tumor that most commonly affects the femur or tibia. It typically occurs in adolescents or young adults.
  • Characterized by a small, well-circumscribed lesion with a central nidus on X-ray.
  • Symptoms include localized pain, especially at night, that is relieved by NSAIDs.
  • Surgical excision of the nidus is the standard treatment. Radiofrequency ablation can be used
  • Pain is often well-controlled with NSAIDs until definitive treatment.

question: A 30-year-old female patient presented with complaints of a gradually progressive swelling around her wrist joint for 3 months. Given below is the image of the X-ray film. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The probable diagnosis is Osteoclastoma.
  • Osteoclastoma, also known as a giant cell tumor, is a locally aggressive and destructive bone tumor that is composed of multinucleated giant cells and stromal cells.
  • Osteoclastoma is most commonly seen in the epiphysis or metaphysis of long bones such as the distal femur, proximal tibia, and distal radius.
  • Soap bubble appearance is the characteristic radiological finding of giant cell tumors.
  • It presents as a lytic lesion with multiple internal septations, giving it a soap bubble appearance.
  • It is usually located in the epiphysis of long bones, such as the distal femur.

X-ray findings in Giant cell tumors (GCTs):

  • Eccentric location, often subchondral.
  • Expansion of the overlying cortex.
  • The cortex may be thinned out.

Lobulated lytic lesions with narrow zones of transition produce a soap bubble appearance.

[[figure-1]]

  • No calcification within the tumor.
  • No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor.
  • The tumor usually does not enter the adjacent joint.

Treatment:

  • The treatment of choice is excision.
  • Followed by reconstruction procedures and bone grafting or polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) insertion.
  • Adjuvant treatments:
    • Liquid nitrogen and phenol have been shown to decrease recurrences.
    • Bisphosphonates like zoledronate or pamidronate
  • Radiotherapy- especially for spine GCTs
  • Drugs:

Denosumab- anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 198, 199, 206, 213, 214.

  • Tumours can arise within the medullary cavity, called enchondromas or on the bone surface, where they are called juxtacortical chondromas.
  • It is the most common type of benign bone tumor of the phalanges of the hand and is usually seen in 10 to 30 years of age.
  • Both Maffucci syndrome and Ollier’s disease are characterised by multiple enchondromas (not solitary).

question: A 20-year-old patient presents with painful swelling in the index finger around the proximal phalanx. An X-ray was done, and it is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: C) Osteochondroma

Explanation:

  • The radiograph shows a well-defined bony protuberance arising from the metaphysis of the distal femur, which is consistent with an osteochondroma.

Osteochondroma:

  • Benign cartilaginous neoplasms arising from physeal cartilage beneath the periosteum.
  • Growth via enchondral ossification, similar to normal bone development.
  • More common in males, usually appearing during adolescence.
  • Affects long bones, especially the femur and humerus.

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Presentation

  • Usually presents as a painless mass.
  • Symptoms may include:
    • Formation of a bursa due to friction.
    • Activity-related discomfort.
  • Rare symptoms:
    • Neuropathic pain from nerve compression.
    • Sudden pain due to fracture.

Osteochondroma: X-ray, Treatment, and Complications

X-ray Appearance

  • Bony protuberance with distinct edges.
  • Widened host bone cortex extending into the osteochondroma.
  • Features may include:
    • Thin outer cortex, cancellous structure.
    • Pedunculated (cauliflower-like) or sessile base.
    • Pedunculated types grow away from joints, toward the diaphysis.

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

MRI to assess the cartilage cap thickness

  • Reserved for cases where malignant transformation is suspected.

[[figure-4]]

Biopsy to rule out malignancy

  • Indicated without symptoms such as pain or rapid growth.

Treatment

  • Asymptomatic osteochondromas: No treatment required. (Option B)
  • Excision indicated for:
    • Large lesions causing pressure.
    • Concern for malignant transformation in adults.

Complications

Complication

Description

Painful bursa formation

Due to friction over the osteochondroma.

Activity-related discomfort

General discomfort with movement.

Nerve compression

Rare, may cause neuropathic symptoms.

Fracture

Uncommon, results in sudden pain.

Malignant transformation

Rare progression to chondrosarcoma, more likely with a cartilage cap >1.5 cm.

  • Malignant transformation risk factors:
    • Large cartilage cap (>1.5 cm on MRI).
    • Osteochondroma location: More common in the trunk, rare in extremities.
    • Risk Factors: Increased size or new pain after skeletal maturity, especially in Multiple Osteochondromas.

Enchondroma (Option A) are benign cartilaginous tumors that typically arise within the medullary canal of long bones, such as the proximal humerus or femur. They are usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on radiographs.

[[figure-5]]

Chondroblastoma (Option B) are rare benign bone tumors that arise in the epiphysis of long bones, such as the proximal humerus or femur. On X-ray, they are seen as round or oval lytic lesions in the epiphysis.

[[figure-6]]

Giant Cell Tumor (Option D) are benign bone tumors that typically arise in the epiphysis of long bones, such as the distal femur or proximal tibia. They may cause pain and swelling and erode adjacent bone, resulting in pathologic fractures. On radiographs, giant cell tumors appear as lytic lesions with a "soap bubble" appearance.

[[figure-7]]



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 192

Incorrect options:

  • It usually presents with a painful, rapidly growing mass.

Option B - Multiple myeloma:

  • Multiple myeloma is a hematological malignancy that affects plasma cells in the bone marrow.
  • It does not present as a palpable bony mass near the metaphysis of a long bone.
  • On an X-ray, multiple myeloma can show lytic lesions throughout the bone, often referred to as "punched-out" lesions.

Option D - Osteoid osteoma

  • Osteoid osteoma is a benign bone tumor that causes localized pain that is relieved by NSAIDs.
  • It is typically found in the cortex of long bones, rather than near the metaphysis.

question: A patient has a painless, palpable bony mass near the metaphysis of a long bone. X-ray done shows the following finding. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Osteosarcoma :

  • Teriparatide is prescribed for treating medication-induced osteonecrosis, but it carries a risk of osteosarcoma, although this is rare. Patients with a higher baseline risk for osteosarcoma, including those with Paget disease of bone, unexplained elevations of alkaline phosphatase, open epiphyses, or prior radiation therapy involving the skeleton, should avoid using teriparatide.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Osteonecrosis of jaw: Osteonecrosis of the jaw can result from bisphosphonates and denosumab. Teriparatide, however, doesn't cause this condition; it's used to treat it.

Option B - Net bone loss: Teriparatide is not responsible for net bone loss or osteoporosis; instead, it is employed in treating postmenopausal and corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis.

Option D - Subtrochanteric fracture of the femur: Teriparatide does not cause subtrochanteric fracture of the femur
question: Which of the following is a complication of intermittent administration of teriparatide?

  • Osteochondroma, also known as exostosis, is characterized by an exophytic growth from the bone. This type of growth appears as a cauliflower-like structure in imaging studies.

Osteochondroma:

  • Benign cartilaginous neoplasms arising from physeal cartilage beneath the periosteum.
  • Growth via enchondral ossification, similar to normal bone development.
  • More common in males, usually appearing during adolescence.
  • Affects long bones, especially the femur and humerus.

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Presentation

  • Usually presents as a painless mass.
  • Symptoms may include:
    • Formation of a bursa due to friction.
    • Activity-related discomfort.
  • Rare symptoms:
    • Neuropathic pain from nerve compression.
    • Sudden pain due to fracture.

Factors affecting malignant transformation:

  • Larger lesions with thicker cartilage caps (especially >1.5 cm).
  • More common in trunk lesions, and rare in extremities.
  • Suspicious changes in size or pain after skeletal maturity in MO patients.

Radiographic Appearance

  • Bony protuberance with well-defined borders.
  • Key radiographic features:
    • Cortex flaring into the osteochondroma. (Option B)
    • Thin outer cortex with inner cancellous structure.
    • Pedunculated (cauliflower-like summit) or broad sessile base.
    • Pedunculated lesions point away from the joint toward the diaphysis.

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]


  • MRI findings:
    • Cartilaginous cap thickness, generally thicker in children and thins with age.

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

Enchondroma (Options A) presents with Asymmetric limb shortening, Swelling of fingers/toes and impaired movement of interphalangeal joints

Osteosarcoma (Options B) Sun-rays appearance is typically seen in osteosarcoma.

Osteomyelitis (Options D) shows periosteal new bone formation (periosteal reaction) by 7-10 days



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 192
question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the clinic complaining of a painless lump on the lateral aspect of his left knee. The radiograph of the patient is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: C) Osteogenic sarcoma

Explanation:

  • Codman’s triangle is seen in Osteogenic sarcoma
  • The elevation of the periosteum in the form of a triangle is known as Codman's triangle.

Osteogenic Sarcoma (Osteosarcoma):

  • Most common primary malignant bone tumor of non-hematopoietic origin/ solid malignant bone tumor.
  • Age group: Bimodal age distribution peaking in adolescence (10–14 years) and again in the seventh decade.
  • Gender: Males >> Female

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • All osteosarcomas are aggressive and metastasize widely through the hematogenous route, typically to the lungs.
  • Despite its aggressiveness, it seldom penetrates the epiphyseal plate.

Histopathology: Anaplastic mesenchymal parenchyma with tumor cells surrounded by osteoid.

Clinical manifestation:

  • Worsening pain and swelling, particularly night pain.
  • Pathological fracture is rare.
  • On examination:
    • Shiny skin with prominent veins over swelling.
    • Poorly defined, warm, and tender swelling.
    • Adjacent joint movement may be limited due to swelling.
    • The tumor may compress neurovascular structures, causing symptoms.
    • Usually reactive enlargement of regional lymph nodes.
  • Associated syndromes with osteosarcoma development:
    • Li–Fraumeni (p53 tumor suppressor gene mutation)
    • Hereditary retinoblastoma syndromes
    • Rothmund–Thomson syndrome

X-ray findings of osteosarcoma:

  • Area of irregular destruction in the metaphysis. The cortex overlying the lesion is eroded.
  • Sun-ray appearance (aggressive periostitis): As the tumor grows into the overlying soft tissues new bone is laid down centrifugally along the blood vessels within the tumor.

[[figure-3]]

  • Codman's triangle: Elevation of periosteum by the growing tumor in the form of a triangle.

[[figure-4]]

CT scan is primarily used to assist with biopsy and disease staging.

Treatment

Combination of therapy:

  • Surgical amputation is the treatment of choice- complete removal of the tumor must be ensured. Limb-salvage procedures have become possible and popular.
  • Radiotherapy
  • Chemotherapy
    • Doxorubicin
    • Cisplatin
    • Ifosfamide
    • Methotrexate
  • Follow-up: Every 6-8 weeks. Evidence of recurrence of the primary tumor or appearance of the secondary (usually in the chest) is diagnosed early and treated.

Osteomyelitis (Options A), Aneurysmal bone cyst (Options B) and Chondrosarcoma (Options D) are not associated with Codman’s triangle.



Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 205, 206, 213, 214
  • Osteosarcoma - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)
question: Codman's triangle is seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is often characterized by an expansile, lytic lesion, and its FNA typically yields a bloody aspirate due to the cystic, vascular nature of the lesion.
  • Hemosiderin-laden macrophages are commonly seen due to prior hemorrhage within the cyst.

Giant cell tumor (GCT) (Option A) can also present as an expansile lytic lesion, but it usually involves the epiphysis without such a significant cystic, vascular component or bloody aspirate on FNA.

Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC)

Giant Cell Tumor (GCT)

Age

Primarily affects children and teenagers

Most common in young adults (15-35 years)

Gender

Equal distribution between males and females

More common in females (Female: Male ratio 1.5:1)

Location

Metaphyses of long bones (femur, tibia, humerus), spine

Epiphyses of long bones (lower end of femur, upper end of tibia)

Symptoms

Pain and swelling; spinal lesions may cause neurological issues

Swelling without pain; late stages show joint limitation and pathological fracture

Histology
  • FNAC: Hemosiderin +
  • Blood-filled cystic spaces separated by fibrous septae
  • FNAC: No hemosiderin
  • Abundant giant cells with multiple nuclei (>150), spindle cells indicating malignancy

Radiology

Osteolytic lesion, multiple septations and fluid-fluid levels on MRI

Thin septa with soap-bubble appearance on X-ray, cortex thin and expanded, no periosteal reaction

Treatment

Curettage, debridement, and in some cases radiation (cautiously)

Surgical excision with PMMA or bone grafting; Denosumab and bisphosphonates as adjunct therapy

Osteosarcoma (Option C): It is a malignant tumor that presents with mixed lytic-sclerotic lesions and periosteal reactions rather than a purely lytic, expansile lesion with a bloody aspirate.


Chondroblastoma (Option D): It is a rare benign tumor that affects the epiphysis, usually seen in younger patients, but it does not typically show a bloody aspirate or hemosiderin deposits on FNA.



Reference:

Bony metastasis is the most common cause of pathological fracture in elderly.

Metastatic Tumors to Bone

Common Metastatic Tumors
  • Lung carcinoma (male)

Clinical Features

A brown tumour (Option C) is associated with hyperparathyroidism, which causes bone resorption and weakening.

Eosinophilic granuloma (a form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis) (Option D) is a rare condition more commonly seen in children or young adults.

explanationHtml:

  • Osteoclastoma is a benign bone tumor that typically presents as a painful, gradually enlarging mass, most commonly located in the epiphyseal region of long bones.

question: A 30-year-old male patient presented with complaints of a gradually progressive swelling around his wrist joint for 3 months. Given below is the X-ray image of the affected wrist. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In a school‑aged child with pain, swelling, systemic symptoms (low‑grade fever), elevated ESR, and a mid‑diaphyseal lesion (“onion‑skin” periosteal reaction on X‑ray), the most likely diagnosis is Ewing sarcoma, a primary malignant bone tumor.

Incorrect Options:

  • Osteosarcoma (Option A) presents in adolescents around the knee (distal femur/proximal tibia) or proximal humerus, rather than the mid-diaphysis, and often lacks systemic symptoms, such as fever.
  • Non‑ossifying fibroma (Option C) is a benign, asymptomatic lesion often discovered incidentally in the metaphysis of long bones, not painful with systemic signs.
  • Osteoid osteoma (Option D) presents with nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs and a characteristic nidus on imaging, but does not cause significant swelling, fever, or elevated ESR like Ewing sarcoma.

question: A 9-year-old child presents with pain and swelling over the mid-shaft of the tibia, associated with low-grade fever and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). An X-ray of the affected limb is shown below. Based on the clinical features and radiographic findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • An enchondroma is a benign cartilage tumor commonly found in the phalanges of young adults. It often presents as a painless incidental finding but can become painful after minor trauma (pathologic fracture).
  • X‑ray typically shows a well‑defined, lytic, expansile lesion with chondroid matrix calcifications (stippled, rings‑and‑arcs) in the medullary cavity.

Incorrect Options:

  • Giant cell tumor (Option A) is locally aggressive and occurs in the epiphysis of long bones (distal femur, proximal tibia, distal radius) after skeletal maturity, not commonly in the phalanges.
  • Brown tumor (Option C) is a lytic lesion seen in hyperparathyroidism, usually with other systemic and biochemical abnormalities (e.g., elevated calcium, PTH), not an isolated phalangeal lesion in a young female.
  • Aneurysmal bone cysts (Option D) are expansile, lytic, fluid‑filled lesions often with a “soap‑bubble” appearance, but they are rare in small bones of the hand and usually more symptomatic with swelling and pain.


Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon's Concise System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 193
question: A 28-year-old female presents to the clinic with a complaint of dull, aching pain in her left hand after accidentally striking her finger against a door frame. On physical examination, there is mild tenderness over the affected area, but the range of motion is preserved. An X-ray of the hand is shown below. Based on the clinical presentation and radiographic findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanations:

  • The patient’s age, distal femur location, and night pain suggest an aggressive primary bone tumor, most likely osteosarcoma. On X-ray, Codman’s triangle is a triangular area of new subperiosteal bone formation at the edge of the lesion where the periosteum is lifted by the tumor. It is a classic sign of aggressive bone tumors and is considered highly suggestive of osteosarcoma.
  • Other features of osteosarcoma, such as sun ray (sunburst) appearance, may also be seen but are less specific than Codman’s triangle.

Incorrect Options:

  • Bone cyst (Option A): Benign lytic lesion, usually asymptomatic, without periosteal reaction or night pain.
  • Onion peel appearance (Option C): Characteristic of Ewing sarcoma, showing layered periosteal reaction.
  • Osteochondroma (Option D): Benign bony projection with cartilage cap, not associated with aggressive periosteal reactions or night pain.


Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, Pages 205-209
question: A 19-year-old male presents with persistent night pain involving the distal femur. An X-ray of the affected bone is shown. What is the most likely radiological appearance seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Trendelenburg gait is characterized by the dropping of the pelvis on the contralateral side due to weakness of the hip abductor muscles (primarily the gluteus medius and minimus) on the stance leg. In this case, the right hip drops when the patient stands on her left leg, indicating weakness in the left hip abductors. Bilateral Trendelenburg gait is called a Waddling gait.

Abnormal Gait types

Antalgic Gait

(Option C)
  • Characterised by a markedly shortened stance phase on the affected side.
  • Pain prompts the patient to shift body weight quickly to the normal leg.
  • Results in reduced time spent on the affected leg.

Short Limb Gait

(Option D)
  • Apparent when the limb is shorter than 2 inches.
  • The body on the affected side moves up and down with weight bearing on the affected leg.
  • It can be due to a congenital short femur or shortening secondary to fracture.

Trendelenburg Gait
  • The body swings to the affected side when weight is borne.
  • Indicates functionally weak hip abductor muscles.
  • Associated conditions include a dislocated hip, congenital coxa vara, DDH, greater trochanter fracture and fractured neck of the femur.

High stepping Gait
  • Occurs due to foot drop; the leg is lifted higher for clearance.
  • First contact with the ground is made by the forefoot rather than the heel.
  • Commonly seen in peroneal nerve palsy or sciatic nerve palsy.

Hand on knee Gait
  • The individual walks with their hand on the knee to prevent buckling.
  • Typically associated with quadriceps deficiency and flexion deformity.
  • Common in polio patients.

Quadriceps Avoidance Gait
  • Characterised by hyperextension of the knee to lock it.
  • Compensates for quadriceps paralysis.

Scissoring Gait

(Option A)
  • Legs cross in front of each other while walking.
  • Caused by spasms of the hip adductors, often associated with cerebral palsy.
  • Results in a stiff-legged appearance.


Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page. 234
  2. Essential Orthopaedics, J. Maheshwari, 5th Edition, Page.347
  3. Waddling gait

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The "tabletop sign" occurs when a patient is unable to place their palms and fingers flat on a surface due to limited joint mobility.
  • This is a hallmark of diabetic cheiroarthropathy, which is characterized by restricted movement in the hands, often starting on the ulnar side and progressing radially.
  • It reflects the thickening and stiffening of the connective tissues around the joints, a common finding in long-standing diabetes.

[[figure-1]]

Tinel’s sign (Option B): Tinel’s sign is used to diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome. Tapping over the median nerve in the wrist produces tingling or "pins and needles" in the hand and fingers, which is indicative of nerve compression.

Kanavel’s sign (Option C): Kanavel’s sign refers to symptoms observed in flexor tenosynovitis, where the finger is held in a flexed position, and there is tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath. This is not seen in diabetic cheiroarthropathy.

Finkelstein’s test (Option D): Finkelstein’s test is used to diagnose de Quervain’s tenosynovitis, a condition affecting the tendons on the thumb side of the wrist.

question: A 55 y/o woman with a 15-year history of poorly controlled diabetes presents with stiffness and reduced movement in her fingers, primarily on the ulnar side. Which clinical sign is specific to this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Initiate intravenous antibiotics and monitor for 24 hours
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical features point to Suppurative tenosynovitis. It is the infection of the flexor tendon sheath in the hand, typically following a penetrating injury.

[[figure-1]]

Prompt initiation of intravenous antibiotics is critical to control the infection and prevent complications like tendon necrosis and spread to nearby structures (e.g., radial or ulnar bursa). Commonly used antibiotics include broad-spectrum penicillin or systemic cephalosporins, which target likely organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus.

Apply a splint and prescribe oral antibiotics (Option A): While splinting is helpful to immobilize the affected finger and reduce pain, oral antibiotics are generally inadequate in severe infections like suppurative tenosynovitis. The infection can rapidly worsen, leading to complications such as tendon necrosis or vascular occlusion.

Immediate surgical drainage (Option B): Surgical drainage is not the first-line treatment in all cases. Early suppurative tenosynovitis can often be managed with IV antibiotics if initiated promptly. Surgical drainage is reserved for cases where there is no response to antibiotics within 24 hours.

Request an X-ray to confirm the diagnosis (Option D): The diagnosis of suppurative tenosynovitis is primarily clinical, based on the classic signs like Kanavel’s signs (flexed posture of the digit, tenderness along the tendon sheath, pain with passive extension). X-rays are generally not useful for diagnosing soft tissue infections like tenosynovitis,



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 449

question: A 45 y/o male presents with redness, swelling, and pain in the thumb after sustaining a puncture wound two days ago. The thumb is held in a flexed position, and the patient experiences severe pain when attempting to straighten it. There is also swelling over the thenar eminence. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctAnswer: C. In the Ilizarov fixator only the cortex of the bone is cut, preserving periosteum.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Ilizarov fixator does carry a risk of pin tract infections, but it is highly effective for managing both infected and uninfected nonunions, addressing all aspects of the condition.

Ring fixator/ Illizarov Fixator

  • Principles of Ilizarov’s Method
    • Distraction Osteogenesis (Law of Tension Force): Pulling living tissue apart at 1 mm/day creates new tissue.
    • A multilevel, multidirectional, multiplanar external fixator is superior to others.
    • Corticotomy: Only the cortex of the bone is cut, preserving periosteum and intramedullary circulation for better new bone quality. (Option C)
  • Indications for Ilizarov's Method
    • Complex Fractures: Effective for open, comminuted, and intra-articular fractures.
    • Compound Fractures: Useful for fractures with bone loss; allows mobilization of bone to cover gaps through distraction.
    • Nonunion: Excellent for managing both infected and uninfected nonunions, addressing all aspects of the condition.
    • Limb Lengthening: Applicable in cases like achondroplasia and other limb shortenings.
    • Deformity Corrections: Effective for corrections due to conditions like polio and cerebral palsy. (Option A ruled out)
  • Disadvantages
    • Long duration of treatment.
    • Risks of pin tract infection and nerve palsy.
    • Potential for joint stiffness.

Rail Fixator

  • Consist of a straight bar placed on one side of the limb (arm, leg, or foot).
  • Connected to the bone by screws, often coated with hydroxyapatite for better grip.
  • Prevents screw loosening.
  • Requires patient or family member adjustments several times a day by turning knobs. (Option B)

The rail fixator is superior to the Ilizarov fixator in treating complex fractures. (Option D): While the rail fixator has its advantages, the Ilizarov fixator is specifically designed to address complex fractures, including open and comminuted types, making it a preferred choice in many cases.



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page. 334-335
  2. External-fixators
