explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The first-line management of a March fracture involves conservative treatment, primarily resting the affected limb and modifying physical activities.
  • This approach allows the bone to heal and prevents the fracture from worsening.
Hairline/March/Stress Fracture

Definition

Hairline fractures, also known as march or stress fractures, are small cracks in the bone that develop due to repetitive stress or overuse, particularly when the bone is subjected to excessive weight or pressure.

[[figure-1]]

Common Sites
  • Metatarsal Bones: Most commonly affect the 2nd metatarsal.

[[figure-2]]

  • March Fracture: Named for its prevalence among military personnel during long marches or drills.
  • Stress fractures can occur in any bone but are most frequently seen in weight-bearing bones.

Clinical Features
  • Patients typically present with complaints of pain in the foot, especially during activity or weight-bearing activities.
  • Swelling may or may not be present, making it an atypical fracture.
  • There is often tenderness at the fracture site, and pain usually worsens with activity.

Diagnosis
  • Digital X-ray: X-rays may show subtle changes or a thin line in the bone but may not always be visible in the early stages.
  • MRI or bone scans can be used if the diagnosis remains unclear, as they are more sensitive in detecting stress fractures.

Treatment
  • Rest: Bed rest for 2-3 weeks is generally recommended to allow the bone to heal.
  • Medication: NSAIDs can be prescribed for pain relief.
  • Orthotic Support: Protective footwear or orthotics may be suggested to reduce stress on the affected bone.
  • Activity Modification: Gradual return to activity is important to prevent recurrence.

Surgical fixation of the metatarsal (Option B):

  • This is generally not recommended for simple stress fractures like March fractures unless there is non-healing or severe displacement.
  • Most cases resolve with rest and proper care.

Application of a leg cast (Option C):

  • While immobilization is important in some fractures, a leg cast is unnecessary for a March fracture.
  • A short walking boot or supportive footwear may be used, but complete immobilization is usually unnecessary.


Immediate return to physical activity (Option D):

  • Continuing physical activity without rest can aggravate a stress fracture, worsening the condition and possibly leading to a complete fracture.


Reference:
  1. Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 962.
  2. Ebnezar Textbook of Orthopedics, 6th edition, Pages 15, 109, 110
  3. March Fracture (Metatarsal Stress Fractures) - NCBI

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • 10-year-old boy who fell onto an outstretched hand, a common mechanism for wrist injuries in children.
  • The intense pain he experienced immediately after the fall aligns with this type of injury.
  • The X-ray findings show a subtle bulging of the cortex in the distal radius without a visible fracture line, which is characteristic of a torus fracture.
  • This injury occurs due to the flexibility of pediatric bones, resulting in compression rather than a complete break.
Torus (buckle) fractures

Definition

Torus fractures, also known as buckle fractures, occur when the periosteum (the outer layer of the bone) buckles or compresses, typically due to axial loading forces. This type of fracture is incomplete.

[[figure-1]]

Common Sites
  • Most frequently affects long bones, especially the tibia (particularly the lower end near the metaphysis, where bones are more spongy and susceptible to compression).
  • The radius is another common site, particularly in falls involving outstretched hands (FOOSH injuries).

Clinical Features
  • There is minimal swelling and pain over the affected site.
  • Unlike complete fractures, there is no visible bone displacement.

Diagnosis

Radiographs show a subtle buckling of the cortex, but there is no break in bone continuity. The imaging may require careful interpretation to differentiate from complete fractures.

Treatment
  • Immobilization with a plaster of Paris (POP) slab for 4–5 weeks is usually sufficient.
  • Surgery is not needed, as these fractures typically heal well with conservative treatment. Follow-up may include monitoring for any signs of healing or complications.

Avulsion fracture (Option A):

  • This occurs when a small piece of bone is pulled off by a ligament or tendon.
  • It is less likely in this scenario, which involves a fall on an outstretched hand and not a joint injury.

Impacted fracture (Option B):

  • This occurs when the broken ends of the bone are driven into each other.
  • It would typically show more bone disruption, which is not seen here.

Greenstick fracture (Option D):

  • This fracture is also common in children and involves a partial break of the bone, where one side breaks and the other bends.
  • It typically presents with a more visible fracture line compared to the subtle bulging seen in a torus fracture.

Wedge Compression Fracture

Wedge-shaped Deformity

Collapse of the anterior portion of the vertebral body results in a wedge-shaped deformity, characteristic of this fracture type.

[[figure-1]]

Most Common Site

Thoracolumbar junction (i.e., segment from T12 to L2)

  • This makes it a safer option compared to CT scans or nuclear imaging, which use radiation.

MRI in bone tumors

  • MRI is more accurate for tumor measurements, radiation planning, and resection planning, particularly when using contrast.

Advantages:

  • Provides high spatial resolution images and excellent tissue discrimination across multiple planes.
  • Features useful for lesion characterization include:
    • Precise anatomical location and extent of the lesion.
    • Extent of perilesional edema in both bone marrow and soft tissue.
    • Degree of extraosseous extension and involvement of neurovascular structures and joints.
    • Signal characteristics that help identify specific tissue components within lesions.
  • MRI is the preferred investigation for suspected spinal cord compression due to pathological vertebral body fractures.
  • MRI does not use ionizing radiation, and it is ideal for detecting bone metastases in pregnant women. (Option B)



Reference:

David Sutton Textbook of Radiology And Imaging, Volume 2, Pages 950, 952.

question: A 33-year-old pregnant woman with a history of breast cancer is suspected to have bone metastases. The oncologist opts for an MRI scan to confirm the diagnosis. What is the primary reason MRI is chosen over other imaging modalities in this pregnant patient?

correctAnswer: B. Represents the reactive hypervascular granulation tissue surrounding a necrotic cavity
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given image shows the Penumbra sign. It indicates the presence of a central abscess filled with pus surrounded by a thin rim of enhanced hypervascular granulation tissue.
  • This sign is specific for intraosseous or subperiosteal abscesses in chronic osteomyelitis.

Acute osteomyelitis

[[figure-1]]

  • MRI can reveal early signs of acute osteomyelitis, such as bone marrow edema, within 1-2 days of infection onset
  • In acute osteomyelitis, the typical high signal intensity of fatty bone marrow on T1-weighted MRI images decreases, reflecting congestion from fluid and pus.
  • In contrast, fluid-sensitive sequences and post-contrast images display high signal intensity, indicating the presence of edema and inflammation.

Chronic osteomyelitis

[[figure-2]]

MRI findings in chronic osteomyelitis can reveal:

  • Abscesses and sinus tracts.
  • Sequestra (Necrotic bone fragments appear as low signal intensity areas on T1, T2, and STIR sequences and do not show enhancement.)
  • Thickened periosteum and cloacae.
  • Granulation tissue, soft tissue inflammation & sinus tracks exhibit T1 hypointensity, T2 and STIR hyperintensity, and enhancement after contrast administration.

Penumbra sign:

  • It indicates low signal intensity in intraosseous and subperiosteal abscesses, with high signal intensity in surrounding fluid-sensitive sequences.
  • It features a thin enhancing rim of hypervascular granulation tissue around a central low-intensity pus-filled cavity. (Option B)



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK594242/

question: A 40-year-old male presents with chronic osteomyelitis of the Femur after an open fracture. He experiences persistent drainage from a sinus tract. MRI is given below. What is the significance of the marked sign in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lateral radiograph of the right elbow showing distal ossification, combined with the history of trauma and symptoms, strongly indicate myositis ossificans traumatica.
  • This condition can develop following injury to ligaments, tendons, periosteum or bones and is often exacerbated by improper treatment such as deep tissue massage.

Myositis ossificans (MO)

  • Heterotopic bone formation within a muscle or any other type of soft tissue (tendons, ligament, fascia and connective tissue).
  • 2 Types:
    • Myositis Ossificans Traumatica (MOT): Acquired
    • Myositis Ossificans Progressiva (MOP): Congenital

Myositis Ossificans Traumatica (MOT)

  • Causes:
    • Ill-advised massage (M/c cause):
    • Trauma
    • Simple blow or repeated minor trauma
    • Dislocations and avulsion injuries

[[figure-1]]




Treatment:

    • Massage following injury is strictly prohibited.
    • Acute stages:
      • Immobilization
      • Medications (diphosphonates, calcitonin, NSAIDs)
      • Active physiotherapy (passive stretching is avoided)
    • Chronic stages:
      • Surgery is the treatment of choice (soft tissue release, excision of bony spur).

question: A 30-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling in her right elbow following a minor fall. She received a deep tissue massage shortly after the injury. Examination reveals tenderness and limited motion in the elbow. The lateral radiograph of the right elbow joint is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In the given scenario, the presence of weakness in abduction and external rotation suggests a rotator cuff injury.
  • MRI is the gold standard investigation for rotator cuff injuries and reveals any discontinuity in the supraspinatus tendon, which is indicative of a tear.

MRI shoulder (rotator cuff injuries)

  • A rotational cuff tear refers to a disruption of tendon fibers.
  • Most often occurs in the supraspinatus tendon, near its insertion or 8 to 15 mm above the greater tuberosity (referred to as the critical zone).

Normal Image of rotator cuff

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Partial Thickness Tear
  • Appears as a focal area of fiber discontinuity filled with fluid signal on T2W images.
  • Fat-suppressed sequences enhance the visibility of the fluid-filled tendon defect.
  • Surface fraying and changes in tendon caliber.

[[figure-3]]

Full Thickness Tear
  • Appears as a focal discontinuity in the tendon, extending from the articular to the bursal surface.
  • Seen as fluid signal intensity on T2-weighted (T2W) images.
  • Fluid may be present in the subacromial-subdeltoid (SASD) bursa and joint space.
  • Secondary signs include tendon retraction, superior translation of the humeral head, and muscle atrophy, can be seen.

question: In the given MRI image of the knee identify the posterior cruciate ligament.

correctAnswer: C. The "Empty Notch Sign" observed on MRI indicates an ACL avulsion injury.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given MRI shows an ACL tear, therefore the "Empty Notch Sign" indicates avulsion at the femoral attachment site.

Anterior cruciate ligament injury

[[figure-1]]

  • Edema and hyperintense signal on T2/fat-sat PD images

  • Visible tear or abnormal contour, often midsubstance of ligament

  • ACL fibers less steep than Blumensaat line; ACL angle >15° indicates rupture

  • Empty Notch Sign: Fluid signal at the femoral attachment site in the intercondylar notch, indicating avulsion. (Option C)

  • Partial tear: normal ACL angle with hyperintense signal

  • Bell-hammer sign: torn ACL stump, typical in partial tears

  • Gap sign: fluid/gap between femoral condyle and mid-ACL, seen in posterolateral bundle tears

Posterior cruciate ligament injury

[[figure-2]]

  • PCL often remains intact (~70%) despite partial or complete disruption.
  • An enlarged and swollen PCL with an AP diameter >7 mm in the vertical portion on sagittal images suggests a tear.
  • A posterior tibial shift of more than 2-3 mm in the mid-medial compartment indicates injury



Reference:
  1. https://radiopaedia.org/articles/anterior-cruciate-ligament-tear
  2. https://radiopaedia.org/articles/posterior-cruciate-ligament-tear

An ACL angle greater than 15° indicates a partial rupture.
The "Empty Notch Sign" observed on MRI indicates an ACL avulsion injury.
A hyperintense signal in the ACL with a normal angle suggests a complete tear rather than a partial tear.

question:
A 28-year-old male athlete presents with a right knee injury sustained during a soccer match. He reports hearing a “pop” sound at the time of injury and is experiencing significant pain and swelling in the knee. On physical examination, there is moderate effusion, and the patient is unable to fully extend the knee. An MRI of the knee is performed, revealing the following findings:

Based on the MRI findings, which of the following statements regarding the patient's injury is most accurate?

correctAnswer: A. Horizontal meniscal tear with parameniscal cyst
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Horizontal meniscal tears are common in degenerative conditions and often seen in patients over 40 years old, typically running parallel to the tibial plateau.
  • In this case, the MRI shows a horizontal tear in the posterior horn of the medial Q meniscus, a common site for such tears.

  • Fluid next to tear signals parameniscal cyst, linked to complete horizontal tears via joint fluid communication

  • Menisci: fibrocartilaginous, crescent-shaped between femoral condyles and tibial plateaus

  • Function: absorb shock, distribute load, stabilize knee

  • MRI: menisci appear hypointense (dark) on all sequences

  • Sagittal MRI: "bow-tie" shape peripherally or opposing triangles centrally

[[figure-1]]

  • Coronal MRI: triangular or wedge-shaped

  • Lateral meniscus horns equal size; on the medial side, the posterior horn of the medial meniscus is larger than the anterior horn

Meniscal tear

Key Characteristics on MRI

Horizontal Tear

Horizontal line of high signal intensity; involves articular surfaces and can cause parameniscal cysts.

Longitudinal Tear (Option B)

Vertically oriented tear; runs parallel to the meniscus axis and often involves the red zone. Usually traumatic in origin.

Radial Tear (Option C)

Perpendicular to the meniscus, disrupts hoop strength, seen as truncation of free edge, does not form parameniscal cysts.

Bucket Handle Tear (Option D)

Longitudinal tear with fragment migration; shows a "double PCL" sign or displaced fragment in the intercondylar notch.

[[figure-2]]



Reference:
  1. David Sutton Textbook of Radiology And Imaging, Volume 2, Page 772.
  2. https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/399552-overview?form=fpf#a2
  3. https://epos.myesr.org/poster/esr/ecr2018/C-1670/
  4. https://radiopaedia.org/articles/meniscal-cyst#

options.text: Horizontal meniscal tear with parameniscal cyst

question: A 45-year-old female presents with chronic knee pain and occasional joint swelling and clicking in the joint. She reports no history of trauma. The MRI findings are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. MRI of the thoracic spine
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

MRI is the investigation of choice for spinal tumors because it provides excellent delineation of vertebral body marrow, allowing detection of both primary and metastatic disease.

MRI Spine is the investigation of choice in:

1. Intervertebral Disc Diseases:

  • Bulge: Symmetric disc extension beyond interspace (lumbar > cervical)

  • Protrusion: Asymmetric disc extension beyond interspace

  • Extrusion: Extreme disc extension beyond interspace

  • Sequestration: Fully separated disc fragment

2. Postoperative Back Pain:

  • Detect residual disc material

  • Identify epidural hematomas or abscesses

  • Diagnose postoperative discitis

3. Spinal Tumors:

  • Excellent marrow detail for primary/metastatic lesions

  • High sensitivity on T1-weighted images

4. Spinal Trauma:

  • Spinal cord injury assessment

  • Epidural hematomas

  • Traumatic disc herniation

  • Soft tissue injuries (e.g., ligament tears) in acute stage

question: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive back pain, weight loss, and leg weakness. There is tenderness over the thoracic spine, raising suspicion of a spinal tumor. What is the investigation of choice to evaluate for a spinal tumor?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of tachycardia, fever, confusion, low PaO2, petechial rashes, and thrombocytopenia, along with the characteristic "snowstorm" appearance on the chest X-ray, indicates Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), commonly associated with fat embolism after multiple fractures.

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)/Fat Embolism

Post-traumatic stress syndrome within 72 hrs of skeletal trauma, usually in 24–48 hrs. Linked to major/multiple fractures and multisystem injuries. Occurs in 10–45% of such cases with 11% mortality.
Pathogenesis: Injury causes fat or platelet clumps to enter vessels, forming emboli that trigger systemic symptoms.

Gurd’s Criteria For Fat Embolism

Major criteria: Minor criteria:
  1. Axillary and subconjunctival petechiae
  2. PaO <60 mm Hg
  3. CNS depression
  1. Pulse >110/min
  2. Pyrexia >38.5°C
  3. Retinal embolism
  4. Fat in urine
  5. Reduced platelet count
  6. Increased ESR
  7. Fat globules in sputum

Diagnostic criteria: At least 1 major criterion + 4 minor criteria required for diagnosis

Diagnostic triad (TPR mnemonic):

  • Thrombocytopenia
  • PaO2<60 mm Hg
  • Rashes

Chest X-ray: Snowstorm appearance (pathognomonic).

[[figure-1]]

Management:

  • Respiratory support: Oxygen or ventilation to restore PaO₂

  • Drugs: Steroids (reduce inflammation), heparin (lipolytic), LM dextran (↑ plasma volume), antibiotics

  • Definitive care: Early fracture fixation

question: A 28-year-old male presents to the hospital after sustaining multiple fractures in a motorcycle accident. Within 36 hours of the trauma, he develops tachycardia, fever, confusion, and a PaO of 55 mm Hg. A chest X-ray is taken and is shown below. He has petechial rashes noted on his conjunctiva and neck, and his platelet count is 120,000/mm³. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child’s foot deformities, including symmetrical first-toe malformations seen on X-ray, episodes of painful swelling in the shoulders and neck, and difficulty in movement indicate Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOH).

Myositis (Fibrodysplasia) ossificans progressiva:

  • It is an extremely rare genetic connective tissue disorder affecting all the skeletal muscles.
  • Characterized by heterotopic ossification.
  • Affects ligaments, tendons, and skeletal muscles, leading to joint immobility.

[[figure-1]]

  • Age Group: typically appears in early childhood, often before age 6, and progresses throughout life.
  • Causes:Mostly sporadic or autosomal dominant; caused by ACVR1 gene mutation in the BMP pathway.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Skeletal Malformations:
      • Most common: shortened great toes with malformed distal first metatarsal and missing or malformed first phalanx

[[figure-2]]

  • Features: Hallux valgus, microdactyly, 5th finger clinodactyly, tibial osteochondromas, cervical spine defects

  • First sign: Painful, tender swellings on back, neck, shoulders

[[figure-3]]

  • Treatment:No definitive treatment. Flare-ups managed with short-term high-dose steroids, NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors, mast cell inhibitors, and bisphosphonates.

question: A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic with concerns about foot deformities. An anteroposterior radiograph of the feet is taken, as shown below. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The “Honda H” sign on a Bone scan refers to a specific pattern of fracture lines seen in the sacrum, which is suggestive of Bilateral sacral insufficiency fractures.
  • Bilateral sacral insufficiency fractures typically occur in elderly patients or those with osteoporosis, chronic steroid use, or other metabolic bone diseases. It can also happen in patients with Rheumatoid arthritis.
  • These fractures are caused by normal or physiological stress on weakened bone.

Acute osteomyelitis (Option A) would typically show localized bone marrow edema with possible abscess formation but does not produce the “Honda H” sign.

Marrow edema (Option B) is a non-specific finding that can result from trauma, infection, or inflammation but lacks the specific fracture pattern of the “Honda H” sign.

Metastatic sacral lesion (Option D) usually appears as destructive or infiltrative lesions on MRI, not the bilateral linear fracture pattern of the “Honda H” sign.

question: A patient presents with low back pain. Bone scan reveals the characteristic "Honda H" sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Pressure epiphysis takes part in joint formation and transmits weight. The head of the humerus is a pressure epiphysis as it forms the shoulder joint and bears load during movements.

Types of Epiphysis:

  1. Pressure Epiphysis – Participates in joint formation and weight transmission (e.g., head of humerus, lower end of radius).
  2. Traction Epiphysis – Non-articular, does not transmit weight (e.g., greater/lesser trochanter of femur, greater/lesser tubercle of humerus, mastoid process).
  3. Atavistic Epiphysis – Once independent but fused for nutrition (e.g., coracoid process of scapula, os trigonum).
  4. Aberrant Epiphysis – Not always present (e.g., head of the first metacarpal, base of other metacarpals).

The other options (elbow joint, wrist joint, and sternum) are not classified as pressure epiphyses.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2564388/

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has:
    • Persistent/recurrent low back pain after completion of anti-tubercular therapy (ATT)
    • Possibility of relapse, drug-resistant tuberculosis, or alternate pathology
  • Needle biopsy is the most appropriate investigation because:
    • It provides tissue diagnosis
    • Confirms active tuberculosis histologically

    • Helps differentiate tuberculosis from malignancy or other spinal infections
    • Prevents unnecessary empirical ATT

Protein electrophoresis (Option A) is mainly useful in the evaluation of plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma and does not establish the diagnosis of spinal tuberculosis.

CT scan (Option C) helps assess bony destruction and the extent of the lesion, but cannot definitively confirm diagnosis or drug resistance without tissue sampling.
